Tabsdata is a distributed, horizontally scalable system that runs on Kubernetes and can be deployed across a variety of Kubernetes providers. Tabsdata is organized into two conceptual layers: a resource layer and an execution layer. The resource layer consists of objects that users create to establish the structure of a Tabsdata workflow. These include objects like Tables and Functions, which determine when a workflow runs, what data flows through it, and what work is applied to that data. The execution layer consists of objects that Tabsdata creates when it reads and acts on resources from the resource layer. These objects make up the running workflow that performs work on data. This includes objects like Execution Plans, Transactions, and Function Runs. Server? Projects? Resource layer Groups? Collections? Functions? Connections? Tables? Execution layer Execution Plan? Transaction? Function Run? Worker?

Functions are Tabsdata's unit of work. A function performs a single discrete step of moving data between external systems and internal Tabsdata Tables. There are three types of Tabsdata Functions: A publisher reads from an external system and writes into Tabsdata tables. A transformer reads from Tabsdata tables and writes into new Tabsdata tables. A subscriber reads from Tabsdata tables and writes out to an external system. Data enters and leaves the server through functionsZoom in Database postgres Publisher Tabsdata Server Table customers Transformer Table customer_orders Subscriber Warehouse snowflake

A unique feature of Tabsdata is that it has its own internal storage for all data produced by functions. Tabsdata tables persistently store the data produced by functions. Every successful function run that returns data creates a new table version that sits alongside all previous versions of the table. persons Tabsdata›Collections›input›persons SchemaSample Schema Table schema defines the structure of a table by listing its columns and their data types. Object Type first_name str last_name str age i64 nationality str city str v2v1version While Tabsdata tables share some similarities to database tables, they also have some key differences. Rather than requiring a predefined schema, each version inside a table carries its own, allowing a table's schema to evolve across versions. This not only makes Tabsdata resilient to schema drift, but also stores a lineage of the table's evolution for observability and debugging. Table version history is available not only to users for viewing, but also to functions for ingestion. Functions can read historical table versions for use cases that require comparing historical data with incoming data.
Table schema defines the structure of a table by listing its columns and their data types. Object Type first_name str last_name str age i64 nationality str city str
Functions and tables declare how data should be moved. Tabsdata's reads these and builds the actual workflow that ingests, transforms, and loads your data.

Traditionally, as more steps are added to a data integration workflow, the more complex it is to orchestrate it. Tabsdata does not have this issue. Function are declarative and declare their own dependencies. Any functions that write to tables used by other functions are upstream dependent to them. Any functions that use tables produced by other functions are downstream dependent to them. When a Function is triggered, Tabsdata identifies its downstream dependencies and automatically builds an Execution Plan, a DAG (directed acytclic graph) that finds and executes all downstream dependencies. Click any node to trace its dependenciesResetZoom in Publisherread_salesPublisherread_customersTablesalesTablecustomersTransformerjoin_ordersTableordersSubscriberpush_orders In addition to automatically orchestrating workflows, Execution plans record everything that occurs during execution, capturing metadata such as: Execution start and stop time Functions executed Function code used Tables read and written Execution status Execution logs

Compute and storage are independently scalable. Each Function runs as an isolated process within the Server's Kubernetes cluster. Storage can be distributed across local file storage or cloud storage providers such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, and Google Cloud Storage.

Authorization uses a direct permission model, where permissions are assigned directly to users rather than through roles. Credentials are stored separately from Functions in a secure credential store. This includes both Tabsdata's internal credentials and the credentials used by Connections to authenticate with external systems. note Even when credentials are provided inline through the CLI, Tabsdata automatically extracts and stores them in the credential store.

Tabsdata runs on Linux for production and macOS or Windows for development. The underlying Kubernetes can be deployed across several providers kminus: A lightweight Kubernetes implementation that runs pods as native Python processes instead of Docker containers. The default provider for local development. eks: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS). aks: Azure Kubernetes Service gke: Google Kubernetes Engine

In Tabsdata, Automatic Orchestration handles the order in which Functions run based on the Tables they read and write. Instead of requiring users to manually define a DAG, Tabsdata uses the declared dependencies between Tables and Functions to determine what needs to run. When a Function is triggered, Tabsdata automatically identifies any downstream Functions that depend on its output and executes them in the appropriate order.

Traditionally, orchestrating a data pipeline involves manually defining a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) that specifies how each step depends on the others and the order in which they should execute. As a pipeline grows or changes, the DAG has to be updated to account for any new or modified dependencies. This also means that adding a new step to a pipeline requires updating its orchestration logic, even if the step's inputs and outputs are already known.

In Tabsdata, Functions do not pass data directly to one another. Instead, Functions write their output to Tabsdata Tables, which can then be read by other Functions. Each Function declares the Tables it reads from and writes to as part of its decorator: Publishers declare the Tables they write to using output_tables. Transformers declare the Tables they read from using input_tables and the Tables they write to using output_tables. Subscribers declare the Tables they read from using input_tables. PublisherTransformerSubscriber Publisher: output_tables writes a Tabsdata Table.@publisher(source=PostgresSrc(...),output_tables=["orders"],)def clean_orders(orders):cleaned = ...return cleanedTabsdata Tableorders Because these dependencies are declared ahead of time, Tabsdata already knows which Functions depend on each other. When a Function writes a new version of a Table, Tabsdata can identify every downstream Function that reads from it. For example, registering a new Transformer that reads from the customers Table automatically adds it to the workflow. The next time customers receives a new version, Tabsdata knows to execute the Transformer without requiring any changes to an existing DAG.

In Tabsdata, new Table versions are what trigger downstream Functions to run. By default, Transformers and Subscribers run whenever one of their input Tables receives a new version, unless a different trigger is specified using trigger_by. Publishers do not have input Tables, so they can be triggered manually, through a cron schedule, or by a Table specified in trigger_by. Stream Publishers are triggered whenever a new batch of data is ready from their stream source. See Execution and Triggers for more information about the available trigger types.

Whenever a Function is triggered, Tabsdata uses the declared Table dependencies to build an Execution Plan containing all the downstream Functions that need to run. The Execution Plan determines the order in which Functions execute, including Functions across different Collections, so that each Function runs after the Tables it depends on have been updated. As the plan executes, each Function reads the data written by the upstream Functions in that same execution. However, Tabsdata does not commit any of the new Table versions until every Function in the Execution Plan has completed successfully. If any Function fails, none of the new Table versions are committed. This prevents partially completed workflows from leaving Tables in inconsistent states. Tabsdata also records which Table versions each Function read and wrote during the execution, allowing users to trace how data was produced and how it moved through the workflow. See Lineage for more information.
A Collection is an organizational layer inside of a group that stores tables and functions. Collections help manage credentials for functions and define transaction boundaries for tables.

A Function is responsible for moving, and sometimes transforming, data from one place to another. Publishers and Subscribers that read from or write data to external systems also need a way to securely access sensitive credentials for those systems. Instead of hardcoding credentials directly into Function logic, Tabsdata abstracts credential management into a separate resource called a Connection. A Connection is defined in a .yaml file and bound to a Collection. Any Function registered to the same Collection can access those credentials at runtime. This allows users to store their credentials once and then securely provision those credentials to as many functions that need them. Learn more about connections here.

Triggering a Tabsdata Function creates an Execution Plan that executes the triggering Function along with any functions downstream dependent to it. Because an Execution Plan can span multiple Functions, Tabsdata needs to determine which data should be committed or rolled back if the Execution Plan fails partway through. Collections act as transaction boundaries within an Execution Plan. Tabsdata treats each participating Collection as a separate transaction and commits data to its Tables only when all participating Functions within that Collection complete successfully. If a Function within the transaction fails, Tabsdata rolls back all changes made to Tables within that transaction.

After creating a Collection, users can register Functions into that collection. If a collection is created inside the sources or destinations group, it can only store publisher or subscriber functions respectively and requires a connection to be bound Deleting a Collection removes the Collection and the resources it contains without affecting other Collections in the Project. See Create a Collection, Update a Collection, and Delete a Collection for step-by-step instructions.

A Connection is a resource that stores the credentials required to access an external system. Publisher and Subscriber Functions need credentials to connect to external systems to read and write data, but they do not store these sensitive credentials directly in their code. Instead, that configuration is defined in a Connection. Connections are .yaml files that contain relevant credentials and are attached to Collections, allowing all functions within that collection to access the required credentials during execution.

Connections are defined using .yaml files. The fields in a Connection depend on the external system and Connection type. For example, an S3 Connection stores the bucket, region, and credentials needed to access files in an S3 bucket. conn-s3.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3SrcConn spec: bucket: 'acme-ingest' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: '$secret:AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID' secret_access_key: '$secret:AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY' bucket:strrequired region:strrequired credentials:AwsAccessSecretKeyrequired base_path:stroptional

Connections are bound to Publisher and Subscriber Collections. A Publisher Collection binds a Publisher to an input Connection. The Publisher defines what data to read from the external system and what Tables to create in Tabsdata, while the Connection provides the configuration and credentials needed to access that system during the Publisher's execution. A Subscriber Collection binds a Subscriber to an output Connection. The Subscriber defines which Tabsdata Tables to read and what data to write, while the Connection provides the configuration and credentials needed to access the destination system during the Subscriber's execution.

When configuring a connection , a credential can be passed directly as secret:<value>, or as a reference to an environment variable, written as $secret:<VARIABLE NAME>. Regardless of the method used, when the connection file is registered into Tabsdata, Tabsdata dehydrates the document by extracting any secrets into a separate secret store and storing a reference to the secret in the file. note For security, once credentials are stored in Tabsdata, they can only be accessed by a Tabsdata Function at runtime.

A connector is the set of Python classes Tabsdata uses to read from or write to one external system. Every built-in connector is part of the tabsdatak.conn package and provides a source class, a destination class, or both, along with the connection types that hold the system's address and credentials. A publisher uses a connector's source class to read from the external system and write into Tabsdata tables. A subscriber uses a connector's destination class to read from Tabsdata tables and write out to the external system. Neither class stores credentials. The address and credentials live on the connection of the collection the function is registered in, so the same connection is shared by every publisher or subscriber in that collection. Kafka and the three CDC connectors provide a stream source class instead of a source class. A stream publisher uses a stream source to consume the external system continuously, and runs each time a batch of messages or changes rolls over instead of on a manual, cron, or table trigger.

Each connector's page covers its connection fields and the options of its classes, and links to a full walkthrough in Tutorials. The Amazon S3 connector lets Tabsdata read files from and write files to Amazon S3. The S3Src connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Amazon S3 into a Tabsdata table. The S3Dest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Amazon S3.
Format Publish Subscribe AUTO? Yes Yes CSV Yes Yes JSON Yes Yes AVRO Yes Yes PARQUET Yes Yes LOG Yes No EXCEL Yes No

The S3Src connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Amazon S3 into a Tabsdata table. See the full publisher walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a AwsAccessSecretKey connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Publisher connection, at the end of this page.

The bucket exists and is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The AWS principal can list the bucket and read every object matched by paths. Compressed objects need include_compressed=True; see include_compressed.

Configure S3Src as the source of a publisher function to select the files that Tabsdata reads from S3. publish_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Src, SrcFileFormat @publisher( source=S3Src( paths=[ "incoming/orders.parquet", ], ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders): return orders paths:list[str]required format:SrcFileFormatoptional format_cfg:dictoptional initial_last_modified:datetimeoptional src_cfg:dictoptional

paths​ Defines the files that the publisher reads from S3. Each path is relative to the base_path configured in S3SrcConn. Source paths: cannot begin or end with / cannot contain empty path segments cannot be . or .., or contain a ${...} token can contain a * glob in the final path segment. * matches any run of characters and ? matches one character; in directory segments, both are literal. For example: S3Src( paths=[ "orders/2026/*.parquet", "customers/customers.csv", ] ) Each element in paths represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function. When a path uses a glob to match multiple files, the matching files are provided through the corresponding publisher input. format​ Sets the format used to read the source files. Supported formats are AUTO, CSV, JSON, AVRO, PARQUET, LOG, and EXCEL. The default is AUTO, which determines the format from the file extension. AUTO resolves the format for each file from its own extension. For a compressed file, that is the extension before the compression extension. A file whose extension names no format fails the run. A source whose files resolve to different formats also fails the run. EXCEL reads .xlsx workbooks only. Pick a sheet with a #n suffix on the path, such as paths=["book.xlsx#2"]; the sheet number starts at 1 and counts hidden sheets, and #0 is refused. Its format_cfg takes has_header. format_cfg​ Sets format-specific reader options. Configuration is keyed by SrcFileFormat. For CSV, has_header=False reads the first row as data. The columns are then named column_0, column_1, ... skip_lines skips that many lines at the start of each file before the header is read. A "" field is read as an empty string. include_compressed​ When True, the publisher reads compressed objects. A path that ends in a compression extension fails validation without it. The compression extensions are .gz, .zlib, .zst, .zstd, .bz2, .xz, .lz4 and .br, plus single-entry .zip and .tar archives. The format comes from the name before the compression extension, so orders.csv.gz is read as CSV. An archive must hold one file, and a name can have only one compression extension. purge​ When True, the publisher deletes each matched object that the cursor skipped, if its modification time is at or after initial_last_modified. purge requires initial_last_modified; without it the run fails with FILE_COMMON_35. Deletion runs for each slot after that slot's frames are read. warning purge deletes data, including a late object that the cursor skipped before the publisher ever read it. It needs delete permission on the source objects. initial_last_modified​ Sets the initial cutoff for incremental ingestion. On the first run, Tabsdata imports files modified at or after the specified timestamp. The cutoff then advances so subsequent runs only import newer files. The value must be timezone-aware, for example datetime(2026, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc). src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. The following options are supported: Option Description tabsdata.src_metadata.drop When True, excludes the @td.file.path metadata column. By default, rows read from S3 include a @td.file.path metadata column containing the s3:// URI of the file the row was read from.

The S3Dest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Amazon S3. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a AwsAccessSecretKey connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Subscriber connection, at the end of this page.
The bucket exists and is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The AWS principal can write objects under the configured base_path. The destination path is relative and does not contain a glob.

Configure S3Dest as the destination of a subscriber function to define where Tabsdata writes files in S3. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Dest, DestFileFormat @subscriber( destination=S3Dest( paths=[ "exports/orders.parquet", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders paths:list[str]required format:DestFileFormatoptional format_cfg:dictoptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

paths​ Defines where the subscriber writes files in S3. Each path is relative to the base_path configured in S3DestConn. Destination paths: cannot begin or end with / cannot contain empty path segments cannot contain globs Each element in paths represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. Destination paths can contain variables that Tabsdata substitutes when the subscriber runs: Variable Value ${EXEC_PLAN_ID} Current execution plan ID. ${TRX_ID} Current transaction ID. ${TRIGGERED_ON} Timestamp in file-safe form, such as 20260604T083428.376Z. Replaces ${EXEC_PLAN_TS}. ${EXEC_PLAN_TS} Timestamp when the execution plan started. Deprecated since 2.3.0; use ${TRIGGERED_ON}. For example: S3Dest( paths=[ "exports/${EXEC_PLAN_ID}/orders.parquet", ] ) Dynamic paths can be used to create a new S3 object for each execution instead of overwriting an existing object. format​ Sets the format used to write the destination file. Supported formats are AUTO, CSV, JSON, AVRO, and PARQUET. The default is AUTO, which determines the format from the destination file extension. format_cfg​ Sets format-specific writer options. Configuration is keyed by DestFileFormat. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration.

Each entry in a publisher's paths is one source slot. A literal path reads one object; a final-segment * glob can read several. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to output_tables. Each slot receives one frame per matched object, oldest object first by modification time and then by name. A slot with no matches receives an empty list. Subdirectories are not searched. initial_last_modified sets the cutoff for the first run. After a successful run, Tabsdata advances the cutoff so the same unchanged objects are not published again. Without initial_last_modified, every run reads every matched object. The cutoff is kept for each slot position and pattern, so reordering paths resets it. A late object whose modification time is older than the newest object already taken is skipped. An object that shares a modification time with another is taken once, and overlapping globs import the same object twice. Each entry in a subscriber's paths is one destination slot and maps by position to a returned value. Use ${EXEC_PLAN_ID}, ${TRX_ID}, or ${TRIGGERED_ON} in a path when every run needs a new object. ${TRIGGERED_ON} is a timestamp in file-safe form, such as 20260604T083428.376Z. ${EXEC_PLAN_TS} still works, but it is deprecated since 2.3.0 and logs a warning. A fixed path writes to the same location again.

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set trigger_by to change when the function runs. Tabsdata validates the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not contact Amazon S3 then. A bad path, credential, or permission fails when the function runs. Globs are allowed only for publisher source paths, and only in the final path segment. Subscriber destination paths cannot contain globs. All configured paths are relative to the connection's base_path.

Amazon S3 publishers use S3SrcConn to define the S3 bucket and credentials used by the publisher. conn-s3-in.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3SrcConn spec: bucket: 'acme-ingest' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' secret_access_key: 'secret:wJalrXUtnFEMI0EXAMPLEKEY' bucket:strrequired region:strrequired credentials:AwsAccessSecretKeyrequired base_path:stroptional conn_cfg:dictoptional

A publisher is registered in a source collection, and a source collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type s3-file-in --file conn-s3-in.yaml Edit the template file with the Amazon S3 connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-s3-in.yaml tdk collection create --name s3_in --conn-file conn-s3-in.yaml Then register the publisher in the collection: tdk fn register --coll s3_in --path publish_orders.py::publish_orders The collection goes in the sources group, because the connection is a source connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be sources. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: S3Src for a collection created with S3SrcConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name s3_in --conn-file conn-s3-in.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

bucket​ The name of the S3 bucket that contains the files to publish. region​ The AWS region where the S3 bucket is located, such as us-east-1. credentials​ The AWS credentials used to access the bucket. AwsAccessSecretKey requires an access_key_id and secret_access_key. base_path​ Sets the base path within the S3 bucket. All paths configured in S3Src are relative to this path. base_path starts with /, cannot end with /, and cannot contain empty path segments. The default is /. For example, with: base_path: /hr the source path: employees/2026.csv refers to: /hr/employees/2026.csv within the configured S3 bucket. conn_cfg​ Optional connector configuration overrides. Keys that start with obstore. configure the object store; see Object Store Options.

Amazon S3 subscribers use S3DestConn to define the S3 bucket and credentials used by the subscriber. conn-s3-out.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3DestConn spec: bucket: 'acme-exports' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' secret_access_key: 'secret:wJalrXUtnFEMI0EXAMPLEKEY' bucket:strrequired region:strrequired credentials:AwsAccessSecretKeyrequired base_path:stroptional conn_cfg:dictoptional

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type s3-file-out --file conn-s3-out.yaml Edit the template file with the Amazon S3 connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-s3-out.yaml tdk collection create --name s3_out --conn-file conn-s3-out.yaml Then register the subscriber in the collection: tdk fn register --coll s3_out --path write_orders.py::write_orders The collection goes in the destinations group, because the connection is a destination connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be destinations. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: S3Dest for a collection created with S3DestConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name s3_out --conn-file conn-s3-out.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

bucket​ The name of the S3 bucket where the subscriber writes files. region​ The AWS region where the S3 bucket is located, such as us-east-1. credentials​ The AWS credentials used to access the bucket. AwsAccessSecretKey requires an access_key_id and secret_access_key. base_path​ Sets the base path within the S3 bucket. All paths configured in S3Dest are relative to this path. base_path starts with /, cannot end with /, and cannot contain empty path segments. The default is /. conn_cfg​ Optional connector configuration overrides. Keys that start with obstore. configure the object store; see Object Store Options.

The BigQuery connector lets Tabsdata write tables into BigQuery. BigQuery is destination-only: there is no publisher-side connector for reading from BigQuery. The BigQueryDest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into BigQuery. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a BigQueryDestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The BigQuery project and dataset exist, and the service account can create and load tables in them. The GCS staging bucket exists. The service account can write staged Parquet files there and BigQuery can load them. The project and dataset are set either in each table name or as connection defaults.

For merge writes, schema evolution, and retry watermarks, see Merging into SQL destinations. Configure BigQueryDest as the destination of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in BigQuery. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.bigquery import BigQueryDest @subscriber( destination=BigQueryDest( tables=[ "orders", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders tables:list[str]required if_table_exists:stroptional schema_evolution:stroptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

tables​ Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in BigQuery. Each element in tables represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. Each name is [[project.]dataset.]table; a bare table or dataset.table is completed from the connection's project/dataset defaults. BigQuery wraps the whole name in one backtick pair, e.g. `my-project.ds.t`. if_table_exists​ "merge" applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key and requires a merge_cfg list. See Merge configuration for a complete example. Controls what happens when the destination table already exists. "append" (the default) adds rows. "replace" drops and recreates the table. schema_evolution​ Controls what happens when the returned frame has a column the table lacks or a wider type. "update" adds and widens columns. "strict" is the default: an append fails in the load job (BIGQUERY_7), and a merge is refused before it runs (SQL_COMMON_10). See Schema Evolution. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration. Supported keys include bigquery.logging_level and bigquery.schema_evolution_engine. The engine key is only for a merge under schema_evolution="update", where it must be "iceberg". See Schema evolution.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" adds rows. "replace" drops and recreates the table. "merge" applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key and needs merge_cfg. With schema_evolution="strict", a frame with a new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit, fails instead of changing the table. "update" adds and widens columns before the load.

schema_evolution decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. "strict", the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. "update" changes the table to fit the frame. On BigQuery, the schema evolution "update" uses depends on if_table_exists: if_table_exists "update" uses Changes to the table "append", "replace" BigQuery's native schema evolution Adds columns and makes columns nullable. It never widens a type. "merge" Iceberg schema evolution, applied by the connector through ALTER TABLE. Needs dest_cfg={"bigquery.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"}. Adds columns and widens types. BigQuery's native schema evolution does not apply to MERGE, so a merge under "update" without the iceberg engine is refused at registration. bigquery.schema_evolution_engine is accepted only on a merge under "update": setting it on "append" or "replace", or on a merge under "strict", is also refused at registration. See Schema Evolution for the types each destination widens.

Each write is staged as Parquet in GCS before the BigQuery load job runs. Both the staging write and the BigQuery load must succeed. Bare table names use the connection's project and dataset. Fully qualified names override those defaults. Tabsdata does not contact GCS or BigQuery when the collection is created. Connection and permission errors appear when the subscriber runs.

BigQuery subscribers use BigQueryDestConn to define the GCS staging location and credentials used by the subscriber. The connector stages each write as parquet in GCS, then runs a load job against BigQuery referencing that object. conn-bigquery.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.bigquery:BigQueryDestConn spec: staging: bucket: 'acme-stage' credentials: kind: gcpJsonCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:GCPJson spec: json: 'secret:{"type": "service_account", ...}' base_path: '/bigquery' credentials: kind: gcpJsonCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:GCPJson spec: json: 'secret:{"type": "service_account", ...}' staging:GCSLocationrequired credentials:GCPJsonrequired project:stroptional dataset:stroptional entity_whitelist:list[str]optional conn_cfg:dictoptional

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type bigquery-bulk-out --file conn-bigquery.yaml Edit the template file with the BigQuery connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-bigquery.yaml tdk collection create --name bigquery_out --conn-file conn-bigquery.yaml Then register the subscriber in the collection: tdk fn register --coll bigquery_out --path write_orders.py::write_orders The collection goes in the destinations group, because the connection is a destination connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be destinations. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: BigQueryDest for a collection created with BigQueryDestConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name bigquery_out --conn-file conn-bigquery.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

staging​ The GCSLocation used as the parquet staging bucket for load jobs: a bucket, credentials (GCP service-account JSON), and base_path (defaults to /, same rules as other connectors' base_path: starts with /, cannot end with /, cannot contain empty path segments). credentials​ The GCP service-account JSON credentials (GCPJson) used to run the BigQuery load job, separate from the credentials on staging used to upload to GCS. project​ The default GCP project id. Required when dataset is set. dataset​ The default BigQuery dataset id. Requires project to be set. entity_whitelist​ A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet. Leave it out. conn_cfg​ Optional connector configuration overrides.

The ClickHouse connector lets Tabsdata subscribers write data from Tabsdata tables into ClickHouse. The connector stages the data as Parquet files in cloud storage, then loads it into ClickHouse from there. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a ClickHouseDestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The ClickHouse HTTP or HTTPS endpoint is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The ClickHouse user can create and write destination tables, and can drop them when replace mode is used. Tabsdata can write to the staging location and ClickHouse can read the staged Parquet files.

Configure ClickHouseDest as the destination of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in ClickHouse. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.clickhouse import ClickHouseDest @subscriber( destination=ClickHouseDest( tables=[ "orders", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return orders tables:list[str]required if_table_exists:"append" | "replace"optional schema_evolution:"strict" | "update"optional dest_cfg:dictoptional

tables​ Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in ClickHouse, as a non-empty list. A table cannot be listed twice, and names that differ only in quoting count as the same. Each name is table or database.table; quote a part with backticks if it has special characters. Each element in tables represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. if_table_exists​ "append" (the default) adds rows to the existing table. "replace" overwrites the table: the first run creates it, and later runs drop and recreate it. schema_evolution​ "strict" (the default) refuses a write that adds a column, brings a wider type whose values do not fit the column, or writes NULL into a non-Nullable column, with SQL_COMMON_10, before anything is loaded. Column order is ignored, a narrower type fits, and a column the frame lacks is written as NULL. "update" adds Nullable columns, makes columns nullable and widens integers up to 64 bits and Float32 to Float64; it never drops or reorders columns. Before 2.3.0 "update" was called "iceberg", which now fails validation. See Schema Evolution. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration. The accepted key is clickhouse.logging_level. ClickHouse always uses Iceberg schema evolution, so clickhouse.schema_evolution_engine is refused at registration.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" adds rows. "replace" drops and recreates the table. Because the table is recreated, any engine, ORDER BY or PARTITION BY set on it is lost; a table the connector creates uses ENGINE = MergeTree() ORDER BY tuple(). To keep a layout, create the table first and use "append". Neither mode runs in a transaction: if the insert fails after "replace", the table is left empty, and a failed create leaves no table. Multiple tables are written one after another. With schema_evolution="strict", a new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit, is refused; "update" applies supported schema changes.

schema_evolution decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. "strict", the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. "update" changes the table to fit the frame. On ClickHouse, "update" uses Iceberg schema evolution, applied by the connector, on "append" and "replace": it adds Nullable columns, makes columns nullable, widens integers up to 64 bits, signed and unsigned, and widens Float32 to Float64. "merge" is not supported.

The connector stages Parquet files before ClickHouse reads them. A run needs both staging access and ClickHouse access. Staged files are deleted after each run, whether or not the write succeeds. The cleanup lists every object under base_path whose first path segment sorts at or below the run's upload ID. Give each subscriber its own base_path: a base_path of / reaches the whole bucket, and two subscribers on one prefix can delete each other's files. The staging credentials need list and delete permission on that prefix, as well as upload. GCS staging needs service-account JSON for uploads and HMAC credentials for ClickHouse's S3-compatible reads. The ClickHouse server reads the staged files itself, so it needs network access to the staging store. S3 uses AWS unless obstore.endpoint is set; Azure uses core.windows.net unless obstore.endpoint is set; GCS always uses storage.googleapis.com and refuses an endpoint with CLICKHOUSE_12. Tabsdata does not contact ClickHouse or the staging service when the collection is created. Those checks happen when the subscriber runs.

ClickHouse subscribers use ClickHouseDestConn to define the server, the credentials, and the cloud storage the data is staged in. conn-clickhouse.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.clickhouse:ClickHouseDestConn spec: host: 'clickhouse.internal' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_writer' password: 'secret:example-password' staging: kind: clickHouseS3Location apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.clickhouse:S3Location spec: bucket: 'acme-staging' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:example-access-key' secret_access_key: 'secret:example-secret-key' base_path: '/clickhouse' host:strrequired port:stroptional database:stroptional secure:stroptional credentials:UserPasswordrequired staging:CloudLocationrequired entity_whitelist:list[str]optional conn_cfg:dictoptional

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type clickhouse-bulk-out --file conn-clickhouse.yaml Edit the template file with the ClickHouse connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-clickhouse.yaml tdk collection create --name clickhouse_out --conn-file conn-clickhouse.yaml Then register the subscriber in the collection: tdk fn register --coll clickhouse_out --path write_orders.py::write_orders The collection goes in the destinations group, because the connection is a destination connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be destinations. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: ClickHouseDest for a collection created with ClickHouseDestConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name clickhouse_out --conn-file conn-clickhouse.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

host, port, database and secure​ host identifies the ClickHouse server. port is the HTTP(S) port, from 1 to 65535, and defaults to "8123". database defaults to "default" and supplies the database for destination table names without one. secure is "true" for HTTPS and "false" (the default) for HTTP. It does not change the port, so set port as well; HTTPS ClickHouse is usually on 8443. credentials​ A UserPassword containing the ClickHouse username and password. Cloud storage credentials are configured separately under staging. staging​ Use one of the location classes from tabsdatak.conn.clickhouse: Location Required fields Credentials S3Location bucket, region, credentials AwsAccessSecretKey AzBlobLocation container, credentials AzureAccountKey GCSLocation bucket, credentials, hmac_credentials GCPJson for uploads and GCPHmac for ClickHouse reads Tabsdata must be able to upload the staged files, and ClickHouse must be able to read them. For GCS, both credential types are required: uploads use the native GCS API, while ClickHouse reads through the S3-compatible endpoint. Keys under cfg on the location configure the object store; see Object Store Options. entity_whitelist​ A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet. Leave it out. conn_cfg​ Optional connector configuration.

The Databricks connector lets Tabsdata run queries against Databricks and write tables into Databricks. The DatabricksSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Databricks into a Tabsdata table. The DatabricksDest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Databricks.

The DatabricksSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Databricks into a Tabsdata table. See the full publisher walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a DatabricksSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Publisher connection, at the end of this page.

The Databricks workspace and SQL warehouse are reachable from the Tabsdata server. The personal access token can use the SQL warehouse and read every table referenced by queries. The configured Unity Catalog volume exists and the token can read and write its staging files.

Configure DatabricksSrc as the source of a publisher function to select the queries that Tabsdata runs against Databricks. publish_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher from tabsdatak.conn.databricks import DatabricksSrc @publisher( source=DatabricksSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM main.default.orders", ], ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders): return orders queries:list[str]required initial_values:dictoptional src_cfg:dictoptional

queries​ Defines the SQL queries the publisher runs against Databricks. Each element in queries represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function. initial_values​ The first-run values for named parameters in queries, written :name. On later runs each parameter takes the value the publisher stored with ctx.set_attr(name, value), so a query can read only the rows added since the last run. Parameters bind values such as IDs and timestamps, not identifiers. Catalog, schema and table names have to be written into the query, or set with catalog and schema on the connection. For example: from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx, publisher from tabsdatak.conn.databricks import DatabricksSrc @publisher( source=DatabricksSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM main.default.orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id"], initial_values={"last_id": 0}, ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> TableFrameSpec: row = orders.max_for("id") if row is not None and row["id"] is not None: ctx.set_attr("last_id", int(row["id"])) return orders src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration.

The DatabricksDest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Databricks. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a DatabricksDestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Subscriber connection, at the end of this page.

The Databricks workspace and SQL warehouse are reachable from the Tabsdata server. The personal access token can use the SQL warehouse and create or write the destination tables. The configured Unity Catalog volume exists and the token can read and write its staging files.

For merge writes, schema evolution, and retry watermarks, see Merging into SQL destinations. Configure DatabricksDest as the destination of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in Databricks. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.databricks import DatabricksDest @subscriber( destination=DatabricksDest( tables=[ "orders", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders tables:list[str]required if_table_exists:stroptional schema_evolution:stroptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

tables​ Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in Databricks. Each element in tables represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. Destination table names can be fully qualified or completed from the connection's catalog/schema defaults. if_table_exists​ "merge" applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key and requires a merge_cfg list. See Merge configuration for a complete example. Controls what happens when the destination table already exists. "append" (the default) adds rows. "replace" overwrites the table. schema_evolution​ Controls what happens when the returned frame has a column the table lacks or a wider type. "update" forwards mergeSchema=true to COPY INTO and sets delta.enableTypeWidening, so new columns are added and types widened. "strict" is the default: an append fails inside COPY INTO (DATABRICKS_9), and a merge is refused before it runs (SQL_COMMON_10). See Schema Evolution. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration.

Each entry in queries produces one source slot. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to output_tables. For incremental reads, put named parameters such as :last_id in a query, set their first values with initial_values, and save the next values with ctx.set_attr() after a successful run.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a returned value. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" adds rows, "replace" overwrites the table, and "merge" applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key. With schema_evolution="update", writes can add columns and widen types; under "strict" a new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit, fails the write.

schema_evolution decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. "strict", the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. "update" changes the table to fit the frame. On Databricks, "update" uses Databricks' native schema evolution on every if_table_exists mode: Delta mergeSchema with type widening on "append" and "replace", and MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION on "merge". It adds columns and widens the types Delta type widening supports. Databricks takes no schema_evolution_engine setting.

Publisher queries and subscriber writes use the configured SQL warehouse. The Unity Catalog volume is the staging area used to move data. One- and two-part table names use the connection's catalog and schema defaults. Fully qualified names override them. Tabsdata does not contact the workspace when the collection is created. Workspace, token, warehouse, volume, and permission errors appear when the function runs.

Databricks publishers use DatabricksSrcConn to define the workspace, token, and warehouse used by the publisher. conn-databricks-in.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.databricks:DatabricksSrcConn spec: host_url: 'secret:https://dbc-00000000.cloud.databricks.com' token: 'secret:dapi0example0token0000' volume: 'main.default.tabsdata_stage' host_url:Secretrequired token:Secretrequired volume:strrequired warehouse:stroptional warehouse_id:stroptional catalog:stroptional schema:stroptional

A publisher is registered in a source collection, and a source collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type databricks-bulk-in --file conn-databricks-in.yaml Edit the template file with the Databricks connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-databricks-in.yaml tdk collection create --name databricks_in --conn-file conn-databricks-in.yaml Then register the publisher in the collection: tdk fn register --coll databricks_in --path publish_orders.py::publish_orders The collection goes in the sources group, because the connection is a source connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be sources. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: DatabricksSrc for a collection created with DatabricksSrcConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name databricks_in --conn-file conn-databricks-in.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

host_url​ The Databricks workspace URL, stored as a secret. token​ The Databricks personal access token used for workspace access. volume​ The managed Databricks volume the connector uses to stage files during reads and writes. warehouse​ The SQL warehouse name. Use this or warehouse_id, not both. warehouse_id​ An alternative to warehouse. The two fields are mutually exclusive. catalog​ The default catalog for partially qualified table names. schema​ The default schema. Requires catalog to be set.

Databricks subscribers use DatabricksDestConn to define the workspace, token, and warehouse used by the subscriber. conn-databricks-out.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.databricks:DatabricksDestConn spec: host_url: 'secret:https://dbc-00000000.cloud.databricks.com' token: 'secret:dapi0example0token0000' volume: 'main.default.tabsdata_stage' host_url:Secretrequired token:Secretrequired volume:strrequired warehouse:stroptional warehouse_id:stroptional catalog:stroptional schema:stroptional

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type databricks-bulk-out --file conn-databricks-out.yaml Edit the template file with the Databricks connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-databricks-out.yaml tdk collection create --name databricks_out --conn-file conn-databricks-out.yaml Then register the subscriber in the collection: tdk fn register --coll databricks_out --path write_orders.py::write_orders The collection goes in the destinations group, because the connection is a destination connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be destinations. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: DatabricksDest for a collection created with DatabricksDestConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name databricks_out --conn-file conn-databricks-out.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

host_url​ The Databricks workspace URL, stored as a secret. token​ The Databricks personal access token used for writes. volume​ The managed volume used for staged files during COPY INTO. warehouse​ The SQL warehouse name. Use this or warehouse_id, not both. warehouse_id​ An alternative to warehouse. The two fields are mutually exclusive. catalog​ The default catalog for partially qualified table names. schema​ The default schema. Requires catalog to be set.

The Db2 connector lets Tabsdata run queries against Db2 and write tables into Db2. The Db2Src connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Db2 into a Tabsdata table. The Db2Dest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Db2.

The Db2Src connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Db2 into a Tabsdata table. See the full publisher walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a Db2SrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Publisher connection, at the end of this page.
The Db2 server is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The connection user can run every query in queries and read every referenced table or view.

Configure Db2Src as the source of a publisher function to select the queries that Tabsdata runs against Db2. publish_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher from tabsdatak.conn.db2 import Db2Src @publisher( source=Db2Src( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM orders", ], ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders): return orders queries:list[str]required initial_values:dictoptional src_cfg:dictoptional

queries​ Defines the SQL queries the publisher runs against Db2. Each element in queries represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function. For example: Db2Src( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM country", "SELECT * FROM city", ], ) initial_values​ The first-run values for named parameters in queries, written :name. On later runs each parameter takes the value the publisher stored with ctx.set_attr(name, value), so a query can read only the rows added since the last run. Db2 folds unquoted identifiers to uppercase, so the column read back is ID. Parameters bind values such as IDs and timestamps, not identifiers. Schema and table names have to be written into the query. For example: from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx, publisher from tabsdatak.conn.db2 import Db2Src @publisher( source=Db2Src( queries=["SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id"], initial_values={"last_id": 0}, ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> TableFrameSpec: row = orders.max_for("ID") if row is not None and row["ID"] is not None: ctx.set_attr("last_id", int(row["ID"])) return orders src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration.

The Db2Dest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Db2. The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a Db2DestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Subscriber connection, at the end of this page.

The Db2 server is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The connection user can create missing destination tables and insert rows. With if_table_exists="replace", it also needs to drop and create tables, and with schema_evolution="update", to alter them, and to run REORG through ADMIN_CMD.

Configure Db2Dest as the destination of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in Db2. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.db2 import Db2Dest @subscriber( destination=Db2Dest( tables=[ "orders", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders tables:list[str]required if_table_exists:stroptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

tables​ Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in Db2. Each element in tables represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. For example: Db2Dest( tables=[ "vendors", "items", ], ) if_table_exists​ Controls what happens when the destination table already has rows. "append" (the default) keeps inserting into the existing rows. "replace" drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame, so the table's schema follows the frame. With transactional=True, the drop, the create and the insert run in one transaction. On "append", schema_evolution decides what happens to a new or wider column. schema_evolution​ "strict" (the default) or "update". A refused write fails with SQL_COMMON_10 before anything is written. See Schema evolution. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration.

Each entry in queries produces one source slot. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to output_tables. Keep those three lists in the same order. Queries run when the publisher is triggered. They are not a continuous change feed. To read incrementally, put named parameters such as :last_id in the query, set their first values with initial_values, and save the next values with ctx.set_attr() after each successful run.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" keeps the rows already in the destination and inserts the returned rows. "replace" drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame. On "append", schema_evolution="update" adds new columns and widens number types; removing a column or changing a non-number type still needs a database migration before the subscriber runs.

schema_evolution decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. "strict", the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. "update" changes the table to fit the frame. On Db2, "update" uses Iceberg schema evolution, applied by the connector, on "append" and "replace": ALTER TABLE … ADD adds columns, and integers, decimals and floats are widened by digits or width. It never drops a column or changes a non-number type. After an ALTER, Db2 also runs REORG through ADMIN_CMD. "merge" is not supported.

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set trigger_by to change when the function runs. Tabsdata checks the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not connect to Db2 then. A bad host, credential, query, or permission fails when the function runs. Every function in the collection uses the same connection. Use another collection when functions need another database or another set of credentials.

Db2 publishers use Db2SrcConn to define the database connection and credentials used by the publisher. conn-db2-in.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.db2:Db2SrcConn spec: uri: 'db2+ibm_db://db.internal:50000/world' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_reader' password: 'secret:example-password' uri:strrequired credentials:UserPasswordrequired entity_whitelist:list[str]optional conn_cfg:dictoptional

The Db2 CDC connector lets Tabsdata capture the changes made to Db2 tables (inserts, updates and deletes) and publish them into Tabsdata tables. With start_from="full", the stream starts with a full load: it takes a consistent snapshot of the tracked tables and then switches to change capture from the exact point of that snapshot, with no gaps. Duplicates are removed under the rules in Full load limits. The Db2CdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to read the change-data (CD) tables that Db2 SQL Replication fills, and write every captured change into a Tabsdata table. Unlike Db2Src, which runs queries on a trigger, a CDC source runs continuously: registering the stream publisher starts a long-lived worker that keeps reading the CD tables until the function is disabled or deleted.

The Db2CdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to capture changes from Db2 into Tabsdata tables. See the full publisher walkthrough The stream publisher is registered in a collection created with a Db2CdcStreamSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

Db2 CDC builds on Db2 SQL Replication: the ASN Capture program (asncap) reads the Db2 log and copies each change of a registered table into that table's CD table. Tabsdata reads the CD tables. SQL Replication is set up in the source database: the ASN capture control tables exist, and asncap is running. Each tracked source table is registered for capture (a row in ASN.IBMSNAP_REGISTER), with an active registration and its own CD table. Every column is registered with its before-image; a registration without before-images is refused. The connecting user can SELECT the CD tables and ASN.IBMSNAP_REGISTER, ASN.IBMSNAP_PRUNCNTL and ASN.IBMSNAP_RESTART, and ASN.IBMSNAP_UOW when starting from "tail" or a timestamp. For start_from="full", the connecting user can also SELECT every tracked source table and EXECUTE the SYSPROC.MON_GET_TRANSACTION_LOG table function (for example through the SYSMON authority), and no tracked table is registered to capture updates as a delete plus an insert (CHG_UPD_TO_DEL_INS = 'Y').

Configure Db2CdcStreamSrc as the source of a @stream_publisher function to select the CD tables whose changes Tabsdata captures. stream_sales_changes.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.db2 import Db2CdcStreamSrc from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @stream_publisher( source=Db2CdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "ASN.CD_ORDERS", "ASN.CD_CUSTOMERS", ], start_from="full", ), batch_max_secs=120, output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], ) def stream_sales_changes( orders: TableFramesSpec, customers: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return concat(orders), concat(customers) tables:list[str]required start_from:"full" | "head" | "tail" | CommitSeqPosition | TableCommitSeqPosition | TimestampPositionrequired columns_format:"columns" | "struct" | "map"optional flatten_columns:booloptional src_cfg:dictoptional batch_max_secs=120 hands the captured changes to the function at least every two minutes. The batch_* parameters decide when a batch of changes is handed to the function, and are the same for every stream source. See Stream Publishers for all of them. A stream publisher differs from a regular publisher in three ways: It has no trigger. Registering it starts the stream worker, which runs until the function is disabled or deleted. Each element of tables is one function parameter, and each parameter receives a list of frames: the changes captured for that table since the previous batch. Fold them with concat, which also returns None when the batch carried nothing for that table. The function must not declare a ctx parameter.

tables​ Defines the CD tables to read, as qualified cd_schema.cd_table names. These are the change-data tables, not the source tables. The connector finds each CD table's source table through ASN.IBMSNAP_REGISTER. Db2 folds unquoted names to uppercase, so write them in uppercase. Each element in tables represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function and to an entry in output_tables. A table listed twice is refused with CONN_37. For example: Db2CdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "ASN.CD_ORDERS", "ASN.CD_CUSTOMERS", ], start_from="tail", ) start_from​ Where the stream starts the first time it runs. Later runs resume from the position the stream has recorded, which it keeps for each CD table separately. "full": a full load of every tracked source table, then the changes captured after it. See Full load. "tail": only changes captured after the stream starts. "head": every change still in each CD table. CommitSeqPosition(seq="..."): one commit sequence for every table, as the hex form of the 16-byte IBMSNAP_COMMITSEQ value. TableCommitSeqPosition(seqs={"ASN.CD_ORDERS": "...", ...}): a commit sequence per CD table, for example after re-snapshotting some tables. Every CD table in tables must be listed; a table left out fails the stream. TimestampPosition(ts=...): from the first commit at or after a point in time, looked up in ASN.IBMSNAP_UOW. A naive datetime is read in the Db2 server's time zone. Full load​ With start_from="full", the stream first emits every row of each tracked source table and then captures the changes from the CD tables. No change is missed between the load and the change capture. Duplicates are removed under the rules in Full load limits. Each table's snapshot is preceded by one LOAD row (@td.cdc.meta.op = "l"), and its rows arrive as inserts. A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. The full load reads the source tables rather than the CD tables, and locks nothing. The changes committed while the tables are read are taken from the CD tables and reconciled with the rows read, and duplicates are removed under the rules in Full load limits. asncap must be running, since the load waits for Capture to reach the end of the load before handing over to the change stream. To resynchronize a destination later, keep start_from="full" and reset the function's stage: tdk fn update --reset-stage <other options> The stream then starts again with a new full load and its LOAD rows. Resetting the stage with any other start_from restarts at that position and sends no LOAD row. Full load limits​ The load holds no snapshot. A change committed while the tables are read is loaded and replayed, then deduplicated under the rules of the MySQL lockless load. The limits are: A keyless table cannot be matched row by row, so its changes inside the window arrive twice. The map format fails the load with CDC_26. A DDL change or a TRUNCATE during the load fails the stream with CDC_23 to CDC_25. A change that Db2 records as CHG_UPD_TO_DEL_INS fails the stream with DB2_35. A load with more changes than tabsdata.cdc.initial_load.max_window_changes fails with CDC_29. columns_format​ How each change row lays out the table's column values: "columns" (the default), "struct" or "map". See Change rows. flatten_columns​ When True (the default), the new column values are written as ordinary top-level columns, so each change row reads like a row of the source table. columns_format then only shapes the old values. See Change rows. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. Only these keys are accepted: Key Default Description tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows 10000 Rows buffered in the worker before they are written out to a file. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_bytes none Bytes buffered before they are written out. Measuring bytes costs time on every change; prefer bounding by rows. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_secs 60 Longest time a change waits in the buffer. tabsdata.cdc.poll.max_secs 1 Longest time one read of the CD tables waits for changes. tabsdata.cdc.poll.idle_secs 1 Pause after a read that found no changes. tabsdata.cdc.fetch_size 100000 Rows fetched per round trip. tabsdata.cdc.chunk_size 100000 Rows per chunk while writing the full load. tabsdata.cdc.initial_load.max_window_changes 100000 Most changes that may be committed to the tracked tables while the full load reads them. Above it, the load fails; run it again at a quieter time or raise the limit. tabsdata.cdc.max_large_text_length 1024 Longest value, in characters, accepted from an unbounded text column. A longer value fails the stream. db2.cdc.logging_level 40 Logging verbosity of the connector, as a Python logging level number (10 debug, 20 info, 30 warning, 40 error). The buffer settings control when captured changes are written to files inside the worker. When those files are handed to the function is controlled by the batch parameters of @stream_publisher.

Every row the stream emits is one change. Besides the column values, each row carries change metadata: Column Type Description @td.cdc.meta.op str The operation: "i" insert, "u" update, "d" delete, "l" load (start of a full load). @td.cdc.meta.tx str The commit sequence of the transaction, in hex. Full load rows carry initial-load. @td.cdc.meta.sq int The change's sequence (IBMSNAP_INTENTSEQ). @td.cdc.meta.ts datetime (UTC) When the transaction committed. Full load rows carry the time the snapshot was taken. @td.cdc.meta.seg decimal The transaction's commit sequence (IBMSNAP_COMMITSEQ). Full load rows carry -1. @td.cdc.meta.ord decimal The change's sequence (IBMSNAP_INTENTSEQ). Ordering by seg and then ord gives the order the changes were committed in. @td.cdc.meta.fmt str The columns_format the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.flat bool The flatten_columns setting the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.sch str A hash of the source table's schema when the change was captured. It changes when the table's columns change. The column values are laid out according to flatten_columns and columns_format: New values Old values flatten_columns=True (default) One top-level column per source column, with the source column's name. Depends on columns_format. columns_format="columns" (default) @td.cdc.data.col.new.<column> per column, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.col.old.<column> per column. columns_format="struct" @td.cdc.data.row.new, one struct, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.row.old, one struct. columns_format="map" @td.cdc.data.map.new, a JSON object as a string, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.map.old, a JSON object as a string. What each operation carries: Operation New values Old values Insert (i) The inserted row. Empty. Update (u) The row after the update. The row before the update. Delete (d) The deleted row. Empty. Load (l) Empty. Empty. Empty values are null columns with "columns", a struct whose fields are all null with "struct", and a JSON object whose values are all null with "map". A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. SQL Replication does not copy LOB or XML values into the CD tables, so those columns always arrive as null. TRUNCATE is not captured. To pick up a truncated table, reset the stage with start_from="full". Use "columns" with flatten_columns=True for changes that land in a table and get queried. Use "struct" or "map" when the source table's schema may change while the stream runs, to carry the values opaquely instead of changing the output table's columns.

The stream reads only what asncap has captured. If Capture stops, the stream sees no new changes until it is running again. If a tracked table is deregistered, its registration is deactivated, Capture cold-starts, or pruning removes CD rows the stream has not read yet, the stream fails with an error explaining what happened. The fix is to restore the registration if needed and run a new full load: reset the stage with start_from="full". A CD table added to tables after the stream started has no recorded position, so the stream fails until a new full load runs.
