The MySQL CDC connector lets Tabsdata capture the changes made to MySQL tables (inserts, updates, deletes and truncates) as they are committed, and publish them into Tabsdata tables. With start_from="full", the stream starts with a full load: it takes a consistent snapshot of the tracked tables and then switches to change capture from the exact point of that snapshot, with no gaps and no duplicates when the global read lock is taken. Where the server refuses the lock, the limits in Full load without the global read lock apply. The full load and the change capture are one stream publisher, so there is nothing to reconcile between them. The MySQLCdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to follow the MySQL binary log (binlog) as a replica would and write every captured change into a Tabsdata table. Unlike MySQLSrc, which runs queries on a trigger, a CDC source runs continuously: registering the stream publisher starts a long-lived worker that keeps reading the binlog until the function is disabled or deleted.

The MySQLCdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to capture changes from MySQL into Tabsdata tables. See the full publisher walkthrough The stream publisher is registered in a collection created with a MySQLCdcStreamSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The server's binlog is set up for row-based capture: log_bin = ON, binlog_format = ROW, binlog_row_image = FULL and gtid_mode = ON. The stream checks these at start and refuses a server that does not have them. The connecting user holds the replication privileges a binlog reader needs (REPLICATION SLAVE and REPLICATION CLIENT). When streaming from a replica, the replica runs with log_replica_updates = ON, and with replica_preserve_commit_order = ON if it applies transactions in parallel. For start_from="full", the connecting user also holds SELECT on every tracked table, and RELOAD where the server grants it, for the global read lock. The tracked tables are InnoDB. Managed services such as Amazon RDS and Aurora refuse the global read lock, and the full load still runs there with the same transactional consistency.

Configure MySQLCdcStreamSrc as the source of a @stream_publisher function to select the tables whose changes Tabsdata captures. stream_sales_changes.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLCdcStreamSrc from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @stream_publisher( source=MySQLCdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "sales.orders", "sales.customers", ], start_from="full", ), batch_max_secs=120, output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], ) def stream_sales_changes( orders: TableFramesSpec, customers: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return concat(orders), concat(customers) tables:list[str]required start_from:"full" | "head" | "tail" | GtidPosition | BinlogPosition | TimestampPositionrequired columns_format:"columns" | "struct" | "map"optional flatten_columns:booloptional src_cfg:dictoptional batch_max_secs=120 hands the captured changes to the function at least every two minutes. The batch_* parameters decide when a batch of changes is handed to the function, and are the same for every stream source. See Stream Publishers for all of them. A stream publisher differs from a regular publisher in three ways: It has no trigger. Registering it starts the stream worker, which runs until the function is disabled or deleted. Each element of tables is one function parameter, and each parameter receives a list of frames: the changes captured for that table since the previous batch. Fold them with concat, which also returns None when the batch carried nothing for that table. The function must not declare a ctx parameter.

tables​ Defines the MySQL tables whose changes are captured, as qualified database.table names. Each element in tables represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function and to an entry in output_tables. A table listed twice is refused with CONN_37. For example: MySQLCdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "sales.orders", "sales.customers", ], start_from="tail", ) start_from​ Where the stream starts the first time it runs. Later runs resume from the position the stream has recorded. "full": a full load of every tracked table, then the changes committed after it. See Full load. "tail": only changes committed after the stream starts. "head": replay from the oldest change still in binlog retention. GtidPosition(gtid="<uuid>:<n>"): after a global transaction id. The given GTIDs count as already read, and the stream starts with the next transaction. A range such as "<uuid>:1-<n>" is accepted too. BinlogPosition(file="mysql-bin.000001", pos=4): from a binlog file and byte offset, as SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS or SHOW BINLOG EVENTS report them. Position 4 is the start of a file. TimestampPosition(ts=...): from the first binlog event at or after a point in time. A naive datetime is read as UTC. A time before the oldest retained binlog is refused. Full load​ With start_from="full", the stream first emits every row of each tracked table and then captures the changes from the exact binlog position of that snapshot. The snapshot is consistent across all the tracked tables, and when the global read lock is taken, no change is missed or repeated between the snapshot and the change capture. Each table's snapshot is preceded by one LOAD row (@td.cdc.meta.op = "l"), and its rows arrive as inserts. A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. The tables are read in one consistent-snapshot transaction. To pin that snapshot to a binlog position, the stream briefly takes the global read lock. The lock is held only while the position is read, not while the tables are scanned. On servers that refuse the lock, such as Amazon RDS and Aurora, the load runs without it; see Full load without the global read lock. To resynchronize a destination later, keep start_from="full" and reset the function's stage: tdk fn update --reset-stage <other options> The stream then starts again with a new full load and its LOAD rows. Resetting the stage with any other start_from restarts at that position and sends no LOAD row. Full load without the global read lock​ Without the lock, the snapshot is not pinned to one binlog position. The connector brackets the load with the binlog position before and after it, and deduplicates the changes that fall inside that window. The lockless load has these limits: A table with a primary key is deduplicated by key. A keyless table cannot be matched row by row, so its changes inside the window arrive twice. A key swap, a TRUNCATE or a schema change during the load fails the stream with CDC_23 to CDC_25. The map format fails the load with CDC_26. A load with more changes in its window than tabsdata.cdc.initial_load.max_window_changes fails with CDC_29. columns_format​ How each change row lays out the table's column values: "columns" (the default), "struct" or "map". See Change rows. flatten_columns​ When True (the default), the new column values are written as ordinary top-level columns, so each change row reads like a row of the source table. columns_format then only shapes the old values. See Change rows. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. Only these keys are accepted: Key Default Description tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows 10000 Rows buffered in the worker before they are written out to a file. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_bytes none Bytes buffered before they are written out. Measuring bytes costs time on every change; prefer bounding by rows. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_secs 60 Longest time a change waits in the buffer. tabsdata.cdc.poll.max_secs 1 Longest time one read of the binlog waits for changes. tabsdata.cdc.poll.idle_secs 1 Pause after a read that found no changes. tabsdata.cdc.max_large_text_length 1024 Longest value, in characters, accepted from an unbounded text column. A longer value fails the stream. tabsdata.cdc.initial_load.max_window_changes 100000 Most changes the full load can hold in its window when it runs without the global read lock. Above it the load fails with CDC_29. tabsdata.cdc.fetch_size 100000 Rows fetched per round trip while reading the full load. tabsdata.cdc.chunk_size 100000 Rows per chunk while writing the full load. mysql.cdc.logging_level 40 Logging verbosity of the connector, as a Python logging level number (10 debug, 20 info, 30 warning, 40 error). The buffer settings control when captured changes are written to files inside the worker. When those files are handed to the function is controlled by the batch parameters of @stream_publisher.

Every row the stream emits is one change. Besides the column values, each row carries change metadata: Column Type Description @td.cdc.meta.op str The operation: "i" insert, "u" update, "d" delete, "t" truncate, "l" load (start of a full load). @td.cdc.meta.tx str The transaction's GTID. Full load rows carry initial-load. @td.cdc.meta.sq int The change's sequence within its transaction. @td.cdc.meta.ts datetime (UTC) When the transaction committed. Full load rows carry the time the snapshot was taken. @td.cdc.meta.seg decimal The transaction's number in its GTID. Full load rows carry -1. @td.cdc.meta.ord decimal The position of the change within the transaction. Ordering by seg and then ord gives the order the changes were committed in. @td.cdc.meta.fmt str The columns_format the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.flat bool The flatten_columns setting the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.sch str A hash of the source table's schema when the change was captured. It changes when the table's columns change. The column values are laid out according to flatten_columns and columns_format: New values Old values flatten_columns=True (default) One top-level column per source column, with the source column's name. Depends on columns_format. columns_format="columns" (default) @td.cdc.data.col.new.<column> per column, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.col.old.<column> per column. columns_format="struct" @td.cdc.data.row.new, one struct, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.row.old, one struct. columns_format="map" @td.cdc.data.map.new, a JSON object as a string, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.map.old, a JSON object as a string. What each operation carries: Operation New values Old values Insert (i) The inserted row. Empty. Update (u) The row after the update. The complete row before the update. Delete (d) The deleted row. Empty. Truncate (t), Load (l) Empty. Empty. Empty values are null columns with "columns", a struct whose fields are all null with "struct", and a JSON object whose values are all null with "map". A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. A TRUNCATE row reports that the source table was truncated. BLOB columns are not captured: they always arrive as null. TIMESTAMP columns are rewritten to the server time zone's wall clock. When that zone is unknown, the connector uses UTC and logs one warning. Use "columns" with flatten_columns=True for changes that land in a table and get queried. Use "struct" or "map" when the source table's schema may change while the stream runs, to carry the values opaquely instead of changing the output table's columns.

MariaDB is not supported. A mariadb:// URI is accepted, but the server check fails with MYSQL_27, because MariaDB has no gtid_mode. MySQL has no replication slot, so a stopped stream holds nothing on the server. It resumes from its recorded GTID, provided the server still retains the binlogs from that point. If they were purged, the stream fails and needs a new full load: reset the stage with start_from="full". A stream follows one source server. Switching it to another server (for example after a failover) is not supported: the new server's changes would be dropped as already published. Start a new stream instead.

uri​ The SQLAlchemy-style connection URI: mysql://host:port/database. Written as a plain value here, but accepts secret: too. credentials​ The database user and password, spliced into the URI at connect time. UserPassword requires a user and password. server_id​ The replica id the stream registers with when it reads the binlog. Defaults to 512. MySQL admits one replica per server_id: a second stream connecting with the same id disconnects the first. Several connectors read or write cloud object storage through an object store client. Keys that start with obstore. configure that client. Set them where the connector takes its other settings: conn_cfg on the connection for the file connectors, and cfg on the staging location for ClickHouse, StarRocks and Druid.

Connector Set with What the keys configure Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage conn_cfg on the connection Reads and writes ClickHouse cfg on the staging location The staging upload, the address ClickHouse reads the files from, and the cleanup StarRocks cfg on the staging location The staging upload. StarRocks reads the files through its own path, which the keys do not change Druid cfg on the staging location The staging upload. The ingestion input source does not use them On the file connectors, a key in conn_cfg overrides the matching credential in the connection. The explorer ignores these keys.

queries​ Defines the SQL queries the publisher runs against Oracle. Each element in queries represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function. For example: OracleSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM country", "SELECT * FROM city", ], ) initial_values​ The first-run values for named parameters in queries, written :name. tables​ Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in Oracle. Each element in tables represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. For example: OracleDest( tables=[ "vendors", "items", ], ) if_table_exists​ Controls what happens when the destination table already has rows. "append" (the default) keeps inserting into the existing rows. "replace" drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame, so the table's schema follows the frame. The drop and the create commit implicitly, so a failed write is not undone. On "append", schema_evolution decides what happens to a new or wider column. schema_evolution​ "strict" (the default) or "update". A refused write fails with SQL_COMMON_10 before anything is written. The ALTER statements "update" runs commit implicitly, so they are not undone if the write fails. See Schema evolution. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration.

Each entry in queries produces one source slot. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to output_tables. Keep those three lists in the same order. Queries run when the publisher is triggered. They are not a continuous change feed. To read incrementally, put named parameters such as :last_id in the query, set their first values with initial_values, and save the next values with ctx.set_attr() after each successful run.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" keeps the rows already in the destination and inserts the returned rows. "replace" drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame. On "append", schema_evolution="update" adds new columns and widens number types; removing a column or changing a non-number type still needs a database migration before the subscriber runs.

schema_evolution decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. "strict", the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. "update" changes the table to fit the frame. On Oracle, "update" uses Iceberg schema evolution, applied by the connector, on "append" and "replace": ALTER TABLE … ADD adds columns, and integers, decimals and floats are widened by digits or width. It never drops a column or changes a non-number type. "merge" is not supported.

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set trigger_by to change when the function runs. Tabsdata checks the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not connect to Oracle then. A bad host, credential, query, or permission fails when the function runs. Every function in the collection uses the same connection. Use another collection when functions need another database or another set of credentials.

The Postgres CDC connector lets Tabsdata capture the changes made to Postgres tables (inserts, updates, deletes and truncates) as they are committed, and publish them into Tabsdata tables. With start_from="full", the stream starts with a full load: it takes a consistent snapshot of the tracked tables and then switches to change capture from the exact point of that snapshot, with no gaps and no duplicates. The full load and the change capture are one stream publisher, so there is nothing to reconcile between them. The PostgresCdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to follow the Postgres write-ahead log (WAL) through a logical replication slot and write every captured change into a Tabsdata table. Unlike PostgresSrc, which runs queries on a trigger, a CDC source runs continuously: registering the stream publisher starts a long-lived worker that keeps reading the WAL until the function is disabled or deleted.

The PostgresCdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to capture changes from Postgres into Tabsdata tables. See the full publisher walkthrough The stream publisher is registered in a collection created with a PostgresCdcStreamSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The server runs with wal_level = logical. The wal2json logical decoding output plugin, version 2.0 or later, is installed on the server. The connecting role has the REPLICATION attribute. Every tracked table has a replica identity: a primary key that is not DEFERRABLE, or REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, or REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX on a unique index. A table without one is refused, because Postgres would drop its updates and deletes from the WAL. A tracked table with large text columns needs REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, or the postgres.cdc.unchanged_large_text_as_null setting described under src_cfg. For start_from="full", the connecting role can also SELECT every tracked table.

Configure PostgresCdcStreamSrc as the source of a @stream_publisher function to select the tables whose changes Tabsdata captures. stream_sales_changes.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresCdcStreamSrc from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @stream_publisher( source=PostgresCdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "public.orders", "public.customers", ], replication_slot="tabsdata_sales", start_from="full", ), batch_max_secs=120, output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], ) def stream_sales_changes( orders: TableFramesSpec, customers: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return concat(orders), concat(customers) tables:list[str]required replication_slot:strrequired start_from:"full" | "head" | "tail" | LsnPositionrequired replication_slot_behavior:"reuse" | "create"optional publication_name:stroptional columns_format:"columns" | "struct" | "map"optional flatten_columns:booloptional src_cfg:dictoptional batch_max_secs=120 hands the captured changes to the function at least every two minutes. The batch_* parameters decide when a batch of changes is handed to the function, and are the same for every stream source. See Stream Publishers for all of them. A stream publisher differs from a regular publisher in three ways: It has no trigger. Registering it starts the stream worker, which runs until the function is disabled or deleted. Each element of tables is one function parameter, and each parameter receives a list of frames: the changes captured for that table since the previous batch. Fold them with concat, which also returns None when the batch carried nothing for that table. The function must not declare a ctx parameter.

tables​ Defines the Postgres tables whose changes are captured, as qualified schema.table names. Each element in tables represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function and to an entry in output_tables. For example: PostgresCdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "public.orders", "public.customers", ], replication_slot="tabsdata_sales", start_from="tail", ) replication_slot​ The logical replication slot the stream reads through. Postgres keeps the WAL the slot has not yet consumed, which is what lets the stream resume where it left off after a restart. Each stream publisher needs its own slot. Tabsdata never drops the slot, not even when the function is deleted. A slot that is no longer read makes the server keep WAL indefinitely, so drop it with pg_drop_replication_slot('<slot>') once its stream is gone. start_from​ Where the stream starts the first time it runs. Later runs resume from the position the stream has recorded. "full": a full load of every tracked table, then the changes committed after it. See Full load. "tail": only changes committed after the stream starts. "head": replay from the oldest WAL the slot retains. LsnPosition(lsn=...): an explicit WAL position, given as the 64-bit integer that pg_current_wal_lsn() - '0/0'::pg_lsn returns. Full load​ With start_from="full", the stream first emits every row of each tracked table and then captures the changes from the exact position of that snapshot. The snapshot is consistent across all the tracked tables, and no change is missed or repeated between the snapshot and the change capture. Each table's snapshot is preceded by one LOAD row (@td.cdc.meta.op = "l"), and its rows arrive as inserts. A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. No table is locked. The snapshot is the one Postgres exports when a replication slot is created: the stream's own slot when the stream creates it, or otherwise a temporary slot that is created for the load and dropped once the load is read. To resynchronize a destination later, keep start_from="full" and reset the function's stage: tdk fn update --reset-stage <other options> The stream then starts again with a new full load and its LOAD rows. Resetting the stage with any other start_from restarts at that position and sends no LOAD row. replication_slot_behavior​ "reuse" (the default) requires the slot to exist already, for example when a DBA provisions it. "create" creates the slot, and does nothing if it already exists. publication_name​ A Postgres publication that scopes what the slot decodes (wal2json's publication_names option). columns_format​ How each change row lays out the table's column values: "columns" (the default), "struct" or "map". See Change rows. flatten_columns​ When True (the default), the new column values are written as ordinary top-level columns, so each change row reads like a row of the source table. columns_format then only shapes the old values. See Change rows. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. Only these keys are accepted: Key Default Description tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows 10000 Rows buffered in the worker before they are written out to a file. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_bytes none Bytes buffered before they are written out. Measuring bytes costs time on every change; prefer bounding by rows. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_secs 60 Longest time a change waits in the buffer. tabsdata.cdc.poll.max_secs 1 Longest time one read of the WAL waits for changes. tabsdata.cdc.poll.idle_secs 1 Pause after a read that found no changes. tabsdata.cdc.max_large_text_length 1024 Longest value, in characters, accepted from an unbounded text column. A longer value fails the stream. tabsdata.cdc.fetch_size 100000 Rows fetched per round trip while reading the full load. tabsdata.cdc.chunk_size 100000 Rows per chunk while writing the full load. postgres.cdc.wal2json_format_version 2 wal2json output format, 1 or 2. Truncates are only captured with 2. postgres.cdc.unchanged_large_text_as_null unset Set to true to accept that, on a table without REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, an update that does not touch a large text column delivers that column as null. When unset, such a table refuses to start the stream. postgres.cdc.accept_gap unset Lets a stopped stream resume past one reported gap between its position and the slot's. Give the value exactly as the error message prints it; it matches no other gap. postgres.cdc.logging_level 40 Logging verbosity of the connector, as a Python logging level number (10 debug, 20 info, 30 warning, 40 error). The buffer settings control when captured changes are written to files inside the worker. When those files are handed to the function is controlled by the batch parameters of @stream_publisher.

Every row the stream emits is one change. Besides the column values, each row carries change metadata: Column Type Description @td.cdc.meta.op str The operation: "i" insert, "u" update, "d" delete, "t" truncate, "l" load (start of a full load). @td.cdc.meta.tx str The source transaction id. Full load rows carry initial-load. @td.cdc.meta.sq int The change's sequence within its transaction. @td.cdc.meta.ts datetime (UTC) When the transaction committed. Full load rows carry the time the snapshot was taken. @td.cdc.meta.seg decimal The position of the transaction's commit in the WAL. Full load rows carry -1. @td.cdc.meta.ord decimal The position of the change within the transaction. Ordering by seg and then ord gives the order the changes were committed in. @td.cdc.meta.fmt str The columns_format the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.flat bool The flatten_columns setting the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.sch str A hash of the source table's schema when the change was captured. It changes when the table's columns change. The column values are laid out according to flatten_columns and columns_format: New values Old values flatten_columns=True (default) One top-level column per source column, with the source column's name. Depends on columns_format. columns_format="columns" (default) @td.cdc.data.col.new.<column> per column, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.col.old.<column> per column. columns_format="struct" @td.cdc.data.row.new, one struct, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.row.old, one struct. columns_format="map" @td.cdc.data.map.new, a JSON object as a string, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.map.old, a JSON object as a string. What each operation carries: Operation New values Old values Insert (i) The inserted row. Empty. Update (u) The row after the update. The row before the update. Postgres logs the complete previous row only for tables with REPLICA IDENTITY FULL; otherwise only the replica identity columns are present. Delete (d) The deleted row. Without REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, only the replica identity columns are present. Empty. Truncate (t), Load (l) Empty. Empty. Empty values are null columns with "columns", a struct whose fields are all null with "struct", and a JSON object whose values are all null with "map". A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. A TRUNCATE row reports that the source table was truncated. bytea and oid columns are not captured: they always arrive as null. Use "columns" with flatten_columns=True for changes that land in a table and get queried. Use "struct" or "map" when the source table's schema may change while the stream runs, to carry the values opaquely instead of changing the output table's columns.

Stopping a stream does not lose changes: the slot keeps the WAL, and the stream resumes from its recorded position. The server also keeps that WAL until the stream consumes it, or until the slot is dropped. If the slot is dropped or invalidated, the server is restored from a backup, or the stream's position no longer matches the server, the stream fails with an error explaining what happened. In most of those cases the fix is a new full load: reset the stage with start_from="full". A slot can only be read by one connection at a time. A stream whose slot is still held by another connection fails after a timeout.

Postgres CDC stream publishers use PostgresCdcStreamSrcConn to define the database connection and credentials used by the stream. conn-postgres-cdc.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.postgres:PostgresCdcStreamSrcConn spec: uri: 'postgres://db.internal:5432/sales' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_cdc' password: 'secret:example-password' uri:strrequired credentials:UserPasswordrequired entity_whitelist:list[str]optional conn_cfg:dictoptional

A stream publisher is registered in a source collection, and a source collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type postgres-cdc --file conn-postgres-cdc.yaml Edit the template file with the Postgres connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-postgres-cdc.yaml tdk collection create --name sales_cdc --conn-file conn-postgres-cdc.yaml Then register the stream publisher in the collection: tdk fn register --coll sales_cdc --path stream_sales_changes.py::stream_sales_changes The collection goes in the sources group, because the connection is a source connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be sources. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: PostgresCdcStreamSrc for a collection created with PostgresCdcStreamSrcConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name sales_cdc --conn-file conn-postgres-cdc.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project. A batch PostgresSrc publisher cannot share this collection, because it uses a different connection (postgres-sql-in).

uri​ The SQLAlchemy-style connection URI: postgres://host:port/database (or postgresql://). Written as a plain value here, but accepts secret: too. credentials​ The database user and password, spliced into the URI at connect time. UserPassword requires a user and password. The role must have the REPLICATION attribute. entity_whitelist​ A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet: it does not limit which tables a stream can track. Leave it out. conn_cfg​ psycopg2 connection keywords such as sslmode, sslrootcert, connect_timeout or application_name. They apply to every connection the stream opens: catalog reads, the full load and the replication connection. The replication slot is configured on the publisher, not on the connection, so one connection can serve several stream publishers as long as each uses its own slot.

The Salesforce connectors let Tabsdata read data from Salesforce into Tabsdata tables. The SalesforceSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to run a SOQL query against Salesforce and write the result into a Tabsdata table. The SalesforceReportSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read Salesforce reports into Tabsdata tables. Both connectors use the same connection class, SalesforceSrcConn, so one collection can hold both kinds of publisher.

The SalesforceSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read the result of a SOQL query into a Tabsdata table. See the full publisher walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a SalesforceSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.
API access is enabled for the Salesforce user. The username, password, and security token are valid for the instance. The user can read every object and field referenced by the SOQL query.

Configure SalesforceSrc as the source of a publisher function to select the SOQL query that Tabsdata runs against Salesforce. publish_accounts.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.salesforce import SalesforceSrc @publisher( source=SalesforceSrc( queries=["SELECT Id, Name FROM Account"], ), output_tables=["accounts"], ) def publish_accounts(accounts: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return accounts queries:list[str]required include_deleted:booloptional initial_last_modified:datetimeoptional api_version:stroptional src_cfg:dictoptional

queries​ A list holding one SOQL query. The list currently takes exactly one entry, and its result maps to the one argument of the publisher function and the one entry in output_tables. include_deleted​ When True, the query also reads deleted rows, through the queryAll endpoint. Defaults to False. initial_last_modified​ A cutoff substituted for any $lastModified token in the query, for example WHERE SystemModStamp > $lastModified, so a run reads only the records changed after it. The cutoff stays the same on every run; the connector does not move it forward. A query that uses $lastModified without initial_last_modified fails with SALESFORCE_11. api_version​ Overrides the Salesforce API version, written <major>.<minor>, for example "60.0". src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. The accepted keys are salesforce.logging_level and tabsdata.src_metadata.drop.

The SalesforceReportSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read Salesforce reports into Tabsdata tables. See the full report walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a SalesforceSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

API access is enabled for the Salesforce user. The user can open every report in reports and read the fields used by its filters. Incremental reads need the last-modified column to be present in the report.

Configure SalesforceReportSrc as the source of a publisher function to select the reports that Tabsdata reads. publish_customers.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.salesforce import SalesforceReportSrc @publisher( source=SalesforceReportSrc( reports=[ "00O000000000001", ], ), output_tables=["customers"], ) def publish_customers(customers: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return customers reports:list[str]required column_name_strategy:"columnName" | "label"optional find_report_by:"id" | "name"optional filter:list[tuple]optional filter_logic:stroptional last_modified_column:stroptional initial_last_modified:datetimeoptional src_cfg:dictoptional

reports​ The reports to read, as report ids (15 or 18 alphanumeric characters) or report names, as a non-empty list. Each element in reports represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function and to an entry in output_tables. column_name_strategy​ "columnName" (the default) names the columns after the report's API column names. "label" uses the display labels. find_report_by​ How an entry of reports is looked up. Unset, an entry that looks like an id is looked up as an id and anything else as a name. "id" or "name" forces one lookup, for an entry that could be either. filter​ A list of (column, operator, value) triples applied on the Salesforce server before the report is downloaded. operator is one of equals, notEqual, lessThan, greaterThan, lessOrEqual, greaterOrEqual, contains, notContain, startsWith, includes or excludes. filter_logic​ A boolean expression over the filter entries, numbered from 1, for example "(1 AND 2) OR 3". last_modified_column and initial_last_modified​ An incremental read: only the rows whose last_modified_column is after initial_last_modified are read. Each of the two requires the other. The cutoff is fixed, so every run filters on the same initial_last_modified value. The condition is added as one more filter, combined with AND onto filter_logic. A naive datetime is read as UTC. If the column is not in the report, the run fails with SALESFORCE_19. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. The accepted keys are salesforce.logging_level and tabsdata.src_metadata.drop.

SalesforceSrc.queries currently takes one SOQL query, which produces the publisher's one source slot. The selected Salesforce fields become columns in that slot. For incremental SOQL reads, include SystemModStamp in the selected fields and compare it with $lastModified. The first run uses initial_last_modified; every run uses initial_last_modified as the cutoff, so the read does not move forward on its own. To read from a later point, change initial_last_modified in the function. Set include_deleted=True when deleted records also need to be returned. Each entry in SalesforceReportSrc.reports produces one source slot. Report ids or names, publisher arguments, and output_tables map by position. Report filters are applied by Salesforce before the rows are downloaded.

SOQL and report publishers use the same SalesforceSrcConn, so both can be registered in one source collection. A report incremental read needs both last_modified_column and initial_last_modified. Without them, the full report is read on each run. A report with more than 2,000 detail rows fails with SALESFORCE_21; it is not truncated. Narrow the report with filter or last_modified_column, or read the data with a SOQL query through SalesforceSrc. Report generation is polled every 5 seconds and fails with SALESFORCE_20 after 600 seconds. HTTP requests time out after 30 seconds to connect and 300 seconds to read. Returning None from the publisher commits a new table version that keeps the previous data. Tabsdata does not contact Salesforce when the collection is created. Login, object, report, field, and API-version errors appear when the function runs.

Salesforce publishers use SalesforceSrcConn to define the Salesforce login used by both connectors. conn-salesforce.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.salesforce:SalesforceSrcConn spec: credentials: kind: salesforceTokenCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.salesforce:SalesforceTokenCredentials spec: username: 'secret:integration@acme.com' password: 'secret:example-password' security_token: 'secret:exampleSecurityToken00' credentials:SalesforceTokenCredentialsrequired instance_url:stroptional category:stroptional objects:list[str]optional entity_whitelist:list[str]optional conn_cfg:dictoptional

A publisher is registered in a source collection, and a source collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type salesforce-sosql-in --file conn-salesforce.yaml Edit the template file with the Salesforce connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-salesforce.yaml tdk collection create --name salesforce_in --conn-file conn-salesforce.yaml Then register the publisher in the collection: tdk fn register --coll salesforce_in --path publish_accounts.py::publish_accounts The collection goes in the sources group, because the connection is a source connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be sources. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: SalesforceSrc or SalesforceReportSrc for a collection created with SalesforceSrcConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name salesforce_in --conn-file conn-salesforce.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project. The template type can be salesforce-sosql-in or salesforce-report-in. Both write the same SalesforceSrcConn, so a collection created from either holds both kinds of publisher.

credentials​ A SalesforceTokenCredentials with the username, password and security_token of the Salesforce user. instance_url​ An explicit instance URL. It must be an https:// URL on a Salesforce domain (salesforce.com, force.com, cloudforce.com or salesforce-setup.com). Accepts secret: too. category and objects​ Hints for entity discovery, used only by the explorer. category has no effect yet. objects is a non-empty list of Salesforce object API names, each 1 to 80 characters, starting with a letter, optionally ending in __c or __r. entity_whitelist​ A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet. Leave it out. conn_cfg​ Optional connector configuration.

Every table destination takes a schema_evolution setting that decides what happens when a write brings a column the destination table does not have, or a value type wider than the column's. The table destinations are Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse, StarRocks, Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle and Db2. The same two values apply to append, replace and merge on all of them, but what each one does differs by destination. Druid cannot enforce a schema, so "update" is its only value and its default.

schema_evolution takes one of two values: Value What it does "strict" Refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column, with error SQL_COMMON_10, before any data is loaded. "update" Adds new columns, widens types and makes columns nullable. It never drops or reorders columns. Under either value, a column the batch lacks is written as NULL on append and keeps its stored value on merge. Renamed in 2.3.0 ClickHouse and StarRocks called update "iceberg" before 2.3.0. A function that still sets schema_evolution="iceberg" fails validation after the upgrade; change it to "update".

What each destination does with a new or wider column, and how it carries out replace: Destination strict append strict replace strict merge update replace mechanism replace atomic Databricks Fails in COPY INTO (DATABRICKS_9) Schema follows the batch Refused before the MERGE (SQL_COMMON_10) Append: mergeSchema and delta.enableTypeWidening. Merge: MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION and widening CREATE OR REPLACE … read_files() LIMIT 0, then COPY INTO No Snowflake Refused before COPY Refused: the schema check runs before the TRUNCATE Refused Append and replace: native ENABLE_SCHEMA_EVOLUTION, adds columns and makes columns nullable. Merge: Iceberg engine, set in dest_cfg; ALTER adds columns and widens VARCHAR length and NUMBER precision TRUNCATE, then COPY INTO; the table definition is kept No BigQuery Fails in the load job (BIGQUERY_7) Schema replaced Refused Append and replace: native, adds columns and relaxes REQUIRED, never widens. Merge: Iceberg engine, set in dest_cfg; ALTER adds and widens, and REQUIRED stays REQUIRED WRITE_TRUNCATE load job Yes ClickHouse Refused before the load on a new column, a wider type whose values do not fit, or a NULL into a non-Nullable column. Column order is ignored, a narrower type fits, a missing column is NULL Schema follows the batch Not supported Adds Nullable columns, makes columns nullable, widens Int8 up to Int64, UInt likewise, and Float32 to Float64 Stage, DROP TABLE IF EXISTS, CREATE … MergeTree() ORDER BY tuple(), INSERT by name No StarRocks Refused before the load on a new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit. A missing column gets its default or NULL Same check, then TRUNCATE and INSERT; the table must exist Not supported ADD COLUMN … NULL; MODIFY COLUMN widens integers, FLOAT to DOUBLE, VARCHAR and DECIMAL, waiting up to 30 minutes for the ALTER job TRUNCATE, then INSERT … SELECT FROM FILES() No Druid Refused at registration Refused at registration Not supported The default and only value: schema discovery adds columns, and a missing column reads as NULL index_parallel with dropExisting over 1970 to 2100 Per datasource Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2 Refused on a new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit (SQL_COMMON_10) Schema follows the batch Not supported ALTER TABLE … ADD; widens integers, decimals and floats by digits or width. Db2 then runs REORG. No drops, and no retyping of non-number columns DROP TABLE IF EXISTS, then the table is created on write Postgres, SQL Server and Db2: inside transactional. MySQL, MariaDB and Oracle: no, and their update ALTERs commit implicitly A write to several tables runs one table after another and is not atomic across tables, except on the relational destinations with transactional=True. The Databricks and BigQuery merge staging tables are real tables named <target>_<8 hex characters>, created next to the target; only Snowflake's is TEMPORARY.

Each destination widens only these types: Destination Widens Snowflake VARCHAR length and NUMBER precision, on merge BigQuery INT64 to BIGNUMERIC to FLOAT64, on merge ClickHouse Integers up to 64 bits, signed and unsigned, and Float32 to Float64 StarRocks Integers, FLOAT to DOUBLE, VARCHAR and DECIMAL Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2 Integers, decimals and floats, by digits or width A change outside these rules fails the write.

Under "update", a destination changes the table in one of two ways. Native schema evolution is the destination's own: the load or merge statement adds the columns. Iceberg schema evolution is applied by the connector: it compares the incoming and destination schemas following Apache Iceberg's evolution rules, and runs the ALTER TABLE statements before the write. It does not convert the destination into an Apache Iceberg table. Destination append and replace merge Databricks Native Native Snowflake, BigQuery Native Iceberg, set in dest_cfg ClickHouse, StarRocks, Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2 Iceberg Not supported Druid Native Not supported Snowflake's and BigQuery's native schema evolution adds columns and makes columns nullable, but never widens a type, and does not apply to MERGE. A Snowflake or BigQuery merge under "update" needs the Iceberg engine set in dest_cfg: dest_cfg={"snowflake.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"} dest_cfg={"bigquery.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"} Without it, the merge is refused at registration. The engine setting is accepted only on a Snowflake or BigQuery merge under "update"; on any other write mode or destination, and under "strict", registration refuses <database>.schema_evolution_engine.

update needs permission to ALTER the destination table. Db2 also runs REORG through ADMIN_CMD after an ALTER, and BigQuery creates and deletes a temporary external table. On the relational destinations, replace drops and recreates the table, so it needs DROP and CREATE. See Merge into SQL destinations for merge, and each destination's page for its other settings.

The Snowflake connector lets Tabsdata write tables into Snowflake. Snowflake is destination-only: there is no publisher-side connector for reading from Snowflake. The SnowflakeDest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Snowflake. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a SnowflakeDestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The Snowflake account is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The configured role can use the warehouse, database, and schema, and can create or write the destination tables. If stage is set, the configured role can use that permanent stage. If it is left out, the connector creates a session-scoped temporary stage.

For merge writes, schema evolution, and retry watermarks, see Merging into SQL destinations. Configure SnowflakeDest as the destination of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in Snowflake. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.snowflake import SnowflakeDest @subscriber( destination=SnowflakeDest( tables=[ "orders", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders tables:list[str]required if_table_exists:stroptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

tables​ Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in Snowflake. Each element in tables represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. Each name is a 1-, 2-, or 3-part name (table, schema.table, or database.schema.table); double-quote a part for a case-sensitive or special-character name. if_table_exists​ "merge" applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key and requires a merge_cfg list. See Merge configuration for a complete example. Controls what happens when the destination table already exists. "append" (the default) adds rows. "replace" issues TRUNCATE before COPY INTO, so the existing schema is preserved. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration. Supported keys include snowflake.logging_level and snowflake.schema_evolution_engine. The engine key is only for a merge under schema_evolution="update", where it must be "iceberg". See Schema evolution.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" adds rows. "replace" truncates before COPY INTO, so the existing table definition stays in place. "merge" applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key and needs merge_cfg.

schema_evolution decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. "strict", the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. "update" changes the table to fit the frame. On Snowflake, the schema evolution "update" uses depends on if_table_exists: if_table_exists "update" uses Changes to the table "append", "replace" Snowflake's native schema evolution, ENABLE_SCHEMA_EVOLUTION Adds columns and makes columns nullable. It never widens a type. "merge" Iceberg schema evolution, applied by the connector through ALTER TABLE. Needs dest_cfg={"snowflake.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"}. Adds columns and widens types. Snowflake's native schema evolution does not apply to MERGE, so a merge under "update" without the iceberg engine is refused at registration. snowflake.schema_evolution_engine is accepted only on a merge under "update": setting it on "append" or "replace", or on a merge under "strict", is also refused at registration. See Schema Evolution for the types each destination widens.

A one-part table name uses the connection's database and schema. Two- and three-part names override one or both defaults. Replace mode truncates the table and keeps its definition. The schema check runs before the truncate, so under schema_evolution="strict" a frame with a new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit, is refused with SQL_COMMON_10 and the table is left as it was. Tabsdata does not connect to Snowflake when the collection is created. Account, role, warehouse, stage, and permission errors appear when the subscriber runs.

Snowflake subscribers use SnowflakeDestConn to define the account, credentials, and default namespace used by the subscriber. conn-snowflake.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.snowflake:SnowflakeDestConn spec: account: 'ABCDEFG-XY12345' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_svc' password: 'secret:CorrectHorseBatteryStaple' account:strrequired credentials:UserPasswordrequired role:stroptional database:stroptional schema:stroptional warehouse:stroptional stage:stroptional conn_cfg:dictoptional

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type snowflake-bulk-out --file conn-snowflake.yaml Edit the template file with the Snowflake connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-snowflake.yaml tdk collection create --name snowflake_out --conn-file conn-snowflake.yaml Then register the subscriber in the collection: tdk fn register --coll snowflake_out --path write_orders.py::write_orders The collection goes in the destinations group, because the connection is a destination connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be destinations. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: SnowflakeDest for a collection created with SnowflakeDestConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name snowflake_out --conn-file conn-snowflake.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

account​ The Snowflake account identifier or locator, such as ABCDEFG-XY12345. credentials​ The Snowflake credentials used to authenticate. UserPassword requires a user and password; a personal access token can be passed as the password. role​ An optional role the connection runs USE for before writing. database​ The default database. Required when schema is set. schema​ The default schema. Requires database to be set. warehouse​ An optional warehouse the connection runs USE WAREHOUSE for. USE WAREHOUSE is only issued when this is set. stage​ An optional permanent stage used for PUT and COPY INTO. When unset, the plugin creates a session-scoped temporary stage instead. conn_cfg​ Optional connector-config overrides, forwarded to snowflake-connector-python.

The StarRocks connector lets Tabsdata Subscribers write data from Tabsdata Tables into StarRocks. The connector stages the data as Parquet files in cloud storage, then loads it into StarRocks through its native FILES() table function. Destination tables in StarRocks must already exist as the connector does not create them automatically. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a StarRocksDestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The StarRocks frontend is reachable from the Tabsdata server. Every destination table already exists. The connector cannot infer its key model or distribution strategy. Tabsdata can write to the staging location and StarRocks can read the staged Parquet files. The StarRocks user can insert into the destination tables and truncate them when replace mode is used.

Configure StarRocksDest as the destination of a Subscriber Function. Each returned frame maps to one entry in tables, in order. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.starrocks import StarRocksDest @subscriber( destination=StarRocksDest( tables=[ "orders", ], ), input_tables=["sales/orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders tables:list[str]required if_table_exists:stroptional schema_evolution:stroptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

tables​ Names of existing StarRocks tables, one per returned frame. A table cannot be listed twice. Names can be table or database.table; an unqualified name uses the Connection's database. Backtick-quote individual name parts containing special characters. Create the destination tables before running the Subscriber. StarRocks table creation requires a physical layout, including a key definition and distribution strategy, that the connector cannot infer from a frame. if_table_exists​ "append" (the default) inserts rows into the existing table. "replace" truncates the existing table and then inserts the returned rows. Neither mode creates a missing table. schema_evolution​ "strict" (the default) refuses a write that adds a column, or brings a wider type whose values do not fit the column, with SQL_COMMON_10, before anything is loaded; a column the frame lacks gets its default or NULL. "update" adds nullable columns and widens integers, FLOAT to DOUBLE, VARCHAR and DECIMAL, waiting up to 30 minutes for the ALTER job to finish. Before 2.3.0 "update" was called "iceberg", which now fails validation. See Schema Evolution. dest_cfg​ Optional destination configuration. The supported key is starrocks.logging_level. StarRocks always uses Iceberg schema evolution, so starrocks.schema_evolution_engine is refused at registration.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the Subscriber Function. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" inserts rows into the existing table. "replace" truncates it first. Neither mode creates a missing table. schema_evolution="strict" refuses a new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit, before the load, on "replace" too, where the check runs before the truncate. Writes are not atomic: a failed "replace" can leave the table empty, and tables load one after another. "update" applies supported changes to the table.

schema_evolution decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. "strict", the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. "update" changes the table to fit the frame. On StarRocks, "update" uses Iceberg schema evolution, applied by the connector, on "append" and "replace": ADD COLUMN … NULL adds columns, and MODIFY COLUMN widens integers, FLOAT to DOUBLE, VARCHAR and DECIMAL, waiting up to 30 minutes for the ALTER job. "merge" is not supported.

Writes are staged as Parquet, then loaded through StarRocks FILES(). The staged files are deleted after each table's load, whether it succeeded or failed, so the staging credentials need delete permission. S3 and Azure staging use one credential set. GCS needs service-account JSON for the upload and HMAC credentials for StarRocks's S3-compatible read. Tabsdata does not contact StarRocks or the staging service when the collection is created. Those checks happen when the subscriber runs.

StarRocksDestConn defines the StarRocks frontend address, database credentials, and cloud staging location. Register the Connection on the Collection where the Subscriber runs. conn-starrocks.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.starrocks:StarRocksDestConn spec: host: 'starrocks-fe.internal' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_writer' password: 'secret:example-password' staging: kind: starRocksS3Location apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.starrocks:S3Location spec: bucket: 'acme-staging' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:example-access-key' secret_access_key: 'secret:example-secret-key' base_path: '/starrocks' host:strrequired port:stroptional database:stroptional credentials:UserPasswordrequired staging:CloudLocationrequired entity_whitelist:list[str]optional conn_cfg:dictoptional

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type starrocks-bulk-out --file conn-starrocks.yaml Edit the template file with the StarRocks connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-starrocks.yaml tdk collection create --name starrocks_out --conn-file conn-starrocks.yaml Then register the subscriber in the collection: tdk fn register --coll starrocks_out --path write_orders.py::write_orders The collection goes in the destinations group, because the connection is a destination connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be destinations. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: StarRocksDest for a collection created with StarRocksDestConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name starrocks_out --conn-file conn-starrocks.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

host, port, and database​ host identifies the StarRocks frontend. port is the MySQL-protocol port, from 1 to 65535, and defaults to "9030". database defaults to "default" and supplies the database for unqualified destination table names. These fields accept strings or secret references. credentials​ A UserPassword containing the StarRocks username and password. Cloud storage credentials are configured separately under staging. staging​ Use one of the location classes from tabsdatak.conn.starrocks: Location Required fields Credentials S3Location bucket, region, credentials AwsAccessSecretKey AzBlobLocation container, credentials AzureAccountKey GCSLocation bucket, credentials, hmac_credentials GCPJson for uploads and GCPHmac for StarRocks reads Tabsdata must be able to upload the staged files, and StarRocks must be able to read them. For GCS, both credential types are required: uploads use the native GCS API, while StarRocks reads through the S3-compatible endpoint. Each location accepts base_path, which defaults to /, and an optional cfg dictionary for storage-client configuration. The keys are listed in Object Store Options. A non-root base_path starts with /, has no trailing /, and contains no empty path segments. entity_whitelist​ A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet. Leave it out. conn_cfg​ Optional connector configuration overrides.

A custom connector is a Python package that defines how Tabsdata connects to an external system. It contains the configuration classes and the code needed to read from or write to that system. Once installed, the connector becomes available as a Publisher source, Subscriber destination, or both. Coding agents working with Tabsdata through tdk can also create custom connectors.

This guide builds a SQLite connector as an example. Create a directory named sqlite_connector with the following files. The Python package lives in src/tabsdata_sqlite. ⌄sqlite_connector pyproject.toml ⌄src ⌄tabsdata_sqlite error.py __init__.py _plugin.py pyproject.toml defines the package, dependencies, and entry points Tabsdata uses to discover the connector. error.py defines errors for invalid configuration and failed reads or writes. __init__.py defines the connection and function configuration classes users import. _plugin.py implements the read and write logic and registers the connector with Tabsdata. Download the complete connector directory using the button beside sqlite_connector, or copy the files below. The highlighted lines are the main parts you would change when adapting this example to another system.

Step 1Define the package and entry points pyproject.toml defines the package metadata, Python dependencies, and entry points Tabsdata uses to load the connector. When adapting this file: Set the package name, version, and description. Add any Python packages the connector needs to dependencies. Define one entry point for each source or destination the package provides. pyproject.toml [build-system] requires = ["setuptools>=69"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [project] name = "tabsdata-conn-sqlite" version = "0.1.0" description = "Tabsdata source and destination connector for SQLite databases." requires-python = ">=3.12" dependencies = [ "tabsdata>=2.1,<2.2", ] [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] [project.entry-points."tabsdatak.connectors"] src_sqlite = "tabsdata_sqlite._plugin:SQLITE_SRC" dest_sqlite = "tabsdata_sqlite._plugin:SQLITE_DEST"

Step 2Define connector errors SqliteRuntimeException extends ConnException for errors that happen while reading or writing data. SqliteErrorCode defines the errors the connector can raise and maps each one to an exception type and message. SQLITE_1 through SQLITE_4 are used when validating the configuration classes in __init__.py. The plugins use: SQLITE_5 when a query fails. SQLITE_6 when the number of returned tables does not match the configured destination tables. SQLITE_7 when a write fails. Message placeholders such as {table} are filled when .exception() is called. error.py from tabsdatak.conn.common.error import ConnException, ConnInitException from tabsdatak.error import ErrorCode, ErrorDef class SqliteRuntimeException(ConnException): """A SQLite read or write failed.""" class SqliteErrorCode(ErrorCode): SQLITE_1 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteSrcConn validation failed") SQLITE_2 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteDestConn validation failed") SQLITE_3 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteSrc validation failed") SQLITE_4 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteDest validation failed") SQLITE_5 = ErrorDef(SqliteRuntimeException, "SQLite query {index} failed") SQLITE_6 = ErrorDef( SqliteRuntimeException, "SQLite received {slots} table(s) for {tables} target table(s)", ) SQLITE_7 = ErrorDef(SqliteRuntimeException, "SQLite write to {table} failed")

Step 3Define connection and function settings __init__.py defines the classes users import from tabsdata_sqlite. StrOrSecretSpec allows a field to accept either a plain string or a Tabsdata secret. The resolve helper returns the underlying value. TableName restricts SQLite table names to letters, numbers, and underscores, with the first character limited to a letter or underscore. SqliteSrcConn and SqliteDestConn define the database path stored in the Collection's connection document. Both extend Conn and require a path field. In the connection document, that value appears as spec.path. SqliteSrc defines the queries a Publisher should run. SqliteDest defines the tables a Subscriber should write to and whether existing tables should be replaced or appended to. The order matters: Query results are returned in the same order as queries. Subscriber results are written in the same order as tables. if_table_exists accepts "append" or "replace" and defaults to "replace". The @_api.dataclass decorator validates each class using the provided error code. kw_only=True requires named arguments, such as SqliteSrcConn(path="/data/shop.db"). __init__.py from typing import Annotated, Literal from pydantic import StringConstraints import tabsdatak._api as _api from tabsdatak.api import Dest, Secret, Src, StrOrSecretSpec from tabsdatak.spi import Conn from tabsdata_sqlite.error import SqliteErrorCode TableName = Annotated[str, StringConstraints(pattern=r"^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$")] def resolve(spec: StrOrSecretSpec) -> str: return spec.value() if isinstance(spec, Secret) else spec @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_1, kw_only=True) class SqliteSrcConn(Conn): """Connection to the SQLite database a publisher reads.""" path: StrOrSecretSpec @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_2, kw_only=True) class SqliteDestConn(Conn): """Connection to the SQLite database a subscriber writes.""" path: StrOrSecretSpec @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_3, kw_only=True) class SqliteSrc(Src): """Queries a publisher runs against SQLite.""" queries: list[str] @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_4, kw_only=True) class SqliteDest(Dest): """SQLite tables that receive a subscriber's returned data.""" tables: list[TableName] if_table_exists: Literal["append", "replace"] = "replace" The connection defines where Tabsdata connects. The Publisher or Subscriber defines what to read or write. During execution, Tabsdata passes both objects to the connector plugin. __init__.py · Connection class SqliteSrcConn(Conn): path: StrOrSecretSpec → conn-sqlite-in.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdata_sqlite:SqliteSrcConn spec: path: str:/data/shop.db __init__.py · Source class SqliteSrc(Src): queries: list[str] → pub_shop.py source=SqliteSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM customers", "SELECT * FROM orders", ], )

Step 4Implement and register the reads and writes _plugin.py contains the connector's runtime logic. The plugins receive the connection and function settings defined in __init__.py. The shared connect helper resolves the configured database path and opens the SQLite connection. SqliteSrcPlugin.read_in: Runs each query from the Publisher configuration. Wraps each query result as a polars LazyFrame. Returns the frames as LazyFrameInputs with to_lazy_frame_inputs, in the same order as src.queries. Each result is wrapped in its own inner list because the connector uses TableMode.SINGLE. If a query fails, the plugin raises SQLITE_5 with the query index and original exception. SqliteDestPlugin.write_out: Checks that the number of returned table slots matches dest.tables. Matches each returned file to the destination table in the same position. Skips any None file reference. Reads each remaining Parquet file. Replaces or appends to the destination table based on dest.if_table_exists. The explicit BEGIN keeps table creation, replacement, and inserts in the same transaction. If a write fails, those changes are rolled back together. note The database path is resolved on the machine running the Function. If Functions run on separate workers, the SQLite file must also be accessible from those workers. SQLITE_SRC and SQLITE_DEST register the connection classes, function settings, and plugin implementations with Tabsdata. Their names must match the entry points defined in pyproject.toml. _plugin.py import sqlite3 from collections.abc import Iterable import polars as pl from tabsdatak.spi import ( DestContext, DestDef, DestPlugin, LazyFrameInput, SrcDef, SrcPlugin, SrcPluginCtx, TableFileSpec, TableMode, to_lazy_frame_inputs, ) from tabsdata_sqlite import ( SqliteDest, SqliteDestConn, SqliteSrc, SqliteSrcConn, resolve, ) from tabsdata_sqlite.error import SqliteErrorCode def connect(conn: SqliteSrcConn | SqliteDestConn) -> sqlite3.Connection: return sqlite3.connect(resolve(conn.path)) class SqliteSrcPlugin(SrcPlugin[SqliteSrcConn, SqliteSrc]): def read_in( self, ctx: SrcPluginCtx, conn: SqliteSrcConn, src: SqliteSrc, ) -> list[Iterable[LazyFrameInput]]: con = connect(conn) try: frames = [] for index, query in enumerate(src.queries): try: frame = pl.read_database(query, con) except Exception as e: raise SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_5.exception(cause=e, index=index) frames.append([frame.lazy()]) return to_lazy_frame_inputs(frames) finally: con.close() class SqliteDestPlugin(DestPlugin[SqliteDestConn, SqliteDest]): def write_out( self, ctx: DestContext, conn: SqliteDestConn, dest: SqliteDest, tables: list[TableFileSpec], ) -> None: if len(tables) != len(dest.tables): raise SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_6.exception( slots=len(tables), tables=len(dest.tables) ) con = connect(conn) try: with con: con.execute("BEGIN") for table, parquet in zip(dest.tables, tables): if parquet is None: continue try: frame = pl.read_parquet(parquet) columns = ", ".join( '"' + c.replace('"', '""') + '"' for c in frame.columns ) if dest.if_table_exists == "replace": con.execute(f'DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "{table}"') con.execute( f'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "{table}" ({columns})' ) marks = ", ".join("?" for _ in frame.columns) con.executemany( f'INSERT INTO "{table}" ({columns}) VALUES ({marks})', frame.iter_rows(), ) except Exception as e: raise SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_7.exception(cause=e, table=table) finally: con.close() SQLITE_SRC = SrcDef( conn=SqliteSrcConn, type_="sqlite-sql-in", system="SQLite", src_version="v1", src=SqliteSrc, table_mode=TableMode.SINGLE, cardinality=lambda src: len(src.queries), plugin=SqliteSrcPlugin, explorer=None, icon=None, ) SQLITE_DEST = DestDef( conn=SqliteDestConn, type_="sqlite-sql-out", system="SQLite", dest_version="v1", dest=SqliteDest, cardinality=lambda dest: len(dest.tables), plugin=SqliteDestPlugin, explorer=None, icon=None, ) type_ is the connector's registration identifier and must be unique across installed connectors. It is different from the type field in a connection document. The connection document's type identifies the Python connection class to instantiate. cardinality tells Tabsdata how many results the source or destination expects. For the source, TableMode.SINGLE means each query result contains one file. This connector does not provide an explorer or icon, so both are set to None.

The connector package must be installed in two places: Wherever tdk runs, so Tabsdata can validate connections and register Functions. In the server's Function environment, so the connector is available when those Functions execute. Step 5aInstall the package where tdk runs From the directory that contains sqlite_connector, run: pip install ./sqlite_connector Step 5bInstall the package in the server's function environment Make the package available to the server, such as through a Git repository. Replace <org> and <repo> with the repository that contains sqlite_connector, then add the package to a requirements file: connectors.txt tabsdata-conn-sqlite @ git+https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git#subdirectory=sqlite_connector Update the Function environment, then restart the instance. Updating the environment stops the instance. tdkserver venv update --name fn --requirements connectors.txt tdkserver start The requirements file replaces the environment's current list of complementary packages. Include every complementary package the server still needs.

Step 6aCreate the connections and attach them to Collections Create connection documents for the source and destination. The type field selects one of the connection classes defined in the connection classes. spec.path provides the required path value. The str: prefix marks it as a literal string. conn-sqlite-in.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdata_sqlite:SqliteSrcConn spec: path: str:/data/shop.db conn-sqlite-out.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdata_sqlite:SqliteDestConn spec: path: str:/data/warehouse.db The source database must already contain the customers and orders tables used by the Publisher. The destination database is created the first time SQLite opens it if it does not already exist. Its parent directory must already exist and be writable. Attach the source connection to a shop Collection in the sources group and the destination connection to a warehouse Collection in the destinations group: tdk collection create --name shop --group sources --conn-file conn-sqlite-in.yaml tdk collection create --name warehouse --group destinations --conn-file conn-sqlite-out.yaml Step 6bUse the source in a Publisher Create pub_shop.py. Set queries on SqliteSrc, which is the source field defined in the function settings. Before pub_shop runs, the source plugin executes both queries and passes their results into the Function. The Function returns those results as the customers and orders Tabsdata tables. pub_shop.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdata_sqlite import SqliteSrc @publisher( source=SqliteSrc(queries=["SELECT * FROM customers", "SELECT * FROM orders"]), output_tables=["customers", "orders"], ) def pub_shop( customers: TableFrameSpec, orders: TableFrameSpec ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return customers, orders Register the Publisher in the shop Collection. It automatically uses the source connection attached to that Collection. tdk fn register --coll shop --path pub_shop.py::pub_shop Step 6cUse the destination in a Subscriber Create sub_warehouse.py. Set tables and if_table_exists on SqliteDest, which are the destination fields defined in the function settings. The Subscriber reads shop/customers and shop/orders, then returns those tables to the destination plugin. Use "replace" to drop and recreate each configured SQLite table on every write. Use "append" to keep the existing rows and add the returned rows. sub_warehouse.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec from tabsdata_sqlite import SqliteDest @subscriber( destination=SqliteDest(tables=["customers", "orders"], if_table_exists="replace"), input_tables=["shop/customers", "shop/orders"], ) def sub_warehouse( customers: TableFrameSpec, orders: TableFrameSpec ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return customers, orders Register the Subscriber in the warehouse Collection. It automatically uses the destination connection attached to that Collection. tdk fn register --coll warehouse --path sub_warehouse.py::sub_warehouse

Data quality checks validate the rows of a Table as a Function writes it. A check is a DataQuality object passed to a Publisher or Transformer through the on_tables argument of its decorator. After the Function succeeds, Tabsdata runs the check against the named output Table, where it can label rows, remove or copy rows that fail, write a summary, or fail the Transaction.
