Data quality checks are available on @publisher, @stream_publisher, and @transformer. @subscriber does not take on_tables. from tabsdatak.api import transformer, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.dataquality import ( AnyFailed, DataQuality, Filter, IsBetween, IsIn, IsNotNull, Summary, ) # transformer that dedupes the raw orders, with a data quality check that moves # rows failing any rule to orders_rejected and writes a summary of the verdicts @transformer( input_tables=["raw_orders"], output_tables=["orders"], on_tables=[ DataQuality( table="orders", classifiers=[ IsNotNull(["order_id"]), IsBetween(["amount"], min_val=0, max_val=10000), IsIn(["status"], values={"open", "shipped", "cancelled"}), ], operators=[ Filter(AnyFailed(), to_table="orders_rejected", include_quality_columns="criteria"), Summary(), ], ), ], ) def clean_orders(raw_orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return raw_orders.unique() A DataQuality check has three parts: table: the output Table the check runs on classifiers: the rules that label each row, at least one operators: what to do with the labels, at least one

A classifier evaluates one or more columns and writes a verdict for each row into a new verdict column. Classifiers fall into two kinds: boolean classifiers decide whether each value passes a rule, and categorizers assign each value to a bin.

Checks Classifiers Null and NaN IsNull, IsNotNull, IsNan, IsNotNan, IsNullOrNan, IsNotNullNorNan Sign of a number IsPositive, IsNegative, IsZero, IsNotZero, IsPositiveOrZero, IsNegativeOrZero Booleans IsTrue, IsFalse Ranges IsBetween, IsNotBetween Sets of values IsIn, IsNotIn Text Matches, DoesNotMatch, HasLength from tabsdatak.dataquality import HasLength, IsBetween, IsIn, IsNotNull, Matches IsNotNull(["order_id", "customer_id"]) IsBetween(["amount"], min_val=0, max_val=10000, closed_on="both") IsIn(["status"], values={"open", "shipped", "cancelled"}) Matches(["email"], pattern=r"^[^@]+@[^@]+$") HasLength(["country_code"], min_len=2, max_len=2) Classifiers share these settings: column_names: the columns to classify. Each entry is a column name, or a (column, verdict_column) tuple that names the verdict column. When omitted, the classifier applies to every user column. on_missing_column: "ignore" (the default) skips a named column that is not in the Table, and "fail" fails the check. on_wrong_type: "ignore" (the default) skips a column whose data type the classifier does not support, and "fail" fails the check. on_wrong_value: "ignore" (the default) gives a null verdict for a value that cannot be evaluated, and "fail" fails the check. tags: labels that scope operators to this classifier. prefix: text added to the start of every verdict column name. Defaults to @td.dq., and "" adds no prefix.

ScaleCategorizer assigns each numeric value to a bin of a scale. The verdict column holds the bin number, or a reserved value for a null, a NaN, or a value below or above the scale. Scale Bin edges LinearScale Equal-width bins LogarithmicScale Spaced logarithmically ExponentialScale Spaced exponentially MonomialScale Bin widths that grow as a power law IdentityScale One bin per integer from tabsdatak.dataquality import InBins, LinearScale, ScaleCategorizer, Select # splits amount into five equal-width bins between 0 and 10000 ScaleCategorizer([("amount", "amount_bin")], scale=LinearScale(0.0, 10000.0, bins=5), prefix="") # copies orders in the top bin, or above the scale, to large_orders Select(InBins(column_name="amount_bin", bins={5, "overflow"}), to_table="large_orders") Bins are numbered from 1. A scale created with use_bin_zero=True gives its minimum value a bin 0 of its own.

Criteria select the rows that the Filter, Select, and Fail operators act on. Criteria Selects rows where AllOk() Every boolean classifier passes AnyFailed() At least one boolean classifier fails InBins(column_name, bins) A categorizer's bin is one of bins NotInBins(column_name, bins) A categorizer's bin is not one of bins AllOk and AnyFailed treat a null or NaN verdict as a failure, unless none_is_ok=True or nan_is_ok=True is set. InBins and NotInBins accept bin numbers from 0 to 100 and the special bins "none", "nan", "underflow", and "overflow".

Operator Effect Enrich() Adds each classifier's verdict column to the Table, or to to_table. No rows are removed. Summary() Writes a summary with one row per classifier, holding its verdict counts or bin counts, to a Table named <table>_dq_summary, or to table. Filter(criteria) Removes the selected rows. They are discarded, or written to to_table. Select(criteria, to_table) Copies the selected rows to to_table, leaving the Table unchanged. Fail(criteria, threshold) Fails the Transaction when the number of selected rows reaches the threshold. Filter and Select take include_quality_columns to choose which verdict columns are carried into to_table: "none" (the default), "criteria", or "all". The checked Table never carries them.

Fail takes a threshold of rows, as a count or as a percentage of the Table: from tabsdatak.dataquality import AnyFailed, Fail, PercentThreshold, RowCountThreshold # fails as soon as one row fails a rule Fail(criteria=AnyFailed(), threshold=RowCountThreshold(1)) # fails when a twentieth of the table fails a rule Fail(criteria=AnyFailed(), threshold=PercentThreshold(5)) A failed Transaction commits none of its Tables.

Tags scope an operator to some of a check's classifiers. An operator with tags applies only to the classifiers that carry a matching tag, and an operator without tags applies to all of them. from tabsdatak.dataquality import ( AnyFailed, DataQuality, Fail, Filter, IsNotNull, Matches, RowCountThreshold, ) DataQuality( table="customers", classifiers=[ IsNotNull(["customer_id"], tags=["critical"]), Matches(["email"], pattern=r"^[^@]+@[^@]+$", tags=["cleanup"]), ], operators=[ # fails the transaction on a missing key Fail(criteria=AnyFailed(tags=["critical"]), threshold=RowCountThreshold(1)), # moves rows with a malformed email aside without failing Filter(AnyFailed(tags=["cleanup"]), to_table="customers_bad_email"), ], )

A Summary records how a Table's data quality looked in one Transaction. Trends keep that history: every time the check runs, its summary is folded into a trend Table that holds the recent runs one by one, plus weekly and monthly totals that reach further back. Reading the trend Table shows whether a rule fails more or less often over time, without keeping every version of the summary. Trends are off by default. Turn them on by passing Trends() to the trends argument of Summary: from tabsdatak.api import transformer, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.dataquality import ( DataQuality, IsBetween, IsIn, IsNotNull, Summary, Trends, ) @transformer( input_tables=["raw_orders"], output_tables=["orders"], on_tables=[ DataQuality( table="orders", classifiers=[ IsNotNull(["order_id"]), IsBetween(["amount"], min_val=0, max_val=10000), IsIn(["status"], values={"open", "shipped", "cancelled"}), ], operators=[Summary(trends=Trends())], ), ], ) def clean_orders(raw_orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return raw_orders.unique() Each run of clean_orders writes orders_dq_summary as before, and Tabsdata then folds that summary into orders_dq_summary_trends. The classifiers run while the data is written, in the same execution of the Function. Tabsdata does not read the Table again afterwards to compute the summary or the trend, so there is no separate quality job and no second pass over the data. The summary and trend Tables are Tabsdata Tables, versioned like any other. Every execution creates a new version of both, so the summary and the trend of any past execution can be read as they were at that point. See Data Quality for the classifiers and operators a check is built from.

The Tabsdata UI recognizes data quality Tables and shows them without any setup. A Table that has data quality checks is marked with a Q next to its name, in the Table list and in the execution plan graph. The data quality summary of the leads Table for one execution, opened from the execution plan graph: 100 rows checked, 10 checks, grouped by column. Each check shows its pass rate and how many rows failed or were null, and the lowest pass rate is called out at the top. The Data Quality Trends tab of the leads Table, with its trend chart expanded: the pass rate of every classifier, execution by execution. Hovering over an execution shows all the pass rates at that point. A Table's data quality shows in two places: The Table's page. A Table with a summary has a Data Quality Summaries tab, and a Table with a trend has a Data Quality Trends tab. Each tab lists the Table's summary or trend Tables; select one to chart it. The execution plan graph. Right-click a Table and open Data Quality > Data Quality Summary or Data Quality Trend to see the summary or trend as it was written by that execution. The trend chart, titled Pass rate by classifier, plots pass_pct for every classifier: Runs, Weeks, and Months switch between the run, week, and month rows of the trend Table. Buckets are in UTC, and weeks start on Monday. The legend button shows or hides individual classifiers, and the expand button opens a larger chart. On the Data Quality Trends tab, a trend Table can be pinned, so that its chart stays on the board while other trend Tables are selected.
documents.s: Data quality in the Tabsdata UI

documents.t: Trends configures the trend Table: its name and how long each tier keeps its rows. from tabsdatak.dataquality import Summary, Trends Summary(trends=Trends()) Summary(trends=Trends(table="orders_quality_history", days=14, weeks=26, months=36)) Summary(trends=Trends(days=7, weeks=13, months=0)) The first keeps the default retention, the second names the Table and keeps longer history, and the third keeps no month tier.

table​ The Table the trend is written to, as a valid table name. Defaults to None, which writes to <target>_dq_summary_trends, where <target> is the Table the DataQuality check runs on. The default name does not follow Summary(table=...): a summary written to orders_quality still gets its trend in orders_dq_summary_trends unless table is set. A name given here is used as is, with no suffix added. The trend Table is created in the same collection as the Function. days​ How many days a run is kept as its own row, as a non-negative integer. Defaults to 7. A run counts towards its week and month from its first execution, so expiring its run row does not remove it from the coarser tiers. 0 keeps no run rows. weeks​ How many weeks a week row is kept, counted from the Monday that starts it, as a non-negative integer. Defaults to 12, which keeps the current week and the 11 before it. 0 keeps no week rows. months​ How many months a month row is kept, counted from the 1st of the month, as a non-negative integer. Defaults to 24, which keeps the current month and the 23 before it. 0 keeps no month rows. At least one of days, weeks, and months must be greater than zero. To keep no trend, leave trends unset.

The trend Table holds four kinds of rows, told apart by the grain column: grain One row per bucket holds run classifier and run The time of the run week classifier and week Monday 00:00 UTC of the week month classifier and month The 1st of the month, 00:00 UTC folded Transaction already counted The time of the run The tiers overlap. A run is added to its week and its month as soon as it happens, not when its run row expires, so the current week row already includes the runs that are still listed one by one, and a month row includes every run of that month. Each tier expires on its own: a week that falls out of the weeks window is still counted in its month row. Weeks and months are bucketed independently, so a week that crosses into a new month is one week row while its runs count towards two month rows. Adding week rows together does not give a month row.

Retention is measured against the newest run folded into the Table, not against the wall clock. With the defaults, after a run on a given day the Table holds: a run row for each run in the 7 days before it a week row for that week and each of the 11 weeks before it a month row for that month and each of the 23 months before it Rows only expire when the trend is updated, so a Table whose check stops running keeps its last rows as they were.

Each folded row records one Transaction whose results the week and month rows already include. It carries the Transaction ID and the time of the run, and no counts. When a summary arrives for a Transaction that has a folded row, for example because the Transaction was recovered, it is not counted a second time. Summaries that arrive out of order are still counted once each. A folded row is kept for as long as the week or month tier could still be holding that run. When both weeks and months are 0, no folded rows are kept.

Column Type Description grain string run, week, month, or folded. bucket datetime (UTC) The run time for run and folded rows, the Monday that starts the week for week rows, and the 1st of the month for month rows. classifier string The verdict column the counts belong to, as in the summary, for example @td.dq.order_id_is_not_null or the name given in a (column, verdict_column) tuple with its prefix. Null on folded rows. runs int64 1 on a run row; the number of runs in the bucket on week and month rows. Null on folded rows. passed int64 Rows that passed the classifier. failed int64 Rows that failed the classifier. nulls int64 Rows with a null verdict. nans int64 Rows with a NaN verdict. pass_pct float64 passed * 100 / (passed + failed). Null and NaN verdicts are left out. Null when passed + failed is 0, and on folded rows. txn string The Transaction ID on run and folded rows. Null on week and month rows. folded_through datetime (UTC) The time of the newest run folded so far. Every row of a version holds the same value. On week and month rows, passed, failed, nulls, and nans are summed over the runs in the bucket, so pass_pct is the share of passing rows across the whole bucket, not an average of the runs' percentages. Like every Tabsdata Table, the trend Table also carries the $td. system columns. Only boolean classifiers are tracked. ScaleCategorizer results appear in the summary but not in the trend Table, and a summary with only categorizers adds no rows to its trend Table. Tags on Summary apply as usual: the trend tracks the classifiers the summary includes.

Registering a Function that declares Summary(trends=Trends(...)) also registers a second Function, the trend Function. The trend Function: is named after the trend Table with _trend appended, for example orders_dq_summary_trends_trend reads the latest summary and the latest version of the trend Table, and writes a new version of the trend Table runs in the same execution as the parent Function, after the summary is written is registered even in a collection that does not otherwise accept transformers Each run writes a new version of the whole trend Table: the previous version is read back, the new summary is merged in, and the rows that fell out of their tier's window are dropped. Earlier versions of the trend Table stay available like any other Table's. The trend Table is linked to the Table the check runs on, not to the summary, and its data versions report that Table as their parent.
documents.s: How the trend Table is maintained

documents.t: The trend Function belongs to the Function that declares the Summary, its parent, and follows it: Updating the parent Function with the same declaration keeps the same trend Function. Changing days, weeks, or months keeps its name. Renaming the trend Table, through table, replaces the trend Function with one named after the new Table. Adding trends to an existing Summary registers a trend Function on the next update. Removing trends, or the whole DataQuality check, deletes the trend Function. The trend Table is kept, frozen, with its history. Deleting the parent Function deletes the trend Function, and leaves their Tables frozen. Registering the parent Function again with tdk fn register --reuse-tables takes the frozen Tables back, history included. Disabling or enabling the parent Function does the same to the trend Function. Moving the check to another Table of the same Function keeps the summary and trend Tables and links them to the new Table. No longer producing the Table the check runs on freezes that Table, its summary, and its trend Table. Deleting the frozen Table also deletes the summary and trend Tables derived from it. The trend Function cannot be managed directly. Updating, patching, deleting, enabling, disabling, or triggering it by name is refused with: Function '<name>' is a child function managed by its parent; it cannot be updated, patched, deleted, enabled or triggered directly Make the change on the parent Function instead.

A sales operations team publishes the Salesforce Lead Lifetime report once a week and wants to know which data entry problems are getting better. The publisher checks every run and keeps a trend: from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, publisher from tabsdatak.conn.salesforce import SalesforceReportSrc from tabsdatak.dataquality import ( DataQuality, HasLength, IsBetween, IsIn, IsNotIn, IsNotNull, IsPositive, Matches, Summary, Trends, ) @publisher( source=SalesforceReportSrc(reports=["Lead Lifetime Report"], find_report_by="name"), output_tables=["leads"], on_tables=[ DataQuality( table="leads", classifiers=[ IsNotNull([("EMAIL", "email_present")]), Matches([("EMAIL", "email_valid")], pattern=r"^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}$"), IsNotNull([("LEAD_SOURCE", "lead_source_present")]), IsNotIn([("COMPANY", "company_provided")], values={"[not provided]", "N/A", "Unknown"}), IsIn([("RATING", "rating_valid")], values={"Hot", "Warm", "Cold"}), IsBetween([("EMPLOYEES", "employees_in_range")], min_val=1, max_val=10_000), HasLength([("LAST_NAME", "last_name_valid")], min_len=2, max_len=80), IsPositive([("ANNUAL_REVENUE", "revenue_positive")]), ], operators=[Summary(trends=Trends(days=35))], ) ], ) def leads_report(leads: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return leads The report runs once a week, so with the default days=7 only the latest run would keep a row of its own. days=35 keeps the last five runs individually. The trend lands in leads_dq_summary_trends, with one classifier per verdict column: @td.dq.email_present, @td.dq.email_valid, and so on. After a few weeks, the trend separates the problems that are being fixed, such as missing emails once the web form makes the field required, from those that hold steady and those that come and go with list imports. For example, the month row for August 2026 might read: grain bucket classifier runs passed failed pass_pct month 2026-08-01 00:00:00 UTC @td.dq.email_present 4 362 38 90.5
documents.s: Tracking a source report run by run

documents.t: Use tdk table data with --sql to look at one tier: tdk table data --coll sales --name leads_dq_summary_trends --sql "SELECT bucket, classifier, runs, failed, pass_pct FROM leads_dq_summary_trends WHERE grain = 'week' ORDER BY classifier, bucket" --print folded_through shows which run the trend has caught up to. The trend Function commits in the same Transaction as the summary, so a committed summary version always has its trend version next to it.

A transformer can take the trend Table as an input like any other Table, for example to publish a weekly quality scorecard for a dashboard: from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["sales/leads_dq_summary_trends"], output_tables=["leads_weekly_quality"], ) def leads_weekly_quality(trends: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return trends.filter(col("grain") == "week").select( "bucket", "classifier", "runs", "passed", "failed", "pass_pct" ) Each new version of the trend Table triggers the transformer, so the scorecard is refreshed after every run of the report.

A pipeline that runs every few minutes produces many run rows. Keeping a day of runs and a quarter of weeks, with no month tier, bounds the Table's size: from tabsdatak.dataquality import Summary, Trends Summary(trends=Trends(days=1, weeks=13, months=0))

Trends are only maintained for boolean classifiers. Categorizer results stay in the summary Table. Retention values are whole numbers of days, weeks, or months, 0 or greater. A negative value, a float, a string, or a boolean is refused with error DQC_32, as is an invalid table name. Setting days, weeks, and months all to 0 is refused with error DQC_33. Leave trends unset to keep no trend. Every Table a check produces must have a unique name, and that includes trend Tables. Two Summary operators with trends on the same check need different table names for their trends, or registration fails with error DQPE_4. Week and month buckets are always in UTC; weeks start on Monday and months on the 1st. There is no option to bucket in another time zone. A tier that was disabled and is later enabled starts from the runs that follow; it is not filled in from older run rows. The trend Function is managed through the Function that declares the Summary. It cannot be triggered, updated, or deleted on its own.

A trigger decides when a Function runs. There are four kinds of triggers: Manually When you run it When a function is executed through the tdk fn trigger CLI Command or through the trigger button in the Tabsdata UI On a schedule At set times When a function is executed on a CRON schedule On new data When an input Table receives new data Execute the Function whenever an input Table receives a new Version. On a stream batch When a batch of streamed data is due Execute the Function each time a stream worker, such as SQL CDC or Kafka, hands over a batch

No matter which trigger fires a function, Tabsdata doesn't run just that one function. It follows the data dependencies and builds an execution plan: the graph of every function that must run as a result, in the correct order, across collections. There is no orchestration for you to wire up.
Every table in an execution plan stays in sync, because new data is only committed if every function in the plan succeeds. A partial failure commits nothing.

A normal publisher pulls a batch of data each time it runs. A streaming publisher stays running continuously, creating new table versions as data arrives: for change-data-capture feeds, log tails, and message queues like Kafka.

An execution plan is the Directed Acyclic Graph that Tabsdata automatically builds and executes whenever a function is triggered. Tabsdata Functions are self describing, allowing Tabsdata to infer a Function's dependencies and automatically fire it when needed.

In other systems, DAG nodes need to be manually wired together, with explicit declaration of what data one node passes to the other. In Tabsdata, Functions never directly pass data to other Functions. Instead, Functions write tabular data into Tables and other Functions use those tables as input. When a Table gets new data, all functions that use it as input get triggered. tip Your Functions are also your data flow. Click on a Publisher, Transformer, or Subscriber to see the Execution Plan that is created if that Function is triggered. Click any node to trace its dependenciesResetZoom in Publisherread_salesPublisherread_customersTablesalesTablecustomersTransformerjoin_ordersTableordersSubscriberpush_orders

Execution plans are idempotent and deterministic. When an execution plan is generated, it contains a full snapshot of metadata and configurations used for the plan; such as start and stop timestamps, function code used for the plan, source data ingested, Table data generated, and data written out of Tabsdata

An Execution Plan is a DAG of all Functions Tabsdata intends to execute. A plan contains transactions, function runs, and workers. Click into each resource to learn more about what they do. A function is triggered creates Execution planOne per function triggered TransactionsOne per collection in the execution plan Function runsOne per function in the transaction WorkersOne per attempted code execution (max 3)

Four commands cover the four levels: tdk plan, tdk trx, tdk fnrun, and tdk worker. See the CLI Guide for what each one accepts. Execution & Triggers covers what fires a plan in the first place, along with the pristine-state guarantee it carries.

A Function Run represents a single execution of a Function in Tabsdata. Whenever a Function is executed as part of an Execution Plan, Tabsdata creates a Function Run to track that individual execution. If an Execution Plan contains multiple Functions, each Function gets its own Function Run. Function Runs allow Tabsdata to track the execution of each Function independently, including its status, logs, inputs, outputs, and the Worker responsible for executing it.

An Execution Plan describes the set of Functions that need to run and the order in which they need to run. Function Runs represent the individual executions that take place within that plan. For example, an Execution Plan containing a Publisher, Transformer, and Subscriber would create a separate Function Run for each Function: Execution Plan ├── Publisher Function Run ├── Transformer Function Run └── Subscriber Function Run This makes it possible to see the status of each individual Function rather than only whether the Execution Plan as a whole succeeded or failed.
documents.s: Function Runs in an Execution Plan

documents.t: Function Runs are executed by Workers. When a Function is ready to run, Tabsdata assigns its Function Run to a Worker. The Worker performs the actual processing required by the Function and reports the status of the Function Run back to Tabsdata. This separation allows multiple Function Runs to be processed independently and, when possible, in parallel. Runs of the same function run one at a time, in trigger order (best effort). In case of failures, function runs can be assigned to new workers and retried.

The data produced by a Function Run is written as part of a Transaction. A successful Function Run can produce changes to one or more Tables, but those changes do not become available simply because the Function Run finished. They become available when the Transaction containing those changes is committed. This allows Tabsdata to keep the execution of an individual Function separate from the process of publishing its output.

Each Function Run has its own status throughout its execution. This makes Function Runs useful for understanding where an Execution Plan is currently running or where a failure occurred. If one Function fails in a plan containing several Functions, you can identify the specific Function Run that failed and inspect its logs without treating the Execution Plan as a single unit.

Because each Function execution is tracked as its own Function Run, Tabsdata can operate on individual runs after they have been created. A failed Function Run can be recovered, allowing Tabsdata to retry that execution without starting the entire workflow again. A completed Function Run can also be replayed, allowing the Function to execute again using the same inputs. Functions can be replayed even if the source data the function relies on has changed.

Function Runs can be inspected through an AI agent connected to Tabsdata, to view their status, logs, and other execution information. AI agent session ❯Show me the logs for function run fr-3f9a2c1e Called tabsdata 1 time (ctrl+o to expand) ⏺ Here's fr-3f9a2c1e's log. ❯What's its status? Called tabsdata 1 time (ctrl+o to expand) ⏺ fr-3f9a2c1e is a Transformer run and finished successfully. See the CLI Guide for the complete set of commands for inspecting, recovering, and replaying Function Runs.

A transaction groups together changes made to Tables within a Collection during an execution plan. These changes are committed together, meaning they become available at the same time. Transactions help Tabsdata maintain pristine state. If an execution plan fails before a transaction is committed, its output is not published and the affected Tables remain in their previous state. This prevents incomplete or partially processed data from becoming available to users or downstream Functions. See Execution & Triggers for more information about pristine state.

In Tabsdata, a Collection acts as a transaction boundary. When an execution plan processes Functions within a Collection, changes made to that Collection's Tables are grouped into a transaction. Once the transaction is successfully committed, all of those changes become available together. This ensures that users and other Functions do not read a Collection while only some of its Tables have been updated.

A single execution plan can process Functions across multiple Collections. Because each Collection has its own transaction, an execution plan may contain multiple transactions. For example, if an execution plan processes Functions across three Collections, each Collection handles and commits its Table changes through its own transaction. This is why execution plans in Tabsdata are multi-transactional.

A worker is the process that executes the code defined in a Tabsdata Function Each worker runs as an isolated process on the Tabsdata server's Kubernetes cluster. Performance optimizations such as Polars Streaming and Lazy Evaluation allow workers to process datasets incrementally, allowing them to handle datasets larger than the memory available on the machine's hardware.

Tabsdata deploys one worker for each execution attempt of the function code. If a worker fails, Tabsdata snapshots the worker's execution log and spins up a new worker to retry the execution. By default, a function run will attempt three executions before stalling. A function is triggered Function runGenerated by the trigger Worker 1Failed Worker 2Failed Worker 3Succeeded Three workers is the default limit. Had the third one failed as well, the function run would stall instead of starting a fourth.
A worker is where a function's output ends up, so its logs are the first place to look when a function run fails: $ tdk worker logs --worker WID Pass --file - to write the log to stdout.
You can retry a single worker without re-running the whole plan: $ tdk worker recover --worker WID

tdk worker list filters down from any level of the plan, so you can start from whichever identifier you already have: $ tdk worker list [--status R] [--coll C] [--fn F] [--plan P] [--trx T] [--fnrun FR] See the CLI Guide for the full set of commands and the status codes each accepts.

A Tabsdata Function is Tabsdata's operational unit of work and defines a single step that reads data from or writes data to a Tabsdata Table. Tabsdata Functions build on the familiar model of a regular Python function, where data comes in through a parameter, the function performs work on that parameter, and the result is returned through the return statement. Tabsdata extends this model to data integration by abstracting data sources and destinations into the simple parameters and return statement of a Python function. Users define their inputs, which can be a SQL query against a database, a file in object storage, or a Tabsdata Table. They then define where they want the output data to be written, whether that is a database table, a file in object storage, or another Tabsdata Table. Tabsdata handles retrieving, converting, and moving the data between those systems. While the data is being passed through the Function, Tabsdata materializes it as a DataFrame object that users can transform through an expression-based API. This allows users to work with tabular data independently of where it is physically stored or how it needs to be moved between systems. PublisherTransformerSubscriber Publisher: Database to Python to Tabsdata Table.@td.publisher(input=database,output=['orders'],)def clean_orders(orders):cleaned = ...return cleanedDatabaseTabsdata Tableorders

There are three types of Tabsdata functions: publishers: read data from external systems and publish data into Tabsdata Tables transformers: read data from Tabsdata Tables and write data into Tabsdata Tables subscribers: read data from Tabsdata Tables and subscribe data into Tabsdata Tables Publishers External SystemTabsdata Table Reads an external system and writes Tabsdata Tables. Transformers Tabsdata TableTabsdata Table Reads Tabsdata Tables and writes new Tabsdata Tables. Subscribers Tabsdata TableExternal System Reads Tabsdata Tables and writes an external system.

The decorator maps declared inputs to the Python callable's parameters. It also maps returned values to output Tables or to destination slots in an external system. The number and order of parameters and returned values must match the corresponding declarations. Publishers and Subscribers use a Connector for the system-specific read or write operation. The Collection's Connection supplies the configuration and credentials used by that Connector. Transformers work entirely with Tabsdata Tables and do not use an external Connection. Output Tables belong to the Collection where the Function is registered. Input Table references can identify Tables in other Collections within the same Project, allowing Functions to connect into a larger workflow.

A parameter or a returned value is None when there is no data at that position. None is not the same as a TableFrame with zero rows: an empty TableFrame is data and replaces the previous data, while None keeps it. None never invalidates data already in Tabsdata. A None parameter has a different meaning for each Function type: Function A parameter is None when Publisher The external system has no new data for that source slot. A slot that takes a list of frames receives None, not an empty list. The Publisher still runs, and can return data anyway. Transformer, Subscriber The requested input version does not exist, the input Table has never been produced, or the Table had no data up to that version. The value alone does not tell these cases apart. A version range, such as orders@HEAD~3..HEAD, reaches a Transformer or Subscriber as a list with one element per version, oldest first. A None element is a version that does not exist or that has no data yet. A range of a fixed size, such as HEAD~3..HEAD, always has that many elements, and its None elements are always at the oldest end, because once a Table has data every later version has data too. A range from INITIAL, such as INITIAL..HEAD, has one element per existing version and can be empty. A returned None has a different meaning for each Function type: Function Returning None for an output Publisher, Transformer Commits a new version of the output Table that holds the same data as the previous version. If the Table has never had data, the new version has no data either. Subscriber Sends no new data to that destination slot. The Connector still runs and decides what None does to the external system; each Connector page describes it under Write behavior. Any returned TableFrame is new data, including an input TableFrame returned unchanged; only None keeps the previous data. A Transformer or Subscriber that reads a version committed from a None receives the previous data as a TableFrame, not None. Such a version also triggers dependent Transformers and Subscribers like any other commit, so a Subscriber runs for it too: return None to leave the external system as it is, or the frame to write the data again. When a Table version has no data, the UI and tdk say so, and say whether the version does not exist or has no data, instead of showing an empty table. tdk writes that message to stderr and exits with a non-zero code.

A Trigger determines when a Function starts. A Transformer or Subscriber without trigger_by runs whenever one of its input Tables commits a new version. A Publisher has no input Tables, so without trigger_by it runs only when triggered manually. Set trigger_by to a schedule, or to one or more Table references, to control what starts the Function.

Registration sends the Function definition, source code, and required bundle metadata to the Server. A Function name must be unique within its Collection. Register a decorated callable from a Python file with: tdk fn register --coll <collection_name> --path <path_to_python_file>::<function_name> Pass --update when the same command should update an existing Function with that name. Registration records the definition; it does not execute the Function. See Register a Function for the full procedure.

A manual Trigger can start any registered Function: tdk fn trigger --coll <collection_name> --name <function_name> The Server evaluates the Function's dependencies and creates an Execution Plan. Each Function included in that plan gets a Function Run, and a Worker executes each attempt. A successful run that produces Tables creates new Table Versions; the Server keeps the registered Function definition after the Worker exits. Function code does not run in the CLI process that sends the command. The CLI requests the Trigger, while the Server coordinates and records the execution.

A publisher reads data from an external system and publishes it to Tabsdata tables. Each run reads the source, calls the function, and commits the returned tables together. Unlike a stream publisher, a regular publisher does not keep reading. It reads the source only when it runs. The publisher must be registered in a source collection whose connection matches the source.

Tabsdata server collection · world? ▶ Trigger publisher Database PostgreSQL ? PostgreSQL · external Reachable Connection conn-postgres.yaml ? Publisher read_world ? Table country ? //world No versions yet Table city ? //world No versions yet

publisher( source, output_tables, trigger_by=None, on_tables=None, ) Parameter Type source Src required output_tables list[str] required trigger_by CronTrigger | TablesTrigger optional on_tables list[OnTablesAction] optional source​ The source to read. The source class decides what is read and how many slots are passed to the function. A SQL source has one slot per query. A file source can read several files into one slot. The source does not contain the server address or credentials. Those come from the connection of the collection where the publisher is registered. The page for each connector lists its source classes and settings. output_tables​ A non-empty list of local table names, one for each value the function returns. A name must start with a letter, use only letters, numbers, and underscores, and be no longer than 64 characters. The source slot count and output table count do not have to match. A publisher can combine several source slots into one table or derive several tables from one slot. trigger_by​ The trigger that starts the publisher automatically: a CronTrigger or TablesTrigger. Without trigger_by, the publisher runs only when triggered manually. See Execution & Triggers. on_tables​ Actions to run on the output tables after the publisher succeeds, such as data quality checks.

read_world.py 1from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresSrc 3 4 1@publisher( 2 source=PostgresSrc( 3 queries=[ 8 "SELECT * FROM country", 9 "SELECT * FROM city", 10 ], 11 ), 4 output_tables=["country", "city"], 13) 56def read_world(country: TableFrameSpec, city: TableFrameSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: 7 return (country, city) 1Function decorator Defines the source and output Tables for the Publisher. 2Plugin class Reads data from the external system. The Collection's Connection provides the address and credentials. 3Queries SQL queries that read the country and city data from Postgres. 4Output tables Tabsdata Tables where the returned data is written. 5Function body Receives the query results and returns the data to write to the output Tables. 6Arguments The country and city arguments receive the query results in the order listed in queries. 7Return The returned data is written to the Tables listed in output_tables, in that order. Returning None for a Table leaves its current version unchanged.

A publisher function has one parameter per source slot and returns one frame per output table. Parameters. Source slots are passed to the function in source order. Annotate a parameter as TableFrameSpec for one frame or TableFramesSpec for a list of frames. A slot is None when the external system has no new data for it; see None inputs and outputs. Context. The function can have a final ctx: TransactionCtx parameter. Use ctx to keep values between successful runs. For example, an incremental SQL publisher can save its last processed ID with ctx.set_attr() and use it in the next query. Type it FunctionCtx to also read the run's identifiers and the project's secrets. Return value. Return values map to output_tables in order. One output can be returned on its own; several outputs are returned as a tuple. Returning None for one output commits a new version that keeps that table's previous data. Slot counts. The number of source slots does not have to match the number of output tables. The function can combine several inputs into one table or create several tables from one input. Tabsdata checks the slot counts and function signature when the publisher is registered.

All publishers in a source collection use the same connection. Each publisher has its own source settings, code, and output tables. The connection is created with the collection. Updating a connection changes how every publisher in that collection reaches the external system.

Register. tdk fn register uploads the publisher. Its collection and connection must already exist. Run. A manual, cron, or table trigger starts a transaction. The source is read before the function runs. Commit. A successful run commits the output tables together. Each commit adds a table version. Update. tdk fn update replaces the code and decorator settings. Delete. Deleting the function stops future runs but does not delete its output tables or their versions. For step-by-step guides on building a publisher for a specific external system, see Publishers under How-to Guides.

When Subscribing data, you may need to dynamically update, delete, and insert records within a single function. Tabsdata supports sql merge writes. Users can specify key columns to match records and an operation column that tells Tabsdata whether to insert, update, or delete each row. The Subscriber returns the changes, and the connector applies them to the destination table. Merge writes are supported by the Snowflake, BigQuery, and Databricks connectors.

To configure a merge, set if_table_exists="merge" on the destination and pass a merge_cfg list containing the key and operation columns for each table. For example, this Subscriber reads order changes from Tabsdata and applies them to ORDERS in Snowflake: from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.snowflake import MergeCfg, SnowflakeDest @subscriber( destination=SnowflakeDest( tables=["ORDERS"], if_table_exists="merge", merge_cfg=[MergeCfg(on=["order_id"], op_column="op")], schema_evolution="update", dest_cfg={"snowflake.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"}, ), input_tables=["capture/order_changes"], ) def load_orders(changes: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return changes Here, on=["order_id"] matches records by order ID, while op_column="op" identifies the column containing the operation. The Function returns the changes from capture/order_changes for the connector to write. Because a Subscriber can write to several tables, the MergeCfg entries must follow the order of tables, and both lists must have the same length. Use a list even for a single table. The merge_cfg setting is required for merge writes and cannot be used with other write modes. The on setting requires at least one key column, and those columns must exist in both the incoming data and the destination when the merge runs. If several columns form the key, all their values must match. MergeCfg is imported from the same connector module as the destination. On Snowflake and BigQuery, a merge under schema_evolution="update" needs "iceberg" set as the schema evolution engine in dest_cfg. See Schema evolution.

After matching records by key, Tabsdata uses the operation column to decide what to write. In the example above, op accepts these values: Marker Operation i Insert the row if its key does not exist in the destination. u Update the row matching its key. d Delete the row matching its key. l Load: the row comes from an initial load. The destination is emptied before the load's rows are inserted. t Truncate: the destination is emptied. An insert leaves an existing record unchanged, while an update or delete does nothing if the record is missing. Uppercase I, U, D, L and T are also accepted, but spaces are not removed, so " d " is invalid. Tabsdata removes rows with invalid or null operations before processing the batch. Because the operation column is used to control the write, Tabsdata excludes it when creating the destination table or updating its schema.

l and t reset the table. When a batch contains one, the changes before the last reset are discarded, and the destination's rows are replaced in one statement by what follows it. A CDC stream that uses start_from="full" or captures table truncates sends these markers.

A record may change several times within the same batch. Tabsdata combines changes with the same key before writing them, using the first and last valid operations to determine the result. These operations follow the row order in the materialized batch, so the order returned by the Function matters: First operation Last operation Result Insert Insert or update Insert using the latest row. Insert Delete No destination write for this key. Update or delete Insert or update Update using the latest row. Update or delete Delete Delete the matching record. For example, i → u → d → i inserts the latest row because the final change adds the record again. With i → u → d, nothing is written because the record was created and deleted in the same batch. For a delete, Tabsdata keeps the data from the last insert or update for that key, or the first row if all operations are deletes. This allows delete records to contain just the key columns and operation. The destination therefore receives the combined change, without storing the intermediate changes as history.

If the destination table does not exist, all three connectors can create it from the staged data's schema, excluding the operation column. The database and schema or dataset must already exist, and the Connection must have the required permissions. For existing tables, Snowflake and BigQuery write columns shared by the incoming data and the destination. Updates leave the keys unchanged, while inserts include them. Columns found only in the destination are left unchanged on updates and omitted from inserts, where the destination's defaults and constraints apply. A batch with a column the destination lacks is refused under schema_evolution="strict", with SQL_COMMON_10, before the merge runs; under update the column is added. Values written to shared columns must still satisfy the destination's types and constraints. Databricks handles column matching through Delta's merge rules, and update uses MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION, which excludes the operation column. The operation marker should therefore use a separate column from the data being written.

Incoming data may contain new columns or values too large for the destination's current column types. Schema evolution controls whether Tabsdata can change the table to accept that data. Set schema_evolution on the destination to choose the behavior. All three destinations default to "strict": Setting Behavior "strict" Refuses a new column, and a wider type unless its values fit the column, with SQL_COMMON_10, before the merge runs. A configured watermark column is an exception. "update" Allows new data columns and supported type widening. strict accepts a wider type when its values fit the column, and an incoming type narrower than the column's. Making a column nullable counts as widening and is refused. A column the batch lacks keeps its stored value. Schema Evolution has the same policy for every table destination and write mode. Snowflake's and BigQuery's native schema evolution does not apply to MERGE. A Snowflake or BigQuery merge under "update" needs the iceberg engine set in dest_cfg, and is refused at registration without it: # SnowflakeDest dest_cfg={"snowflake.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"} # BigQueryDest dest_cfg={"bigquery.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"} The iceberg engine compares the incoming and destination schemas and applies supported changes through ALTER TABLE. It controls how schemas are compared; it does not convert the destination into an Apache Iceberg table. Under "strict", a merge that sets the engine is refused at registration. Databricks uses Delta's MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION for schema_evolution="update", so it does not require a schema_evolution_engine setting. On each merge, Tabsdata also sets the destination table's delta.enableTypeWidening property to true for update or false for strict.

Type widening allows a column to store larger values, such as longer strings or numbers with greater precision. The supported changes depend on the destination: Destination Supported widening Snowflake Wider VARCHAR lengths and greater NUMBER precision at the same scale. The connector does not widen between different base types. BigQuery Supported numeric promotions, including INT64 → NUMERIC → BIGNUMERIC → FLOAT64, and wider type parameters. Databricks Type changes supported by Delta type widening. Setting schema_evolution="update" allows these supported changes. If the incoming data requires a conversion outside these rules, the write can still fail.

A Subscriber may retry a write after data has already reached the destination. To recognize these retries, Tabsdata can store the Transaction ID in a watermark column. If that ID is already in the table, Tabsdata skips the write. Set watermark_column on the destination to enable this check: SnowflakeDest( tables=["ORDERS"], if_table_exists="merge", merge_cfg=[MergeCfg(on=["order_id"], op_column="op")], watermark_column="wm", ) The configured name applies to all tables listed in the destination. If the column is missing, Tabsdata adds it even when schema_evolution="strict". Existing rows have NULL in the new column, while inserted and updated rows receive the current Transaction ID. The watermark name must differ from the key columns and operation column, following the destination's rules for uppercase and lowercase names. Watermarks work with append and merge, but not with replace. Retries use the same Transaction ID, while new Transactions have different IDs and write normally. The check depends on a matching ID remaining in the destination. A batch containing only deletes leaves no new watermark value.

The connectors differ in how they stage data, change schemas, and match column names: Behavior Snowflake BigQuery Databricks Staging Snowflake stage, then a TEMPORARY table GCS, then a staging table <target>_<8 hex characters> beside the target Unity Catalog volume, then a staging table <target>_<8 hex characters> beside the target Schema changes under update Connector applies ALTER TABLE using Iceberg schema comparison Connector applies ALTER TABLE using Iceberg schema comparison Delta merge schema evolution Engine for merge iceberg, required under update iceberg, required under update No engine setting Column names Unquoted names resolve as uppercase; double quotes preserve case Case-insensitive; backticks quote names Case-insensitive; backticks quote names The BigQuery and Databricks staging tables are real tables, so the Connection needs permission to create and drop them, and a run that is killed can leave one behind. For example, Snowflake resolves an unquoted order_id as uppercase, so on=["order_id"] matches a stored ORDER_ID column. BigQuery and Databricks match column names without considering case, including when those names are quoted. BigQuery also requires destination table names to be enclosed in backticks, as in tables=["`orders`"].

Tabsdata checks the configuration before writing and validates the incoming data during execution. The following conditions can cause the merge to fail: Condition Result Merge mode without merge_cfg, or merge_cfg without merge mode Configuration error. merge_cfg is not a list, or its length differs from tables Configuration error. Empty on, or an operation column that matches a key Configuration error. Snowflake or BigQuery merge under update without schema_evolution_engine="iceberg", or under strict with an engine set Refused at registration. The same table listed twice in tables Refused at registration (CONN_37). Databricks compares names ignoring case, Snowflake folds unquoted parts to uppercase, and BigQuery compares them verbatim. A watermark with replace, or a watermark name that matches a key or operation column Configuration error. Missing operation or key columns in the incoming batch Runtime error. A new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit, under strict Refused before the merge (SQL_COMMON_10). No shared data columns between the batch and destination Runtime error. Several incoming columns match the same configured column name Runtime error. For field definitions, see the MergeCfg API reference for Snowflake, BigQuery, and Databricks.

A stream publisher reads data continuously from a stream source, such as a CDC log or a Kafka topic, and publishes it into Tabsdata tables in batches. A regular publisher runs when it is triggered and reads what is in the source at that moment. A stream publisher has no trigger. Registering it starts a worker that keeps reading the source, collects what it reads, and runs the function once per batch. The batch_* parameters of @stream_publisher decide when a batch is complete. These sources work with @stream_publisher: Source Reads Page PostgresCdcStreamSrc Postgres changes, from the WAL Postgres CDC MySQLCdcStreamSrc MySQL changes, from the binlog MySQL CDC Db2CdcStreamSrc Db2 changes, from the SQL Replication CD tables Db2 CDC KafkaStreamSrc Messages from Kafka topics Kafka All of them use the batch parameters described on this page.

Tabsdata server collection · events? ▶ Start stream Kafka topic Kafka ? Kafka · external Reachable Connection conn-kafka.yaml ? Stream Publisher stream_page_views ? Table page_views ? //events No versions yet

stream_sales_changes.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresCdcStreamSrc from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @stream_publisher( source=PostgresCdcStreamSrc( tables=["public.orders", "public.customers"], replication_slot="tabsdata_sales", start_from="full", ), output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], batch_max_secs=300, batch_max_rows=50_000, ) def stream_sales_changes( orders: TableFramesSpec, customers: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return concat(orders), concat(customers) source is the stream source. Its connection comes from the collection the function is registered in, as for any publisher. output_tables are the Tabsdata tables the function writes, in the order the function returns them. batch_max_secs and batch_max_rows decide when a batch is handed to the function: here, every 5 minutes, or sooner once 50,000 changes are waiting, but never more often than once a minute. The function receives one parameter per source slot. Each parameter is a list of frames: the data read for that slot since the previous batch. concat combines them into one frame.

stream_publisher( source, output_tables, *, batch_min_secs=None, batch_max_secs=None, batch_max_rows=None, batch_max_bytes=None, batch_idle_secs=None, on_tables=None, flush_interval_mins=None, ) Parameter Type source StreamSrc required output_tables list[str] required batch_min_secs int optional batch_max_secs int optional batch_max_rows int optional batch_max_bytes int optional batch_idle_secs int optional on_tables list[OnTablesAction] optional flush_interval_mins int deprecated source and output_tables can be given by position or by name. The other parameters must be given by name. source​ The stream source to read: one of the sources in the table above. output_tables​ The tables the function writes, as a non-empty list of table names. The number of output tables does not have to match the number of source slots. on_tables​ Actions to run on the output tables, such as data quality checks, as for a regular publisher.

A batch is everything the worker has read since the previous batch. Each batch runs the function once, and the function's output tables are committed together: every batch adds one version to each output table. Parameter Default Description batch_min_secs 60 The shortest time between two batches, in seconds. Never less than 60. batch_max_secs none Seconds after the previous batch at which data that is waiting is handed to the function. batch_max_rows none Rows waiting that make a batch due. batch_max_bytes none Bytes waiting that make a batch due. batch_idle_secs none Seconds after the previous batch at which, if no data is waiting, the function runs with an empty batch. At least one of batch_max_secs, batch_max_rows and batch_max_bytes is required.

The worker checks after every read from the source. Counting from the previous batch (or from when the worker started): When data is waiting, a batch is due once batch_min_secs have passed and any of these is true: batch_max_secs have passed, at least batch_max_rows rows are waiting, at least batch_max_bytes bytes are waiting. When no data is waiting, nothing happens, unless batch_idle_secs is set. Once batch_idle_secs have passed, the function runs with an empty batch. As a result: batch_min_secs is a floor for every other setting. If 50,000 rows arrive 10 seconds after a batch, they wait until batch_min_secs have passed, and more rows keep joining them in the meantime. batch_max_rows and batch_max_bytes make a batch due; they do not cap its size. A batch holds everything that is waiting when it closes, which can be more than the threshold. Rows and bytes are counted over all the slots of the source together, not per table. For a CDC source, one row is one change. Bytes are approximate: the size of the data files already written plus an estimate of what is still in memory. batch_max_secs counts from the previous batch, not from when the data arrived. After a quiet period longer than batch_max_secs, the first data to arrive is handed over right away. Batches are processed one at a time, in order. Tabsdata looks for new batches about every 30 seconds, so a batch can start up to that long after it is due. If the function takes longer than the batch interval, batches queue up and are processed in turn.
documents.s: When a batch is handed to the function

documents.t: The batch parameters are checked when the function is decorated. A violation raises error API_29: batch_min_secs, batch_max_secs and batch_idle_secs must be whole numbers of seconds, at least 60. batch_max_rows and batch_max_bytes must be whole numbers, at least 1. batch_max_secs must be at least batch_min_secs. batch_idle_secs must be at least batch_max_secs, or, without batch_max_secs, at least batch_min_secs. At least one of batch_max_secs, batch_max_rows and batch_max_bytes must be set.

Goal Parameters Result Steady, bounded latency batch_max_secs=120 A batch every 2 minutes while data arrives. Size first, with a time bound batch_max_rows=100_000, batch_max_secs=900 A batch as soon as 100,000 rows are waiting, and at least every 15 minutes. Large batches, few runs batch_min_secs=600, batch_max_secs=3600 At most one batch every 10 minutes, and at least one an hour while data arrives. Runs even when the source is quiet batch_max_secs=300, batch_idle_secs=3600 A batch every 5 minutes while data arrives, and an empty run every hour when nothing arrives, for example to keep downstream functions on a schedule.

Stream sources also have buffer settings in their src_cfg, such as tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows or tabsdata.kafka.buffer.max_rows. Buffer settings and batch parameters work at different levels: Buffer settings decide when the worker writes what it has read from memory to a data file. They bound the worker's memory. Batch parameters decide when the files written so far, and anything still in memory, are handed to the function as one batch. Most streams only need the batch parameters. The buffer settings of each source are listed on its connector page.

stream_sales_changes.py 1from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher 2from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresCdcStreamSrc 3from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat 4 5 1@stream_publisher( 2 source=PostgresCdcStreamSrc( 3 tables=["public.orders", "public.customers"], 9 replication_slot="tabsdata_sales", 10 start_from="full", 11 ), 4 output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], 5 batch_max_secs=300, 14 batch_max_rows=50_000, 15) 67def stream_sales_changes( 17 orders: TableFramesSpec, 18 customers: TableFramesSpec, 19) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: 8 return concat(orders), concat(customers) 1Function decorator Defines the stream source, output Tables, and the conditions that make a batch due. 2Stream source Reads changes continuously from Postgres. The Collection's Connection provides the server address and credentials. 3Source slots Each tracked table is one source slot, in the order listed. 4Output tables Tabsdata Tables that receive the values returned by the function. 5Batch parameters A batch is due after five minutes or when 50,000 rows are waiting, whichever happens first after the minimum interval. 6Function body Receives one list of frames per source slot and returns one frame per output Table. 7Arguments The arguments receive the frames collected for each source slot since the previous batch. 8Return concat combines each slot's frames. The returned values map to output_tables in order.

A stream publisher function has one parameter per source slot, annotated TableFramesSpec, and returns one TableFrameSpec per output table. Slots. A CDC source has one slot per entry in its tables, in the same order. A Kafka source has a single slot. Parameters. Each parameter receives a list of frames with the data read for that slot since the previous batch. For a CDC source, the list holds at most one frame. For Kafka, it can hold several, possibly with different schemas; combine them with concat(frames, how="diagonal_relaxed") if their columns can differ. Empty batches. A slot with no new data receives an empty list. concat of an empty list returns None. Return value. A tuple with one element per output table, in the order of output_tables. With a single output table, the frame can be returned on its own. Returning None for a table means no new data: it commits a new version that holds the same data as the previous version. No other parameters. A stream publisher cannot declare a ctx parameter or any parameter beyond its slots. concat is imported from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions.

Register. tdk fn register starts the worker. The function must be registered in a source collection whose connection matches the source; see the source's connector page. Disable and enable. tdk stream disable stops the worker; tdk stream enable starts it again, from where it stopped. tdk stream list shows the stream publishers and their state. Update. tdk fn update restarts the worker with the new code and settings. It resumes from where it stopped. Delete. Deleting the function stops the worker. Check the source's connector page for anything left on the source system, such as a Postgres replication slot. Failures. If the worker fails, Tabsdata restarts it, waiting one minute after the first failure and doubling the wait after each further failure, up to 30 minutes. Start over. tdk fn update --reset-stage discards the stream's recorded position. The stream starts again as if it were new: from the source's starting position, or with a new full load for a CDC source with start_from="full". On a restart, the stream reads again whatever it had not yet handed to the function. A CDC stream publishes every change once, even across restarts. A Kafka stream is at least once: after a restart, some messages may be published again.

The full load of a CDC source (start_from="full") is not subject to the batch parameters. It is handed to the function as one batch, covering every tracked table, as soon as it has been read. If the load fails or is interrupted, it is discarded and runs again from the start. The batch parameters apply to the changes that follow.

flush_interval_mins was the only batch setting before 2.2.0. It is deprecated, and is converted to batch_max_secs = flush_interval_mins * 60, so it must be at least 1. It cannot be combined with any batch_* parameter. Doing so raises error API_30. It raises a Python DeprecationWarning when the function is decorated, and the worker logs a warning when it starts. Python hides DeprecationWarning by default, so the worker log is where the warning shows. To migrate, replace flush_interval_mins=N with batch_max_secs=N * 60.

A subscriber reads Tabsdata tables and writes to an external system. The function can filter, rename, or otherwise prepare the data before it is written. A subscriber belongs to a destination collection. That collection's connection provides the address and credentials for the destination.

Tabsdata server collection · warehouse? ▶ Trigger subscriber Table vendors ? //sales Committed Table items ? //sales Committed Connection conn-mysql-dest.yaml ? Subscriber write_sales ? Database MySQL ? MySQL · external Not yet synced

subscriber( destination, input_tables, trigger_by=None, ) Parameter Type destination Dest required input_tables list[str] required trigger_by CronTrigger | TablesTrigger | AllTablesTrigger optional destination​ The destination to write to. The destination class decides where the data is written and how many slots the function must return. The destination uses the connection of the collection where the subscriber is registered. The page for each connector lists its destination classes and settings. input_tables​ A non-empty list of table references in the form [collection/]table[@versions]. Omit the collection for a table in the subscriber's collection. Use @versions to select a version, a version range, a comma-separated list, or NEW. Each entry maps to one function parameter, in list order. trigger_by​ The trigger that starts the subscriber automatically: a CronTrigger, TablesTrigger, or AllTablesTrigger. Without trigger_by, a commit to any input table triggers the subscriber. A subscriber can also be run manually. The trigger decides when the function runs. The version selector in input_tables decides which data it sends. See Execution & Triggers.

sales-sub.py 1from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec 2import tabsdatak.api.tableframe as tdf 3from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLDest 4 5 1@subscriber( 2 destination=MySQLDest( 8 tables=["vendors", "items"], 9 if_table_exists="replace", 10 ), 3 input_tables=["sales/vendors", "sales/items"], 12) 45def write_sales(vendors: TableFrameSpec, items: TableFrameSpec): 6 vendors = vendors.filter(tdf.col("active") == 1) 7 return (vendors, items) 1Function decorator Defines the input Tables and destination for the Subscriber. 2Plugin class Writes data to the external system. The Collection's Connection provides the address and credentials. 3Input tables Tabsdata Tables to read. This Subscriber reads vendors and items from the sales Collection. 4Function body Receives the input data and returns the data to write to MySQL. 5Arguments The vendors and items arguments receive the data from input_tables in the order listed. 6Body code Filters the vendors to include only active vendors. 7Return The returned data is written to the destination Tables in the order listed in tables. Returning None for a Table skips the write.

A subscriber function has one parameter per input table and returns one frame per destination slot. Parameters. Inputs are passed to the function in input_tables order. Annotate a parameter as TableFrameSpec for one frame or TableFramesSpec for a list of frames. An input read at @NEW, a v..v range or a v,v list must be typed TableFramesSpec; TableFrameSpec is refused at registration. An input is None when the requested version does not exist or has no data; see None inputs and outputs. Context. The function can have a final ctx: TransactionCtx parameter to keep values between successful runs. Type it FunctionCtx to also read the run's identifiers and the project's secrets. Return value. Return values map to the destination slots in destination order. One slot can be returned on its own; several slots are returned as a tuple. Returning None for a slot sends no new data to it, and the Connector decides what that does to the external system. Slot counts. The number of input tables does not have to match the number of destination slots. The function can combine several inputs into one write or create several destination tables from one input. Tabsdata checks the slot counts and function signature when the subscriber is registered.

All subscribers in a destination collection use the same connection. Each subscriber has its own input tables, destination settings, and code. Input tables can come from the subscriber's collection or another collection. Updating the collection's connection changes how every subscriber in that collection reaches the external system.

Register. tdk fn register uploads the subscriber. Its collection and connection must already exist. Run. A manual, scheduled, or table trigger starts a transaction and resolves the requested input versions. Write. The function's returned frames are handed to the destination. The transaction succeeds only after the destination write succeeds. Update. tdk fn update replaces the code and decorator settings. Delete. Deleting the function stops future writes. It does not remove data already written to the external system. For step-by-step guides on building a subscriber for a specific external system, see Subscribers under How-to Guides. For inserts, updates, and deletes into Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks, see Merging into SQL destinations.
A transformer reads Tabsdata tables, transforms their data, and writes the result back to Tabsdata. It does not read or write an external system, so it does not use a connection.

collection · world? collection · insights · data product? ▶ Trigger transformer Table country ? //world Committed Table city ? //world Committed Transformer find_big_cities ? Table big_cities ? //insights No versions yet

transformer( input_tables, output_tables, trigger_by=None, on_tables=None, ) Parameter Type input_tables list[str] required output_tables list[str] required trigger_by CronTrigger | TablesTrigger | AllTablesTrigger optional on_tables list[OnTablesAction] optional input_tables​ A non-empty list of table references in the form [collection/]table[@versions]. Omit the collection for a table in the transformer's collection. Use @versions to select a version, a version range, a comma-separated list, or NEW. Each entry maps to one function parameter. A single-version reference receives a TableFrameSpec; a reference that selects several versions receives a TableFramesSpec. output_tables​ A non-empty list of local table names, one for each value returned by the function. The output tables belong to the transformer's collection. Each name must start with a letter, contain only letters, numbers, and underscores, and be no longer than 64 characters. trigger_by​ The trigger that starts the transformer automatically: a CronTrigger, TablesTrigger, or AllTablesTrigger. Without trigger_by, a commit to any input table triggers the transformer. A transformer can also be run manually. The trigger decides when the function runs. The version selector in input_tables decides which versions it reads. See Execution & Triggers. on_tables​ Actions to run on the output tables after the transformer succeeds, such as data quality checks.

find_big_cities.py 1from tabsdatak.api import transformer, TableFrameSpec 2import tabsdatak.api.tableframe as tdf 3 4 1@transformer( 2 input_tables=["world/country", "world/city"], 3 output_tables=["big_cities"], 8) 45def find_big_cities(country: TableFrameSpec, city: TableFrameSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: 6 countries = country.rename({"name": "country_name"}).drop( 11 ["population", "continent"] 12 ) 13 joined = city.join(countries, left_on="country_code", right_on="code") 7 return (joined.filter(tdf.col("population") > 3_000_000),) 1Function decorator Defines the input and output Tables for the Transformer. 2Input tables Tabsdata Tables to read. Use collection/table to reference a Table in another Collection. 3Output tables Tables where the transformed data is written. These belong to the Transformer's Collection. 4Function body Reads the country and city data, joins it, and returns cities with a population above three million. 5Arguments The arguments receive the data from input_tables in the order listed. An argument is None if the requested Table version does not exist. 6Body code Renames the country name column, removes unused columns, and joins the country and city data. 7Return The returned data is written to the Tables listed in output_tables, in that order. Returning None for a Table leaves its current version unchanged.

A transformer function has one parameter per input table and returns one frame per output table. Parameters. Inputs are passed to the function in input_tables order. Annotate a parameter as TableFrameSpec for one frame or TableFramesSpec for a list of frames. An input read at @NEW, a v..v range or a v,v list must be typed TableFramesSpec; TableFrameSpec is refused at registration. An input is None when the requested version does not exist or has no data; see None inputs and outputs. Context. The function can have a final ctx: TransactionCtx parameter to keep values between successful runs. Type it FunctionCtx to also read the run's identifiers and the project's secrets. Return value. Return values map to output_tables in order. One output can be returned on its own; several outputs are returned as a tuple. Returning None for one output commits a new version that keeps that table's previous data. Tabsdata checks the input count, output count, and function signature when the transformer is registered.

A transformer can read tables from its own collection or another collection. Its output tables are always local to the collection where the transformer is registered. Table references are resolved when a run starts. When a trigger starts a larger execution plan, Tabsdata passes the versions produced for that transaction through the plan so downstream transformers read a consistent set of data.

Register. tdk fn register uploads the transformer to its collection. No connection is required. Run. A manual, scheduled, or table trigger starts a transaction and resolves the requested input versions. Commit. A successful run commits the output tables together. Each commit adds a table version. Update. tdk fn update replaces the code and decorator settings. Delete. Deleting the function stops future runs but does not delete its output tables or their versions. For step-by-step guidance on building a transformer, see Transformers under How-to Guides.

Grok parses lines of text, such as the lines of a log file, into typed columns. The grok method of a TableFrame matches a Grok pattern against a string column and appends one column for each capture listed in a schema. Grok is usually applied in the Publisher that reads the log file, so the Table it writes is already structured. Because grok is a TableFrame method, it can also be used in a Transformer on a Table that holds raw text. For a full walkthrough that reads a log file and publishes the parsed rows, see Publish data from log files with Grok.

grok takes three arguments: The name of the string column to parse, or an expression that resolves to one A Grok pattern whose named captures become the new columns A schema that maps each capture name to a ColumnDefinition from tabsdatak.tableframe.grok import ColumnDefinition from tabsdatak.tableframe.datatypes import String, Int32, Int64 PATTERN = ( r"%{IPV4:client_ip} " r"%{USER:ident} " r"%{USER:auth} " r"\[%{HTTPDATE:timestamp}\] " r'"%{WORD:method} ' r'%{URIPATHPARAM:request} ' r'HTTP/%{NUMBER:http_version}" ' r"%{INT:response_code} %{INT:bytes}" ) SCHEMA = { "client_ip": ColumnDefinition("ip_address", String), "method": ColumnDefinition("http_method", String), "response_code": ColumnDefinition("status_code", Int32), "bytes": ColumnDefinition("response_bytes", Int64), "timestamp": ColumnDefinition("request_time", String), } parsed = lines.grok("column_0", PATTERN, SCHEMA) lines column_0 203.0.113.10 - - [10/Oct/2026:13:55:01 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 512 not a log line 2 rows parsed column_0str ip_addressstr http_methodstr status_codei32 response_bytesi64 request_timestr 203.0.113.10 - - [10/Oct/2026:13:55:01 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 512 203.0.113.10 GET 200 512 10/Oct/2026:13:55:01 +0000 not a log line null null null null null 2 rows The result keeps every existing column and follows these rules: One column is added for each entry in the schema, in schema order. Captures that are not in the schema are not added. The pattern above captures ident, auth, request, and http_version, but none of them become columns. The captured text is cast to the dtype in the capture's ColumnDefinition. A row whose text does not match the pattern gets null in every new column, so a malformed line never fails the Function.

A capture is written as %{PATTERN:capture}, where PATTERN is a predefined pattern name and capture is the name the schema refers to. Text between captures must match literally, so characters that have a meaning in regular expressions, such as [ and ], are escaped with a backslash. The full capture syntax is %{name:alias:extract:definition}: name: a predefined pattern name, such as IPV4, WORD, or INT alias: the capture name extract: reserved for future use definition: a regular expression, required when no predefined name is given Tabsdata includes 320 predefined patterns from the Elasticsearch Grok pattern library. Commonly used patterns for log files include: Pattern Matches IPV4 An IPv4 address WORD A single word INT An integer NUMBER An integer or decimal number TIMESTAMP_ISO8601 An ISO 8601 timestamp HTTPDATE A timestamp in web server access log format LOGLEVEL A log level, such as INFO or ERROR UUID A UUID URI A URI DATA Any text, matching as little as possible GREEDYDATA Any text, matching as much as possible COMBINEDAPACHELOG A full Apache combined log line SYSLOGBASE The header of a syslog line

The schema is a dictionary keyed by capture name. Each value is a ColumnDefinition from tabsdatak.tableframe.grok with two fields: name: the name of the new column. None keeps the capture name, and any other value renames the column. dtype: the data type the captured text is cast to, from tabsdatak.tableframe.datatypes.
