Defaults to String. from tabsdatak.tableframe.grok import ColumnDefinition from tabsdatak.tableframe.datatypes import String PATTERN = r"%{TIMESTAMP_ISO8601:ts} %{LOGLEVEL:level} %{WORD:service}: %{GREEDYDATA:message}" SCHEMA = { "ts": ColumnDefinition(None, String), "level": ColumnDefinition("level", String), "service": ColumnDefinition("service", String), "message": ColumnDefinition("message", String), }

When a pattern uses the same capture name more than once, each repeat is numbered: the first keeps the name, and later ones get a [1], [2], … suffix. The schema refers to repeats by those numbered names. from tabsdatak.tableframe.grok import ColumnDefinition from tabsdatak.tableframe.datatypes import String, Int64 PATTERN = r"%{WORD:city}-%{INT:year} to %{WORD:city}-%{INT:year}" SCHEMA = { "city": ColumnDefinition("from_city", String), "city[1]": ColumnDefinition("to_city", String), "year[1]": ColumnDefinition("to_year", Int64), } The grok_fields helper lists the capture names a pattern produces, which is useful for building the schema of a long pattern: from tabsdata.expansions.tableframe.features.grok.engine import grok_fields grok_fields(r"%{WORD:city}-%{INT:year} to %{WORD:city}-%{INT:year}") # ['city', 'city[1]', 'year', 'year[1]']

A Group is an organizational layer inside a tabsdata project that organizes workflow steps according to their role in the workflow. By default, all tabsdata projects come with three groups: sources, default, and destinations the sources group stores everything related to ingesting data from external systems the default group stores everything related to transforming data inside tabsdata the destinations group stores everything related to loading data into external systems Groups separate workflow resources based on type of data movementZoom in Database postgres Tabsdata Server sources Publisher load_users Table users default Transformer rank_users Table top_users destinations Subscriber sync_users Warehouse snowflake

The sources, default, and destinations groups are special groups that must exist in your workflow. They are dedicated spaces for registering publisher and subscriber functions and cannot be modified, duplicated, or removed from your project. Outside these three system groups, users can create any number of groups to organize their transformer functions.

Groups are useful for separating workflow steps that happen across tabsdata server boundaries (ingestion, load) from workflow steps that happen inside the tabsdata server (transform). Groups are also useful for separating data transformation workflow steps by the type of data transformation being done. For example, a popular data design pattern is the Medallion Architecture for Data Integration, which breaks data transformation into three layers: Bronze: Layer that ingests raw source data from external systems with the goal of having as close of a representation to data in the external system Silver: Layer that cleans, dedupes, normalizes, and joins related entities Gold: Layer that applies granular, business-specific transformations and creates "consumer-ready" tables. Users looking to implement this design pattern in tabsdata can do so with five groups within Tabsdata: two built-in groups (sources, destinations) and three custom groups (bronze, silver, gold). External systems GroupsourcesPublishers Ingest from external systems. Built in GroupbronzeTransformers Raw data, kept as close to the external system as possible. User created GroupsilverTransformers Cleaned, deduped, normalized, and joined. User created GroupgoldTransformers Business-specific transformations, consumer-ready tables. User created GroupdestinationsSubscribers Write out to external systems. Built in External systems

The Projects view in the Tabsdata UI shows how data moves between Groups, including the number of Tables, rows, and bytes moving through each stage. s3_src7,000,000 rows · 202.9 MBin 2 tablesbronze7,000,000 rows · 202.9 MBin 2 tablessilver3,739,484 rows · 122.5 MBin 1 tablegold934,871 rows · 30.6 MBin 1 tablesnowflake_out934,871 rows · 30.6 MBin 1 table

The sources, default, and destinations Groups are created with every Project. These system Groups cannot be renamed or deleted. Custom Groups can be created, renamed, and deleted within a Project. See Create a Group, Update a Group, and Delete a Group for step-by-step instructions.

To upgrade Tabsdata, install the new version in a clean virtual environment and run tdkserver upgrade from it. The upgrade keeps the instance's custom configuration, for example additional virtual environment requirements. Create a new virtual environment​ Create a new, clean virtual environment for the new version, as in Create a Python virtual environment, with a new name such as tabsdata-new or .venv-new. Do not install the new version in the environment of the version you are upgrading from. Install the new version​ In the new virtual environment, install Tabsdata as in Install Tabsdata. Upgrade the server​ From the new virtual environment, run: tdkserver upgrade The upgrade stops the Tabsdata Server and leaves it stopped. To start it again as soon as the upgrade completes, pass --apply true: tdkserver upgrade --apply true Without --apply true, start the server with tdkserver start when you are ready. tdkserver upgrade upgrades the instance named tabsdata unless --instance names another; see tdkserver upgrade for every option. Remove the previous virtual environment​ Once the upgrade is complete, the virtual environment of the previous version is no longer used and can be deleted. Upgrade the clients​ Every machine that runs tdk needs the new version too. On each one, create a new virtual environment and install the new version, as in the first two steps. Then run the AI agent configuration again from the new virtual environment, starting with tdk ai agents install. See Configure Your AI Agent.

Tabsdata is an open-source, distributed, horizontally scalable data integration platform that allows users to turn their Python functions into automated, AI-friendly workflows that move and transform data between a variety of different systems. Built atop Kubernetes and the Polars DataFrame API, Tabsdata can be deployed on almost any machine that runs Python, requires no admin permissions or Docker dependency, and allows users to move and transform tabular data through an expression-based Pythonic interface. With the Tabsdata skill installed, a coding agent can also build and analyze workflows through tdk.

Lightweight deployment requirements Python-native implementation Automatic DAG Orchestraton Automated data versioning and storage Automatic state and metadata retention Coding agent integration Connectors Tabsdata can be deployed on almost any machine and requires only Python as a dependency. See Architecture Overview for more detail on how these pieces fit together.
Install Tabsdata -- get the server running locally. Configure Your AI Agent -- install the Tabsdata skill for your coding agent. Run Your First Data Integration -- build a working flow end to end.

The documentation is also published in llms.txt format for AI agents: llms.txt: an index of the guide, tutorial and server administration pages, one line per page. llms-full.txt: the full text of every page in that index, in one file of about 1 MB, which can exceed an agent's context window. Any page is available as markdown at its URL with .md appended. This page, for example, is at /guide/introduction.md.
You can join the Tabsdata community on Github or Slack.
We appreciate all contributions, from reporting bugs to implementing new features. You can access the Tabsdata Github repository here.
For license information, see the Tabsdata website.

Any number of factors can evolve over the course of a data pipeline's lifecycle, including the shape of processed data, the logic used to move and transform that data, and when specific data was scheduled to be processed. This is called Data Lineage. Tabsdata's built-in data lineage automatically stores immutable versions of tables and functions as they are modified, preserving a record of how your workflows change over time. This allows users to travel back to historical versions of table data, examine the code that produced them, and see how their workflow logic has evolved.

All Tabsdata functions declare the Tables they read from and write to. This allows Tabsdata to infer dependencies and execution order, a core mechanic that enables Automatic Orchestration and Execution Plans. PublisherTransformerSubscriber Publisher: output_tables writes a Tabsdata Table.@publisher(source=PostgresSrc(...),output_tables=["orders"],)def clean_orders(orders):cleaned = ...return cleanedTabsdata Tableorders Because dependencies are declared ahead of time, Tabsdata automatically links each table version to the function and function code that produced it. These versions are then grouped into an execution plan, along with the other tables and functions affected by the execution. Version 1Version 2Version 3 Version 3 of the customers table was written by version 2 of the pub_customers function.Functionpub_customersVersionsVersion 1Oct 12Version 2Oct 24Code@publisher( source=PostgresSrc(queries=[ "SELECT customer_id, name, email, region, " "signup_date::date AS signup_date " "FROM customers", ]), output_tables=["customers"],)def pub_customers(customers): return customersTablecustomersVersionsVersion 1Oct 20Version 2Oct 24Version 3Oct 27SamplenameemailregionAna Ruizana@example.comEMEABen Okaforben@example.comAMERChen Weichen@example.comAPAC5 rowsFunction version 2Created Oct 27, 09:13

Each time a Function run successfully returns data, Tabsdata creates a new, immutable table version while preserving all previous versions of the table's data and schema. Functions can also read previous Table versions. An input written as customers@HEAD^ reads the version before the latest, and customers@HEAD~2..HEAD reads a range of versions ending at the latest. HEADHEAD^HEAD~2..HEAD Uses the latest version of customers as input. A transformer with input_tables set to customers@HEAD.@transformer(input_tables=["customers@HEAD"],output_tables=["customers_report"],)def report(customers):...

Each Table version stores its own schema, so a Table's version history records changes to its schema as well as its data. Comparing the schema of one Table version with another shows which columns were added, removed, or changed type.
Functions have their own version history. Whenever a Function is updated, Tabsdata creates a new Function version, retaining a changelog of all previous versions of the function's code.
In the Tabsdata User Interface, lineage can be viewed from Tables, Execution Plans, and Functions.

Opening a Table shows three tabs: Schema, Lineage, and Sample. The Lineage tab shows a graph of the Execution Plan that wrote the selected table version. This execution plan is unique to the specific table version, and exploring the lineage of other versions can show the evolution of a particular execution plan. orders_clean Tabsdata›Collections›sales›orders_clean SchemaLineageSample Schema Table schema defines the structure of a table by listing its columns and their data types. Object Type order_id i64 customer_id i64 amount f64 ordered_at datetime

The living semantic catalog is the record the Tabsdata Server keeps of what every connected source and destination holds and how that data can be used. Each source and destination collection has an entry in it: the entities its connection exposes, their fields, and an AI-generated classification of the data. Tabsdata builds the catalog on its own. Soon after a source or destination collection is created, the server connects to the external system, fetches its metadata, and classifies what it found. The catalog is living because it follows the external systems: when their metadata changes, the connection is classified again, so nobody curates the catalog by hand and it reflects what the systems contain as of the last refresh. Agents connected to Tabsdata read the catalog when a user asks them to publish from or subscribe to an external system, and use it to tell the user what data is there and how to use it.

Creating a source or destination collection with its connection starts the process. Nothing else is needed from the user. Soon after the collection is created, the server runs a probe against the external system with the collection's connection. The probe first checks that the system can be reached with the credentials the connection holds. The probe then reads the system's own metadata: the entities it holds, such as tables, reports, files, objects, or topics, and the fields of each entity. Tabsdata stores the entities with their names and fields, and a fingerprint of the whole schema. Data is not copied into the catalog. The server's classifier sends the entity list and the collection's description to the configured AI model, together with a few sample rows when the server allows sampling (catalog.maintenance_samples). The model's answer is recorded as the connection's classification. The entities and their classification become the connection's entry in the catalog, searchable by keyword and by meaning. The probe repeats on a schedule, and the classification is redone whenever the metadata the probe finds has changed. See Keeping It Current.

The probe reads the metadata the external system already keeps about itself, through the same connector that later moves the data. Each entity is stored with its fully qualified name, its kind, and its fields, plus details that depend on the system. System Entities Recorded for each entity SQL databases: Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2 tables and views, by database and schema columns with type, primary key, and column comments Databricks tables, by Unity Catalog catalog and schema columns with type and comments Salesforce reports, by folder, with their report id; SOQL objects report columns; object fields and whether they are required Object stores and files: Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, local files buckets and prefixes the file patterns found under each prefix, their format, and the columns read from them MongoDB collections, by database collection type (collection, view, time series), indexes, and validators Kafka topics partition count
documents.s: What Is Fetched From Each System

documents.t: To classify a connection, the server gives the configured AI model a compact description of the whole connection and asks for a structured judgement of the data. The model receives every entity with its fields, grouped the way the system groups them (database and schema, folder, bucket, namespace), the collection's description, and any sample rows the classifier read. The result is one classification per connection: Field What it says Label a short name for the data, such as "Customer data" or "Market signals" Domain the business domain: CRM, finance, marketing, engineering, operations, product, HR, supply chain, security, infrastructure, IoT, analytics, ecommerce Contains what the data holds, one item per subject Use cases what this data is typically used for Sensitivity public, internal, confidential, or restricted Freshness real-time, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, or static Typical sources where this kind of data usually comes from Search terms the synonyms and business words people would search for it by Names, comments, and sample values read from the external system are passed to the model as data, never as instructions, and sample values are never copied into the classification. Each classification records the fingerprint of the schema it was made from. Comparing that fingerprint with the current one tells Tabsdata when the classification is out of date.

Tabsdata re-reads each connection's metadata on a schedule and whenever a user or an agent asks for a refresh. The schedule is set by catalog.refresh_interval in the server configuration, which is 24 hours as shipped. On every read, the probe compares the fingerprint of the metadata it found with the stored fingerprint. If the fingerprints match, the catalog keeps its entities and its classification. If they differ, because of a new table, an altered table, a new report, or a new file pattern, the stored entities are replaced. Because the stored classification was made for the old schema, the connection is then classified again in full. Tabsdata never attempts a partial update: the model sees the whole connection every time, so the label, the subjects, and the search terms stay consistent with everything the connection now holds. A classification can also be requested by hand, for example after a collection's description was improved, and the connection is classified again on the next sweep. An existing classification can be discarded, and the next sweep then redoes it.

When a user asks an agent connected to Tabsdata to publish from or subscribe to an external system, the agent reads the catalog before it writes any code. To find data, the agent searches the catalog across every connection the user can see. A question like "Where do we keep invoices?" becomes a search by keyword and by meaning over collection names and descriptions, entity names, fields, and the classification's search terms, and the agent answers from the hits instead of guessing names. To describe one source or destination collection, the agent lists the collection's entities and their fields, and says what the classification found the data to be and how sensitive and how fresh it is. To propose a function, the agent works from the entities in the catalog. For a source, the agent proposes a publisher over the entities that matter, with the real column names and types. For a destination, the agent proposes a subscriber for the tables to deliver, written to the entities the destination exposes. See Configure Your AI Agent to set up an agent with Tabsdata.

The catalog is read and maintained with tdk. Every command takes -P <project> and names a source or destination collection, because each connection belongs to exactly one collection. Task Command Show the connection's catalog status: last check, last refresh, entity count, and whether the entity list was truncated tdk connection get -n <collection> List the entities and, with --fields, their fields tdk connection entities -n <collection> [--fields] [--filter fqn:lk:<glob>] Check that the external system can be reached tdk connection check -n <collection> Re-read the metadata now tdk connection refresh -n <collection> Show the classification and whether the schema changed since it was made tdk ai catalog show -n <collection> Classify the connection again on the next sweep tdk ai catalog classify -n <collection> Discard the classification so the next sweep redoes it tdk ai catalog unclassify -n <collection> Search every connection you can see, by keyword and by meaning tdk ai search connections --query "<words>" Viewing a connection's catalog status and its classification requires permission to view the project. Listing its entities, checking it, refreshing it, reading sample rows, and requesting a classification require permission to develop in the project. Discarding a classification requires permission to manage the project.
documents.s: Working With the Catalog in tdk

A custom connector allows Tabsdata to connect to external systems that are not officially supported by the current suite of Tabsdata connectors. Custom Connectors are Python packages that can be coded by hand or by coding agents working with Tabsdata through tdk.

This guide builds a SQLite connector as an example. Create a directory named sqlite_connector with the following files. The Python package lives in src/tabsdata_sqlite. ⌄sqlite_connector pyproject.toml ⌄src ⌄tabsdata_sqlite error.py __init__.py _plugin.py pyproject.toml defines the package, dependencies, and entry points Tabsdata uses to discover the connector. error.py defines errors for invalid configuration and failed reads or writes. __init__.py defines the connection and function configuration classes users import. _plugin.py implements the read and write logic and registers the connector with Tabsdata. tip Download the connector template using the button at the top right of the file tree, or copy the files below. The highlighted lines are the main parts you would change when adapting this example to another system.

pyproject.toml defines the package metadata, Python dependencies, and entry points Tabsdata uses to load the connector. When adapting this file: Set the package name, version, and description. Add any Python packages the connector needs to dependencies. Define one entry point for each source or destination the package provides. pyproject.toml [build-system] requires = ["setuptools>=69"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [project] name = "tabsdata-conn-sqlite" version = "0.1.0" description = "Tabsdata source and destination connector for SQLite databases." requires-python = ">=3.12" dependencies = [ "tabsdata>=2.1,<2.2", ] [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] [project.entry-points."tabsdatak.connectors"] src_sqlite = "tabsdata_sqlite._plugin:SQLITE_SRC" dest_sqlite = "tabsdata_sqlite._plugin:SQLITE_DEST"

error.py defines the different errors that can occur during connector usage. SQLITE_1 through SQLITE_4 are assigned to the configuration classes in __init__.py and report invalid connection or function settings. SQLITE_1 when the source connection document fails validation (invalid credentials) SQLITE_1 when the destination connection document fails validation (invalid credentials) SQLITE_3 when the source connector fails validation (missing/invalid arguments provided) SQLITE_4 when the destination connector fails validation (missing/invalid arguments provided) You can define additional error codes in error.py and raise them in _plugin.py to handle failures during execution. SQLITE_5 when a query fails. SQLITE_6 when the number of returned tables does not match the configured destination tables. SQLITE_7 when a write fails. Message placeholders such as {table} are filled when .exception() is called. error.py from tabsdatak.conn.common.error import ConnException, ConnInitException from tabsdatak.error import ErrorCode, ErrorDef class SqliteRuntimeException(ConnException): """A SQLite read or write failed.""" class SqliteErrorCode(ErrorCode): SQLITE_1 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteSrcConn validation failed") SQLITE_2 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteDestConn validation failed") SQLITE_3 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteSrc validation failed") SQLITE_4 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteDest validation failed") SQLITE_5 = ErrorDef(SqliteRuntimeException, "SQLite query {index} failed") SQLITE_6 = ErrorDef( SqliteRuntimeException, "SQLite received {slots} table(s) for {tables} target table(s)", ) SQLITE_7 = ErrorDef(SqliteRuntimeException, "SQLite write to {table} failed")

__init__.py defines the classes users import from tabsdata_sqlite and what arguments these classes can accept. SqliteSrcConn: Connection Document for Source Connectors SqliteSrc: Source Connector SqliteDestConn: Connection for Destination Connectors SqliteDest: Destination Connector Within each class, define the configuration fields and their types. Pass the appropriate validation error code as the first argument to the @_api.dataclass decorator. @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_1, kw_only=True) class SqliteSrcConn(Conn): """Connection to the SQLite database a publisher reads.""" path: StrOrSecretSpec tip The SqlLiteSrcConn above is configured to accept a single path argument as either a string or a secret. If this condition is not met, it throws the SQLite_1 error code. __init__.py from typing import Annotated, Literal from pydantic import StringConstraints import tabsdatak._api as _api from tabsdatak.api import Dest, Secret, Src, StrOrSecretSpec from tabsdatak.spi import Conn from tabsdata_sqlite.error import SqliteErrorCode TableName = Annotated[str, StringConstraints(pattern=r"^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$")] def resolve(spec: StrOrSecretSpec) -> str: return spec.value() if isinstance(spec, Secret) else spec @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_1, kw_only=True) class SqliteSrcConn(Conn): """Connection to the SQLite database a publisher reads.""" path: StrOrSecretSpec @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_2, kw_only=True) class SqliteDestConn(Conn): """Connection to the SQLite database a subscriber writes.""" path: StrOrSecretSpec @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_3, kw_only=True) class SqliteSrc(Src): """Queries a publisher runs against SQLite.""" queries: list[str] @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_4, kw_only=True) class SqliteDest(Dest): """SQLite tables that receive a subscriber's returned data.""" tables: list[TableName] if_table_exists: Literal["append", "replace"] = "replace" Under this configuration, the source connection defines where Tabsdata connects the source connector defines what query to read from the database the destination connection defines where Tabsdata connects the destination connector defines what Tabsdata tables are written into SQLite and whether to append or replace existing tables. During execution, Tabsdata passes both objects to the connector plugin. __init__.py · Connection class SqliteSrcConn(Conn): path: StrOrSecretSpec → conn-sqlite-in.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdata_sqlite:SqliteSrcConn spec: path: str:/data/shop.db __init__.py · Source class SqliteSrc(Src): queries: list[str] → pub_shop.py source=SqliteSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM customers", "SELECT * FROM orders", ], )

_plugin.py contains the connector's runtime logic that uses the inputs defined in __init__.py SqliteSrcPlugin.read_in: Runs each query from the Publisher configuration. Wraps each query result as a polars LazyFrame. Returns the frames as LazyFrameInputs with to_lazy_frame_inputs, in the same order as src.queries. If a query fails, the plugin raises SQLITE_5 with the query index and original exception. SqliteDestPlugin.write_out: Checks that the number of returned table slots matches dest.tables. Matches each returned file to the destination table in the same position. Skips any None file reference. Reads each remaining Parquet file. Replaces or appends to the destination table based on dest.if_table_exists. _plugin.py import sqlite3 from collections.abc import Iterable import polars as pl from tabsdatak.spi import ( DestContext, DestDef, DestPlugin, LazyFrameInput, SrcDef, SrcPlugin, SrcPluginCtx, TableFileSpec, TableMode, to_lazy_frame_inputs, ) from tabsdata_sqlite import ( SqliteDest, SqliteDestConn, SqliteSrc, SqliteSrcConn, resolve, ) from tabsdata_sqlite.error import SqliteErrorCode def connect(conn: SqliteSrcConn | SqliteDestConn) -> sqlite3.Connection: return sqlite3.connect(resolve(conn.path)) class SqliteSrcPlugin(SrcPlugin[SqliteSrcConn, SqliteSrc]): def read_in( self, ctx: SrcPluginCtx, conn: SqliteSrcConn, src: SqliteSrc, ) -> list[Iterable[LazyFrameInput]]: con = connect(conn) try: frames = [] for index, query in enumerate(src.queries): try: frame = pl.read_database(query, con) except Exception as e: raise SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_5.exception(cause=e, index=index) frames.append([frame.lazy()]) return to_lazy_frame_inputs(frames) finally: con.close() class SqliteDestPlugin(DestPlugin[SqliteDestConn, SqliteDest]): def write_out( self, ctx: DestContext, conn: SqliteDestConn, dest: SqliteDest, tables: list[TableFileSpec], ) -> None: if len(tables) != len(dest.tables): raise SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_6.exception( slots=len(tables), tables=len(dest.tables) ) con = connect(conn) try: with con: con.execute("BEGIN") for table, parquet in zip(dest.tables, tables): if parquet is None: continue try: frame = pl.read_parquet(parquet) columns = ", ".join( '"' + c.replace('"', '""') + '"' for c in frame.columns ) if dest.if_table_exists == "replace": con.execute(f'DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "{table}"') con.execute( f'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "{table}" ({columns})' ) marks = ", ".join("?" for _ in frame.columns) con.executemany( f'INSERT INTO "{table}" ({columns}) VALUES ({marks})', frame.iter_rows(), ) except Exception as e: raise SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_7.exception(cause=e, table=table) finally: con.close() SQLITE_SRC = SrcDef( conn=SqliteSrcConn, type_="sqlite-sql-in", system="SQLite", src_version="v1", src=SqliteSrc, table_mode=TableMode.SINGLE, cardinality=lambda src: len(src.queries), plugin=SqliteSrcPlugin, explorer=None, icon=None, ) SQLITE_DEST = DestDef( conn=SqliteDestConn, type_="sqlite-sql-out", system="SQLite", dest_version="v1", dest=SqliteDest, cardinality=lambda dest: len(dest.tables), plugin=SqliteDestPlugin, explorer=None, icon=None, )

The connector package must be installed in two places: Wherever tdk runs locally, so Tabsdata can validate connections and register Functions. In the server's Function environment, so the connector is available when those Functions execute. Local Git PyPI Step 1Install the local package where tdk runs From the directory containing sqlite_connector, run: pip install ./sqlite_connector Step 2Add the local package to the server's Function environment requirements.txt tabsdata-conn-sqlite @ file:///absolute/path/to/sqlite_connector Step 3Update the server's Function environment tdkserver venv update \ --name fn \ --requirements requirements.txt danger This command overwrites Tabsdata's existing list of package requirements. Include every complementary package the environment still needs, not just the new one being added. Step 1Install the Git package where tdk runs Replace <org> and <repo> with the repository containing the connector: pip install "git+https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git#subdirectory=sqlite_connector" Step 2Add the Git package to the server's Function environment requirements.txt tabsdata-conn-sqlite @ git+https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git#subdirectory=sqlite_connector Step 3Update the server's Function environment After tdkserver quickstart has created the instance, update its fn environment to include the package. tdkserver venv update \ --instance <TABSDATA_INSTANCE> \ --name fn \ --requirements requirements.txt danger This command overwrites Tabsdata's existing list of package requirements. Include every complementary package the environment still needs, not just the new one being added. Step 1Install the published package where tdk runs After publishing the connector to PyPI, install its package: pip install tabsdata-conn-sqlite==0.1.0 Step 2Add the published package to the server's Function environment requirements.txt tabsdata-conn-sqlite==0.1.0 Step 3Update the server's Function environment After tdkserver quickstart has created the instance, update its fn environment to include the package. tdkserver venv update \ --instance <TABSDATA_INSTANCE> \ --name fn \ --requirements requirements.txt danger This command overwrites Tabsdata's existing list of package requirements. Include every complementary package the environment still needs, not just the new one being added.

Step 4Generate the connection documents This works as long as SQLITE_SRC and SQLITE_DEST are registered through the tabsdatak.connectors entry points in pyproject.toml. tip Run tdk connection types to confirm that tdk can discover both custom connector types. Generate the appropriate connection template: Source Destination tdk connection template --type sqlite-sql-in --file conn-sqlite-in.yaml tdk connection template --type sqlite-sql-out --file conn-sqlite-out.yaml Step 5Fill out the connection documents The spec field contains the arguments defined in __init__.py. A completed document will look like this: Source Destination conn-sqlite-in.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdata_sqlite:SqliteSrcConn spec: path: str:/data/shop.db conn-sqlite-out.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdata_sqlite:SqliteDestConn spec: path: str:/data/warehouse.db Step 6Attach the connections to Collections New Collection Existing Collection Create a new collection and attach the filled-out connection document. Source Destination tdk collection create --name shop --group sources --conn-file conn-sqlite-in.yaml tdk collection create --name warehouse --group destinations --conn-file conn-sqlite-out.yaml Update an existing collection with the filled-out connection document. Source Destination tdk collection update --name shop --conn-file conn-sqlite-in.yaml tdk collection update --name warehouse --conn-file conn-sqlite-out.yaml

Publisher Subscriber pub_shop.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdata_sqlite import SqliteSrc @publisher( source=SqliteSrc(queries=["SELECT * FROM customers", "SELECT * FROM orders"]), output_tables=["customers", "orders"], ) def pub_shop( customers: TableFrameSpec, orders: TableFrameSpec ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return customers, orders Register into Tabsdata​ tdk fn register --coll shop --path pub_shop.py::pub_shop sub_warehouse.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec from tabsdata_sqlite import SqliteDest @subscriber( destination=SqliteDest(tables=["customers", "orders"], if_table_exists="replace"), input_tables=["shop/customers", "shop/orders"], ) def sub_warehouse( customers: TableFrameSpec, orders: TableFrameSpec ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return customers, orders Register into Tabsdata​ tdk fn register --coll warehouse --path sub_warehouse.py::sub_warehouse
