tdk fn register --coll warehouse --path sub_warehouse.py::sub_warehouse

A Project is the top-level workspace inside a Tabsdata Server. Projects organize related workflows and their resources while isolating them from other Projects on the same Server. This allows multiple teams to share a single Server without interfering with each other's work.

Most Tabsdata operations are performed within the context of a Project. You can set a default Project for the tdk CLI using: tdk set --proj sales_analytics The selected Project remains the default for subsequent commands. Commands that support the --proj option can target a different Project without changing the default.

Creating a Project establishes an empty workspace within an existing Server. Groups and Collections can then be created to organize the Functions and Tables that make up your workflows. Deleting a Project removes the Project and its resources without affecting other Projects on the Server. See Create a Project, Update a Project, and Delete a Project for step-by-step instructions.

A Project can hold secrets: named groups of keys and values, such as the credentials of an API that its Functions call. Every Function of the Project can read them while it runs. Project secrets are for values your own function code needs. Credentials that a connector uses to read from or write to an external system stay in Connections.

Write the secrets in a YAML file. Each top-level entry is a secret, and each secret maps its keys to their values: weather_api: token: abc123 # the value itself account: $secret:WEATHER_ACCOUNT # read from the WEATHER_ACCOUNT environment variable region: # no value: keep the value already stored A value written as $secret:<VARIABLE> is read from that environment variable in the shell that runs tdk, so the value never has to be written in the file. A key with no value keeps the value already stored, or is empty if there is none; write "" to store an empty value. NOTE: Only project admins can manage project secrets. Pass the file when you create or update the Project: tdk project create --name sales_analytics --secrets-file secrets.yaml tdk project update --name sales_analytics --secrets-file secrets.yaml warning Each update replaces all the secrets of the Project. A secret or key left out of the file is removed. To see which secrets a Project holds, run: tdk project secrets --name sales_analytics It lists each secret and its keys. Values are never shown, and there is no way to read them back out of Tabsdata.

Give the Function a final ctx: FunctionCtx parameter and read a value by secret and key: from tabsdatak.api import FunctionCtx, TableFrame, transformer @transformer(input_tables=["cities"], output_tables=["forecast"]) def forecast(cities: TableFrame, ctx: FunctionCtx) -> TableFrame: token = ctx.secret("weather_api", "token") # or, in one string: ctx.secret("weather_api.token") ... Secret and key names are not case-sensitive. ctx.secret_names lists the secrets of the Project, and ctx.secret_keys("weather_api") the keys of one of them. Reading a secret or key that does not exist raises KeyError. note Only Function code receives Project secrets. Connector plugins do not, and the values are not placed in the Function's environment variables.

Before you start Finish Install Tabsdata and Configure Your AI Agent first, and make sure the server is running. This quickstart uses a coding agent with the Tabsdata skill. To deploy and run Tabsdata without an LLM, switch to the developer doc mirror. How to Switch Mirrors We will be building a Tabsdata Workflow that: ingests a local persons.csv into a Tabsdata table called persons builds a second table called people that drops the age column and adds a full_name column writes people back to your file system as people.jsonl ▶ Trigger execution planReset🔍 Zoom inClick any node for what it does Local File Local File Publisher qs_pub Pending Table persons Pending Transformer qs_tfr Pending Table people Pending Subscriber qs_sub Pending Local File Local File Not written yet Step 1Get the example project tdk examples extract --name quickstart-ai --dir qs-example ⌄qs-example ⌄input-data persons.csv ⌄output-data conn-input.yaml conn-output.yaml README.txt Creates qs-example/, which contains the source data persons.csv and two connection files. Step 2Login to Tabsdata and start your LLM Log in, then start your agent from the same terminal: Claude Code Codex tdk login --server localhost --user admin --password tabsdata claude tdk login --server localhost --user admin --password tabsdata codex Step 3Prompt your LLM to build a Tabsdata workflow Give the following prompt to your LLM: Build a tabsdata workflow that 1. ingests `qs-example/input-data/persons.csv` 2. creates a new column for the full name and drops the age column, 3. writes the result as a .jsonl to the `output-data` folder More info can be found under `qs-example/README.md` AI agent session ❯Build a tabsdata workflow that 1. ingests qs-example/input-data/persons.csv 2. creates a new column for the full name and drops the age column, 3. writes the result as a .jsonl to the output-data folder More info can be found under qs-example/README.md Read 1 file, listed 1 directory (ctrl+o to expand) ⏺ persons.csv has first_name, last_name and age. Three functions cover this: a publisher for the CSV, a transformer for the column changes, and a subscriber for the .jsonl. Getting the connection and publisher guides. Called tabsdata 3 times (ctrl+o to expand) ⏺ Writing conn-input.yaml, then a source collection pointed at input-data. Called tabsdata 2 times (ctrl+o to expand) ⏺ Registering the publisher that produces persons. @publisher( source=LocalFileSrc(paths=["persons.csv"], format=SrcFileFormat.CSV), output_tables=["persons"], ) def ingest_persons(rows: TableFramesSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return rows[0] if rows else None Called tabsdata 2 times (ctrl+o to expand) ⏺ Registered and committed. Now the transformer — full_name from first_name and last_name, age dropped. @transformer( input_tables=["persons"], output_tables=["people"], ) def build_people(persons: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return persons.with_columns( (col("first_name") + " " + col("last_name")).alias("full_name"), ).drop("first_name", "last_name", "age") Called tabsdata 2 times (ctrl+o to expand) ⏺ Registered and committed. Last, the subscriber writing people out as .jsonl. Getting the connection and subscriber guides. Called tabsdata 3 times (ctrl+o to expand) ⏺ Writing conn-output.yaml, then a destination collection pointed at output-data. Called tabsdata 2 times (ctrl+o to expand) ⏺ Registering the subscriber. @subscriber( input_tables=["people"], destination=LocalFileDest(paths=["people.jsonl"], format=DestFileFormat.JSON), ) def export_people(people: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return people Called tabsdata 3 times (ctrl+o to expand) ⏺ Registered. The publisher's commit triggered the transformer, which triggered the subscriber, all in one execution plan — committed, 0 failures. ⏺ people.jsonl is live in qs-example/output-data/: ┌──────────────┐ │ full_name │ ├──────────────┤ │ Ada Lovelace │ ├──────────────┤ │ Grace Hopper │ └──────────────┘ Step 4Check Workflow Execution ⌄qs-example ⌄input-data persons.csv ⌄output-data people.jsonl conn-input.yaml conn-output.yaml README.txt After your LLM finishes processing your request, you should have a new people.jsonl file in the qs-example/output-data/ folder. Step 5Open the UI Go to http://localhost:2457 and log in with admin / tabsdata. You'll see your project, its collections, and the tables the flow just produced.

Credentials used by Publisher and Subscriber Functions are stored in Connections. Connections are credential stores that are indirectly attached to a function and enable the function access to specific credentials. A Project can also hold secrets that its Functions read directly. See Project Secrets. To register a credential into Tabsdata, the user must generate a .yaml connection document template through the tdk connection template cli command and fill in the required credentials. Once the document is completed, it must be attached to a collection through the tdk collection create or tdk collection update cli command. During connection registration, Tabsdata dehydrates the Connection document by extracting its credentials into a separate secret store and replacing them in the stored Connection with references to those secrets. COLLECTIONWRITTEN INTOREGISTERED INTOUSED BYpasswordconnection documentConnectionFunction Once stored, credentials are only made available to a Function when it runs. In fact, once credentials are in Tabsdata, there is no way to read them out of the system. This is by design, ensuring your secrets are always secure. When a coding agent builds workflows for you, it can only pass credentials into Tabsdata that you give it. Understand the security implications of providing credentials to your LLM before you do. There are several ways to pass secrets to an LLM for creating connections.

The most secure option is to create the Connection outside of the agent. You can ask the agent to generate a Connection template, then add the credentials yourself, and register the Connection with Tabsdata using the tdk collection create or tdk connection update` CLI command. The agent can then create or register Functions against the Collection without ever accessing the credentials required. This keeps the credentials out of the agent's context and session history.

Connection templates can reference credentials using $secret:<VARIABLE>. When working through an agent, the environment variable must be available to the process running the LLM and the Tabsdata server. This means the variable must be set in the shell environment before both processes are started. This avoids placing the credential directly in the agent prompt, but still gives the agent process access to it. Environment variables may also be visible to other processes running in the same environment. For these reasons, environment variables are better suited for development and testing than for long-lived production credentials. Adding or updating secrets also requires restarting both the agent and the Tabsdata server with the updated shell environment. warning Storing credentials in environment variables does not prevent the agent from accessing their values. However, it allows the agent to pass the environment variable name as a literal to the Tabsdata server, which can then resolve the value server-side. This reduces the likelihood of the secret being captured in the agent's transcript.

You can also provide credentials directly to the agent and have it create the Connection for you. This is the simplest option, but the credential passes through the agent's context and may be stored in its session history. Credentials provided this way may be at increased risk for exposure.
documents.s: Provide Credentials Directly to the Agent

documents.t: In scenarios where the agent is requesting multiple points of data, or in sessions where providing credentials directly inline requires pasting the same content multiple times, you can pass all relevant data into a .txt file and pass the path to the agent during your session warning Putting credentials in a file and asking an agent to read that file does not prevent the agent from accessing them. Once the agent reads the file, the credentials have passed through the agent just as if they were provided directly.

A Tabsdata Server is the top-level Tabsdata process deployed on a machine. It stores and manages Tabsdata resources, executes workflows, stores tabular data, and isolates Tabsdata processes from other processes running on the machine. You can interact with a Server through the Tabsdata UI, the tdk CLI, or the Python API, and coding agents work with it through tdk.

The main units of work within Tabsdata are Functions, which perform work on data, and Tables, which store data produced by Functions. As the the top-level process Tabsdata, Servers store Functions and Tables as well as several organizational layers that nest functions and tables: Projects are the top-level workspaces within a Server. Projects isolate their resources and workflows from those in other Projects, allowing multiple teams or workflows to share a single Server without interfering with one another. Groups organize resources according to their role in a workflow. For example, a Project might have separate Groups for ingesting source data, cleaning data, and loading processed data. Collections define transaction boundaries for their Tables, determining how data is committed or rolled back during an execution. Collections are also credential stores that can provide Functions inside them with the credentials needed to connect to external systems. Server Projects Groups Collections FunctionsConnectionsTables

A Tabsdata server uses three dedicated endpoints when running: A public endpoint runs on port 2457 by default. The Tabsdata UI, tdk CLI, and Python API use this endpoint to communicate with the Server. A private endpoint runs on port 2458 by default. Tabsdata services use this endpoint for internal communication. An AI agent endpoint runs on port 2459 by default. The Tabsdata Conversational agent, Tabby, uses this endpoint. Using default port configuration, the default local URI for the public endpoint is: http://localhost:2457 You can connect to a Server using several interfaces: The Tabsdata UI provides a browser-based interface for managing resources, running workflows, and inspecting results. The tdk CLI provides command-line access to the Server. The Python API provides programmatic access from Python applications. Coding agents work with the Server through tdk, guided by the Tabsdata skill.

The tdkserver CLI manages the Server lifecycle, including initializing, creating, starting, and stopping a Server. See Deploy Tabsdata on k-minus for Quickstart and the complete local Server lifecycle. For a managed Kubernetes deployment, choose AWS EKS, Azure AKS, or Google GKE. To connect an AI agent, see Configure Your AI Agent.

A service token is a credential owned by a user that automation such as CI jobs, schedulers and scripts uses to call Tabsdata as that user, without a password. A service token acts with a narrowed subset of its owner's permissions: project development work only.

Each user account holds at most two service tokens, in slots 1 and 2. With two slots, you can create a new token while the old one is still in use. A token starts with tdst_ and is displayed only once, when it is created. The server stores only a SHA-256 digest of the token and can never show it again. Every token is created with a lifetime in days. The deployment's service_tokens.max_days setting is the ceiling (90 in the shipped configurations). A token that never expires (-1) works only where max_days is -1. If max_days is not set, service tokens are disabled on that deployment. A token stops working when any of the following happens: the token expires the owner or an administrator revokes the token the owner's account is disabled the owner's account is deleted Changing the owner's password does not affect existing tokens. A session started with a token is never renewed, and lasts until the token expires or is revoked. Clients send the token in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header.

To rotate a token without downtime: Create a token in the free slot. Move your consumers to the new token. Wait until Last used for the old slot stops changing. Last used updates about every ten minutes. Revoke the old slot.

Open Account → Service tokens. The page shows Slot 1 and Slot 2. A filled slot shows the token's prefix (tdst_v1_<hint>…), its comment, and when the token was created, when it expires and when it was last used. To create a token, click Create token in an empty slot. Choose Expires after a number of days (90 by default) or Never expires, add an optional comment of up to 200 characters, then click Create token. Click Copy in the Token created in slot N panel. The token is shown only on this page. After you click Dismiss or leave the page, you can't get the token back. If you lose it, revoke the slot and create a new token. To revoke a token, click Revoke in a filled slot, then Revoke token. Every client using that token stops working immediately.

To manage tokens, log in with your username and password first. tdk auth service-token create --slot 1 --expires-in-days 90 --comment "nightly CI" tdk auth service-token list tdk auth service-token revoke --slot 1 create prints the token once. --expires-in-days has no default: pass a positive number, or -1 for a token that never expires. create is refused if the slot already has a token. Revoke that slot first. list shows each slot's hint, comment, creation time, expiry and Last used (updated about every ten minutes). To run commands as a token, export the token and log in. With no value, --token reads the TDK_TOKEN environment variable, so the token never appears in shell history: export TDK_TOKEN=tdst_v1_... tdk login --server https://tabsdata.example.com --token --token cannot be combined with --user or --password. A token login is never renewed. When the token expires or is revoked, log in again with a new token. See tdk auth for every flag of the service-token commands.
documents.s: Managing tokens with the tdk CLI

documents.t: A token carries two of its owner's project permissions, view_project and develop_project, in the projects where the owner holds them. A token never has more permissions than its owner. The server reads the owner's current grants every time the token is used. If an administrator removes a project grant from the owner, the token loses that grant immediately. Higher roles count. If the owner has manage_project on a project, the token gets develop_project there. A system admin's token can therefore do development work in every project. Area What the token can do Projects List and read the owner's projects; read their groups, metrics, snapshots and in-flight work Collections Create, update, delete and read collections; read a collection's connection Functions Register, update, patch, enable, delete and trigger functions; read history, executions and bundles Tables Read schema, samples, data versions and lineage; download data; delete tables Runs List plans, transactions and function runs; cancel and recover them; replay function runs Workers List workers and read or tail their logs Identity GET /auth/info (who am I) and read its own token record

Every other operation is refused with 403 This operation cannot be performed with a service token, even when the owner holds the permission. A leaked token therefore can't grant access, create accounts or create another token. Not carried What this blocks for a token manage_access (system) Managing users, permission grants and other users' tokens manage_roles (system) Creating, editing and assigning roles create_projects (system) Creating projects manage_project (project) Updating or deleting a project; creating, changing or deleting its groups Token management Creating, listing or revoking tokens, including its own. A token can't create its own replacement Account self-service Changing the owner's password; refreshing or extending its own session An administrator with manage_access can list and revoke any user's tokens through the REST API (/users/{user}/service-tokens), using a password session.
documents.s: Permissions a token does not carry

documents.t: Tabby is the built-in Tabsdata agent, opened from the Tabby page of the User Interface. Tabby answers questions about the resources on a Tabsdata Server and, when the Server allows it, creates and changes them on request. AITabby Did any execution plans fail in customer_management? No. The 10 most recent execution plans in customer_management all finished, and each one committed 5 function runs with no errors. The three latest: Execution plan Triggered by Status Duration ep20260924-14 salesforce/ingest_opportunities Finished 11s ep20260924-13 salesforce/ingest_leads Finished 12s ep20260924-12 salesforce/ingest_customers Finished 12s Each plan runs the Salesforce ingest for one entity, then its bronze, silver, and gold transformers and the Snowflake load. anthropic claude-sonnet-4-6 Ask anything about your data flows… (⌘K) ↑ The UI demo includes the Tabby page. Messages cannot be sent from the demo. Open Tabby in the UI demo

Tabby runs in the Server's AI agent service, on port 2459 by default, and requires an Anthropic or OpenAI API key. When no key is configured, the Server starts without the AI agent service and Tabby is unavailable. The key is set when the instance is created, with --config anthropic-key=… or --config openai-key=…: tdkserver quickstart --config anthropic-key=env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY To add or change the key on an existing instance, download the instance's config, set api_key under ai_providers.anthropic or ai_providers.openai in aiagent.yaml, and apply the change: tdkserver config get --with-secrets tdkserver config put --apply note Tabby runs in the Server's AI Agent process, on port 2459. The process starts only when an API key is provided during server initialization, and Tabby needs that key to be valid.

Open Tabby from the side navigation, or press ⌘K from any page to ask Tabby about the page you are viewing. A new chat offers four starting prompts: Set up a data flow Connect to an external system Check executions health Show me what Tabsdata can do Other pages suggest prompts for what they show. A Collection page, for example, suggests listing its Functions, listing its Tables, and creating a Publisher.

Commands are typed into the message box. Command Description /help Show available commands /new Start a new conversation /clear Clear the current conversation /export Export the conversation as Markdown /models List available providers and models /provider <name> Switch AI provider /model <name> Switch to a specific model, by full or partial name /health Show agent health and status /pop [name] Open resources from the conversation in new tabs, or one resource by name The provider and model can also be switched from the selector above the message box.

Chats are stored on the Server and can be continued later. From a chat, you can: Search the chat's messages Export the chat as Markdown Stop a response while it is being generated Retry a response that failed

Tabby can write a custom connector for a system that Tabsdata does not support natively. Tabby's reference includes the connector interface in tabsdatak.spi, and every connector installed on the Server, including custom ones, is part of what Tabby knows. Installing the connector remains a manual step. See Custom Connectors.
Whether Tabby can create, change, or delete resources is set by allow_writes in the Server's aiagent.yaml config.

Tables are a unique feature of Tabsdata. Unlike other data integration tools that discard intermediate data after execution, Tabsdata stores the data produced by functions in persistent, versioned Tables. Tables make it easier to monitor and debug workflows, inspect data from previous executions, track schema changes over time, and understand how data moves through a Project. Because Tables persist between executions, they can also be used as inputs by other functions and allow Tabsdata to automatically orchestrate workflows based on new data being committed.

Every Table maintains a complete version history. Each successful function execution that writes data to a Table creates a new version containing its own data and schema. Previous versions remain available, allowing users and functions to access the state of a Table from a specific execution. Each version also includes metadata about the execution that produced it and the function code used during that execution. persons Tabsdata›Collections›input›persons SchemaSample Schema Table schema defines the structure of a table by listing its columns and their data types. Object Type first_name str last_name str age i64 nationality str city str v2v1version Because each Table version maintains its own schema, schema changes between executions do not cause previous versions of the Table to become invalid.
Table schema defines the structure of a table by listing its columns and their data types. Object Type first_name str last_name str age i64 nationality str city str

Tables store the data that moves through a Tabsdata workflow. Functions read from and write to Tables depending on their role in the workflow. Publisher functions ingest data from external systems and write it to Tabsdata Tables. Tabsdata server collection · world? ▶ Trigger publisher Database PostgreSQL ? PostgreSQL · external Reachable Connection conn-postgres.yaml ? Publisher read_world ? Table country ? //world No versions yet Table city ? //world No versions yet Transformer functions read from Tabsdata Tables, transform the data, and write the results to new Tables. collection · world? collection · insights · data product? ▶ Trigger transformer Table country ? //world Committed Table city ? //world Committed Transformer find_big_cities ? Table big_cities ? //insights No versions yet Subscriber functions read from Tabsdata Tables and write the data to external systems. Tabsdata server collection · warehouse? ▶ Trigger subscriber Table vendors ? //sales Committed Table items ? //sales Committed Connection conn-mysql-dest.yaml ? Subscriber write_sales ? Database MySQL ? MySQL · external Not yet synced

Functions refer to their input Tables using the following format: [collection/]table[@version] If the Collection is omitted, Tabsdata looks for the Table within the Function's own Collection. For example: persons input/persons input/persons@HEAD The version can be used to select a specific version or set of versions of the Table: HEAD selects the latest version. HEAD^ selects the version immediately before HEAD. HEAD~N selects a version relative to HEAD. INITIAL selects the first version. A specific version ID selects that version. Comma-separated version IDs select multiple versions. a..b selects a range of versions. If no version is specified, the Function reads from HEAD. Tables can also be referenced across Collections within the same Project. Tables in another Project cannot be referenced.

Tables whose names begin with _ are private Tables. Private Tables can only be read by Functions within their own Collection. This makes them useful for intermediate data that needs to move between Functions in a Collection without being accessible to the rest of the Project. For example: _cleaned_customers A Function in the same Collection can use _cleaned_customers as an input, while Functions in other Collections cannot access it.

A new Table commit can also trigger downstream Functions. Transformers and Subscribers are automatically triggered when a new commit is made to one of their input Tables. This allows data to continue moving through a workflow as upstream Functions complete. A commit does not necessarily mean that the data itself changed. When a Publisher writes multiple Tables, it creates a new commit for each Table on every successful execution, even if the rows in a Table are identical to its previous version. Each commit can trigger Functions that use that Table as an input. See Working with Triggers to control which input Tables trigger a Function.
A transformer reads data from one or more Tabsdata tables, transforms them, and writes transformed data to new or existing tables in the Tabsdata server.

Here is an example transformer named process_sales. It reads three tabsdata tables, sums the sales_value data by sales_rep, and writes the resultant tables back to the Tabsdata server. There is a data quality check on the us_sales_by_sales_rep table. It filters out rows where rep_id is NULL, routing them to a separate clean_nulls quarantine table. The main us_sales_by_sales_rep table output only contains rows with valid (non-NULL) rep IDs. This transformer executes automatically as soon as a new commit occurs on any of its input tables: import tabsdata as td @td.transformer( input_tables=["us_sales", "eu_sales", "emea_sales"], output_tables=[ "us_sales_by_sales_rep", "eu_sales_by_sales_rep", "emea_sales_by_sales_rep", ], on_output_tables=[ dq.DataQuality( table="us_sales_by_sales_rep", classifiers=[ dq.IsNull("rep_id", tags="nulls"), ], operators=[ dq.Filter( criteria=dq.AnyFailed(tags="nulls", none_is_ok=False), to_table="clean_nulls", include_quality_columns="criteria", ), ], ) ], ) def process_sales(tf1: td.TableFrame, tf2: td.TableFrame, tf3: td.TableFrame): tf1 = tf1.group_by(td.col("sales_rep")).agg(td.col("sales_value").sum()) tf2 = tf2.group_by(td.col("sales_rep")).agg(td.col("sales_value").sum()) tf3 = tf3.group_by(td.col("sales_rep")).agg(td.col("sales_value").sum()) return tf1, tf2, tf3 note After defining the function, you need to register it with a Tabsdata collection and execute it. For more information, see Register a Function and Execute a Function. When you define a transformer, you specify the name of the transformer, the Tabsdata tables to read, and the names of the Tabsdata tables to write to. By default a transformer is triggered by a new commit to any of its input tables. To create and run a transformer, complete the following tasks: Define a transformer - Define a transformer to configure the parameters that govern the transformations of tables in the Tabsdata server. Register the transformer - Register the transformer with a Tabsdata collection. A transformer can read from tables in any Tabsdata collection, but can only write output tables to the collection that it is registered with. For information about registering functions, see here. Execute the transformer - Execute the transformer by initiating a trigger. Once executed, the transformer processes data from the specified input tables as defined in the function logic, then writes the results to tables in the Tabsdata server. By default, a commit on any of the input tables triggers a transformer. However, you can use any Tabsdata table as a trigger. For more information about executing a function, see here.

The following code uses placeholder values for defining a transformer: import tabsdata as td @td.transformer( input_tables=["<input_table1>", "<collection_name>/<input_table2>"], output_tables=["<output_table1>", "<output_table2>"], on_output_tables=[ dq.DataQuality( table="<output_table1>", classifiers=[ dq.IsNull("<table1_column1>", tags="nulls"), dq.IsPositive("<table1_column2>", tags="positive"), ], operators=[ dq.Enrich(), # add dq columns to `output_table1` dq.Summary(), # writes `output_table1_dq_summary` dq.Filter( criteria=dq.AnyFailed(tags="nulls", none_is_ok=False), to_table="output_table_nulls", include_quality_columns="criteria", ), ], ) ], trigger_by=["<trigger_table1>", "<trigger_table2>"], ) def <transformer_name>("<table_frame1>": td.TableFrame, "<table_frame2>"": td.TableFrame): <function_logic> return <table_frame_output1>, <table_frame_output2> note After defining the function, you need to register it with a Tabsdata collection and execute it. For more information, see Register a Function and Execute a Function. Following properties are defined in the setup code above:

<input_table_1> is the name of an input table in the collection that the function is registered with. <collection_name>/<input_table_2> is an input table from a collection that the transformer is not registered with. Tabsdata stores all the commits of a table in the Tabsdata server. Hence, you can have multiple commits of the same table in the input. You can read more about it here.
<output_table1>, <output_table2>… are the names of the Tabsdata tables to publish to.

A transformer may receive and return a None value instead of a TableFrame parameter or return value. When a transformer receives a None value instead of a TableFrame it means that the requested version does not exist, the input table has never been produced, or the table had no data up to that version. For example, a transformer that has a dependency on the previous version of one the tables it produces, has a None value as an input on its first execution since the input table doesn’t exist yet. When a transformer returns a None value instead of a TableFrame, it commits a new version of the associated table that holds the same data as the previous version. This helps in avoiding the creation of multiple copies of the same data.
documents.s: None as an input and output

documents.t: <trigger_table1>, <trigger_table2>… are the names of the tables in the Tabsdata server. A new commit to any of these tables triggers the publisher. All listed trigger tables must exist in the server before registering the publisher. Defining trigger tables is optional. If you don’t define the trigger_by property, the transformer will get triggered by any of its input tables. If you define the trigger_by property, then only those tables listed in the property can automatically trigger the transformer. For more information, see Working with Triggers.
<transformer_name> is the name for the transformer that you are configuring. It has be unique within all functions registered in a collection.

<function_logic> governs the processing performed by the publisher. You can specify function logic to be a simple write or to perform additional processing, such as dropping nulls, before writing data to output tables. For more information about the function logic that you can include, see Working with Tables. <table_frame1>, <table_frame2>… are the names for the variables that temporarily store source data for processing. <table_frame_output1>, <table_frame_output2>… are the output from the function that are stored as Tabsdata tables with names as defined in the tables property. Consequently, the number of tables returned from the function have to exactly match the number of tables defined in the tables property.
Triggers execute Tabsdata functions. A trigger can be initiated manually through a CLI command or the UI, automatically by a new commit to its associated table, or through Crontab configurations.

Manual triggers are initiated by a CLI command or the UI. For example, you can trigger a publisher to read sales data from a database table and publish it to the Tabsdata server. You can manually trigger any Tabsdata function, even those with a specified automated trigger.

To trigger a function, use the following command in a command line interface: $ tdk fn trigger --coll <collection_name> --name <function_name> Where: <collection_name> is the name of the collection in the Tabsdata server that the function is registered with. <function_name> is the name of the function to be executed. This name is defined when the function is registered.

Click on the collection name “tutorial” on the left hand side or from the collection list to open the view containing further details regarding the collection. Click on “Publishers” to open the publishers registered in the collection. Open the publisher details by clicking on “pub” in the list. Click on trigger on the top right to trigger the execution of the publisher. You can monitor the status of trigger through this diagram.

Automated triggers are initiated by a new commit to one of the tables associated with the function. For example, you might define an inventory subscriber function that exports data from a Tabsdata inventory table to AWS S3 every time the inventory table receives a commit. Note that a commit does not always include changes in the table data. For example, a publisher that writes to three tables performs a commit to all three tables with each execution, irrespective of whether there is a change in data for any of the tables. Since, the functions are automatically triggered which in turn create a new commit to other tables, Tabsdata enables a cascading workflow of updates to downstream tables.

Triggers in Tabsdata functions are defined using the trigger_by property. There are three ways to configure it: Select a configuration to see what it does and how it looks in code. 1Not defined2Empty array3Non-empty array Default behavior When trigger_by is omitted, the behavior depends on the kind of function: Publishers have no trigger by default, so the publisher can only be triggered manually. Transformers and subscribers are triggered by a commit to any of their input tables. To trigger on a different set of tables, define trigger_by with a non-empty array. transformer.pyNot defined @td.transformer( input_tables=["sales"], output_tables=["sales_by_rep"], ) def summarize(sales: tdf.TableFrame) -> tdf.TableFrame: return sales

With Crontab triggers, Publishers, Subscribers, and Transformers can be configured to run periodically within Tabsdata without the need for manual triggers or external schedulers. Similar to automated triggers, you work with the trigger_by parameter. However, unlike automated triggers, the trigger_by parameter must be configured with a CronTrigger object. The CronTrigger object requires a Unix crontab mask and accepts optional start and end parameters. note Tabsdata uses the UTC timezone to interpret all crontab schedules.

The mask Parameter​ The mask parameter defines the frequency of the execution. It follows the standard Unix crontab specification consisting of 5 elements with minute precision. Syntax: Minute Hour Day Month Day-of-Week Extensions: Non-standard extensions (e.g., @hourly, @daily) are not supported. Examples​ Mask Description 0,30 * * * * Runs every 30 minutes (at the top of the hour and at minute 30). 0 0 * * * Runs daily at the beginning of the day (00:00 UTC). 0 22 * * FRI Runs at 10:00 PM (22:00 UTC) every Friday. References​ Open Group Base Specification: Crontab Wikipedia: Cron The start and end Parameters​ These optional parameters define a specific window of time during which the schedule is valid. Format: - A Python datetime object with timezone information. An ISO 8601 string in the UTC timezone (e.g., 2024-01-01T12:00:00Z). Behavior: - If specified: Tabsdata will only trigger the function based on the mask between the start and end times. If omitted: Tabsdata will trigger the function indefinitely based on the mask, starting from the moment the function is successfully registered.

The execution of Crontab triggers is dependent on the enabled status of the function. Registration: When registering or updating a function, it can be set as enabled (default) or disabled via the tdk command line interface. Runtime Control: An existing function can be toggled between enabled and disabled states with tdk fn enable / tdk fn disable. - Enabled: Tabsdata will trigger the function according to the defined crontab mask. Disabled: Tabsdata will ignore the crontab mask and the function will not trigger automatically.

The following is an example of a Publisher configured to trigger at the beginning of every hour. from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc @publisher( trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), source=MySQLSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM my_table"], ), output_tables=["my_table"], ) def my_publisher(my_table: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return my_table The connection details (host, credentials) live on the collection's connection file, not in the function. See MySQL for the full setup.

A scheduled trigger runs a Function at fixed times, whether or not any upstream data has changed. Publishers, Transformers, and Subscribers can all use one. Configure it by passing a CronTrigger to trigger_by. from tabsdatak.api import CronTrigger, publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc @publisher( trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"), source=MySQLSrc(queries=["SELECT * FROM sales"]), output_tables=["sales"], ) def read_sales(sales: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return sales

The first argument is a standard Unix crontab mask with five fields and minute precision: Minute Hour Day Month Day-of-Week Mask Runs 0,30 * * * * every 30 minutes, on the hour and at minute 30 0 0 * * * daily at 00:00 0 22 * * FRI Fridays at 22:00 Non-standard shorthands such as @hourly and @daily are not supported. note All crontab schedules are interpreted in UTC.

CronTrigger also takes optional start and end parameters, each either a timezone-aware Python datetime or an ISO 8601 string in UTC (2026-01-01T12:00:00Z). With them set, the mask only fires between those two times. With them omitted, it fires indefinitely from the moment the Function is registered.

A cron schedule only runs while its Function is enabled. Registration defaults to enabled, and tdk fn register takes --enabled / --disabled explicitly. An already-registered Function is toggled with tdk fn enable and tdk fn disable. A disabled Function ignores its mask entirely. It does not queue missed runs and fire them on re-enable.
The example above names a MySQL query but carries no host and no password. Those live on the Collection's Connection. See Connections.

A manual trigger runs a Function on demand, from the CLI or the UI. Nothing about the Function's definition needs to change to allow it: every Function can be triggered by hand, including one that already has a cron or Table trigger configured.
tdk fn trigger --coll <collection_name> --name <function_name> <function_name> is the name the Function was registered under, not the name of its file.

A Publisher reads no Tabsdata Tables, so there is nothing upstream that could fire it. With no trigger_by on the decorator, a Publisher runs only when triggered manually. Transformers and Subscribers behave differently, because they do have input Tables. Left unconfigured, they run on a commit to any of them. See Table Commit Triggers.

Triggering one Function does not run only that Function. Tabsdata builds an Execution Plan covering every downstream Function that has to run as a result, and nothing commits unless all of them succeed. For the UI walkthrough and the full trigger_by reference, see Working with Triggers.
documents.s: What a manual trigger actually starts

documents.t: A stream trigger runs a Function each time a batch of streamed data is due. It is the only trigger a @stream_publisher has: that decorator takes no trigger_by at all. from tabsdatak.api import stream_publisher, TableFramesSpec, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.kafka import KafkaStreamSrc from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @stream_publisher( source=KafkaStreamSrc( topic="users", data_format="avro", schema=AVRO_SCHEMA, ), batch_max_secs=300, batch_max_rows=500, output_tables=["users"], ) def ingest(users: TableFramesSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return concat(users)

A stream worker reads the source continuously. What it reads is buffered in memory and written out to data files as the buffer fills. When a batch is due, the files written so far, and anything still in memory, are staged and handed to the Function as one batch. The Function runs once per batch and commits a new Version of each of its output Tables. The worker is long-lived and independent of the Function. It keeps reading while the previous batch is being processed, so a slow Function does not drop records. Batches are processed one at a time, in order, and if the Function takes longer than the batch interval, batches queue up and are processed in turn.
documents.s: How a batch becomes a run

documents.t: The batch_* parameters of @stream_publisher decide when a batch is due: batch_min_secs is the shortest time between two batches, and never less than 60 seconds. Once batch_min_secs have passed, a batch is due when batch_max_secs have passed, or when at least batch_max_rows rows or batch_max_bytes bytes are waiting. At least one of the three is required. With no data waiting, nothing runs, unless batch_idle_secs is set. Once batch_idle_secs have passed, the Function runs with an empty batch. Tabsdata looks for new batches about every 30 seconds, so a batch can start up to that long after it is due. See Batch parameters for the full rules and examples. The buffer settings in a source's src_cfg, such as tabsdata.kafka.buffer.max_rows, only decide when the worker writes what it has read to a file. They do not make a batch due.

Source System Output Tables KafkaStreamSrc Apache Kafka the Tables named in output_tables MySQLCdcStreamSrc MySQL one per tracked Table PostgresCdcStreamSrc PostgreSQL one per tracked Table Db2CdcStreamSrc IBM Db2 one per tracked Table All four are registered as stream sources, which tdk connection types shows in the Mode column as Stream Source. Like ordinary sources they belong to a sources Collection, and the address and credentials live on that Collection's Connection rather than on the source object. The CDC sources track a list of qualified Table names and resume from a stored position. Postgres additionally requires a logical replication slot, since the WAL it reads is retained on the server until the consumer confirms it. See Postgres CDC, MySQL CDC, Db2 CDC, and Kafka.

A @stream_publisher differs from the other decorators in three ways: It takes one TableFramesSpec parameter per source slot, always in array mode, because a batch is a list of frames rather than a single frame. It returns one TableFrame per output Table, the same as a Publisher. It must not declare a ctx parameter. It runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction, so there is no TrxCtx at the call boundary and declaring one fails registration. See Stream Publishers for the decorator's parameters and lifecycle.

A Table trigger runs a Function whenever one of the Tables it watches receives a new Version. This is what makes a pipeline cascade: a Publisher commits, the Transformers reading that Table run, they commit in turn, and the chain continues to the Subscribers at the end. Configure it with the trigger_by list on the decorator.

Omitted. Transformers and Subscribers fire on a commit to any of their input Tables. Publishers have no input Tables, so they get no automatic trigger at all and run manually or on a schedule. An empty list. trigger_by=[] disables automatic triggering. Use it when a Transformer or Subscriber should read its input Tables but not wake up when they change. A non-empty list. The Function watches exactly the Tables named and nothing else. This is how you trigger on a subset of the input Tables, or on a Table the Function does not read at all. @transformer( trigger_by=["sales", "inventory/stock"], input_tables=["sales"], output_tables=["sales_by_rep"], ) def summarize(sales: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return sales

Write a Table outside the Function's own Collection as collection/table, as inventory/stock does above. Unqualified names resolve inside the Function's own Collection. Cross-Collection references work only within a single Project. A reference that crosses Projects surfaces as Dependency table '<x>' does not exist, because the row is not visible rather than missing. A Table cannot trigger the Function that writes it.

Every run that returns data commits a new Version, whether or not the rows differ from the previous one. A Publisher writing three Tables commits all three on every run, so a Function watching any of them fires each time, even for the Tables whose contents were identical. Returning None from a slot also commits a new Version, one that keeps the Table's previous data, so downstream Functions watching that Table fire for it too. See None inputs and outputs.
documents.s: A commit is not the same as a change

documents.t: The Tabsdata User Interface (UI) is a web interface for inspecting and managing the resources within a Tabsdata Server. When running Tabsdata locally, the UI is available at http://localhost:2457, where 2457 is the Server's default public port. Sign in using the same username and password used with the tdk CLI. The UI demo provides a read-only Tabsdata Server with three Projects and existing execution history. Actions that create, modify, trigger, or delete resources are disabled. Explore the UI

The Overview page summarizes activity across every Project in the Server. For each Project, the page shows: Tables committed Rows committed Running Executions Warnings Errors Activity can be viewed across six time ranges.

The Projects page shows activity for the selected Project, including data that is currently in flight and data that has already been committed. The page also includes a graph of committed data over time. From the UI, you can: Create Projects Share Projects Switch the currently selected Project Most pages in the UI are scoped to the selected Project. Use the Project selector in the side panel to switch between Projects.

The Collections page lists the Collections within the selected Project. Opening a Collection shows its: Functions Tables Connection configuration Sensitive credentials stored in a Connection are hidden from the UI. From the UI, you can also: Create, edit, and delete Collections Grant a Collection access to Tables in another Collection Remove previously granted access

Opening a Function shows the code registered with Tabsdata and its version history. Function versions are retained so you can inspect previous versions, including the version used for a particular Function Run. From the UI, you can: Trigger a Function Delete a Function Editing a Function's code is performed using tdk rather than through the UI.

Opening a Table shows its schema, sample rows, and version history. Each Table version includes the Execution that wrote it, allowing changes in the Table to be traced back to the Execution that produced them. The Table page also includes Run SQL query, which lets you edit and run a SQL query against the Table's sample data. From the UI, you can also delete a Table.

The Executions page shows the Execution Plans created within the selected Project. Execution Plans are separated into: Active Issues Finished Opening an Execution Plan shows a graph of its execution flow and provides access to the Transactions, Function Runs, and Workers created as part of the Execution. Transactions, Function Runs, and Workers can each be filtered by status.

Opening a Worker provides access to the logs produced while it was running. Worker logs can be: Viewed in the UI Viewed in their raw form Downloaded When a Function Run fails, its Worker logs contain the output and errors produced during execution.

The Executions area also shows the triggers configured for the Project, including: Cron Triggers Stream Sources This lets you inspect both what causes Functions to run and the Execution Plans created when they run.
The Search page searches for resources across the Tabsdata Server. Use Search to locate a resource without navigating through its Project and Collection.

Tabby is the built-in Tabsdata agent for interacting with and inspecting a Tabsdata Server. See Tabby for setup, commands, and an example chat. Tabby requires an Anthropic or OpenAI API key to be configured on the Server. From Tabby, you can: Start a new chat Continue existing chats Stop a response while it is being generated Search previous messages Export a chat as Markdown Use page-specific suggested prompts Run a Server health check Suggested prompts depend on the page you are viewing. For example, a Collection page may include prompts for listing Functions or creating a Publisher. The Run health check action generates an AI-written report about the current health of the Server.

The Security page manages users, roles, and permissions for the Tabsdata Server. From the UI, you can: Create, edit, and delete users Create and delete roles Add users to roles Remove users from roles Grant permissions Remove permissions
The System page shows the status and runtime information for the Tabsdata Server.

The Account page shows information about the currently signed-in user. From the UI, you can also: Change your password Log out Switch between light and dark themes Pin resources to the side panel Clear pinned resources The Server's SSL certificate can also be downloaded from the login page.
